In the end, Denis Villeneuve was all too right: Your television isn’t big enough for the scope of his “Dune,” but that’s only because this lifeless spice opera is told on such a comically massive scale that a screen of any size would struggle to contain it. Likewise, no story — let alone the misshapen first half of one — could ever hope to support the enormity of what Villeneuve tries to build over the course of these interminable 155 minutes (someone mentions that time is measured differently on Arrakis), or the sheer weight of the self-serious portent that he pounds into every shot. For all of Villeneuve’s awe-inducing vision, he loses sight of why Frank Herbert’s foundational sci-fi opus is worthy of this epic spectacle in the first place. Such are the pitfalls of making a movie so large that not even its director can see around the sets. How big is “Dune”? We’re talkin’ slabs upon slabs of angular concrete as far as the eye can see, spaceships that seem to displace entire oceans when they emerge from the seabeds of Caladan, and sandworms so large they could eat the Graboids from “Tremors” like bar nuts. Even yoked kings Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista look like tabletop miniatures when placed against its backdrops, as if cinematographer Greig Fraser discovered a way to shoot deep focus and tilt-shift at the same time. So why, for all of its unparalleled immensity, does watching “Dune” amount to the cinematic equivalent of being handed a novelty-sized check made out for six dollars? Why is the scope of Villeneuve’s dream betrayed by the dull shallowness of its reality to the point that his film’s most astounding effects — which are every bit as tactile and transportive as those in “Blade Runner 2049” — feel more like optical illusions? Why does this “Dune” feel so small? ~this review continues on IndieWire~

The biggest problem, though, is Hans Zimmer, whose score is incredibly loud and unremittingly the dominant sound for more of the movie’s 155 minutes than not. Zimmer’s approach to musical cultural appropriation has been blithe since at least 1994’s The Lion King , while his subsequent rise to Coachella fame has accelerated improbably. Both worlds collide in Dune ’s score, a nightmare barrage of field-filling drums punctuated by the odd muezzin-ish call to prayer—given how fraught the material already is (brown-skinned desert peoples vs. The Man), the Orientalist tinting is poorly thought through. Every time I went to the multiplex in summer 2016, I’d walk past an auditorium booming the thunderous punching-sounds foleys and Zimmer’s score from Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice , and it never failed to make my life a little more unpleasant. Five years later, the most cogent thought I emerged from Dune with was, “Hans Zimmer must be stopped .” More here .

Longer review/ramblings coming very soon. ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Dune may, in the end, prove to be unfilmable after all. Frank Herbert’s vision was one of such an epic scope that it just doesn’t seem to find a right fit in the cinematic medium. Villeneuve however tries his very, very best to fit it in there no matter what. He creates a universe so grand that it barely fits the cinema screen. One scene with unimaginably big spaceships gets put to shame by the next scene with even bigger spaceships. Spaceships the size of planets move about the universe to carry this epic story and yet, for all that stupendous spectacle, Dune feels painfully hollow. Villeneuve wants to take his sweet time to ease us into this complex saga and does so formidably at certain points, but he also gets caught up in the uncontrollable scale of it all to such a degree that the human factor almost crumbles under the weight of the story’s grandeur. The all-star cast is scrambled through the film like a joke, with some actors popping up for only a few minutes to deliver a faint impression of what their character wants and needs. Chalamet’s Paul Atreides serves perhaps the only worthwhile character arc that has some weight to it while most of the people swarming around him leave a faint impression at best. Their frail, human existence simply cannot live up to the immensity of Arrakis or the universe at large. Villeneuve lost his grasp when trying to combine the epic with the intimate and only got a little bit of both without realizing how to combine the two and make them add up to each other. And still, as much as this film is overshadowed by its epic nature, those moments are in hindsight, as flat as all the rest of it. Spectacular, grand imagery with nothing to say other than: “This is big. This is huge!” The Villeneuve-fanbase has clearly already deemed this a masterpiece despite having had zero chance to see this with a critical eye but I could bet on my life that what will stay with them about this won’t be the story but simply the visual spectacle. And Dune is so much more than that. It’s a human spectacle that happens to play on a massive scale but even with Villeneuve’s plan to split this in two to give everything its supposed bit of gravitas, Dune (part one) falls painfully short. At best it’s an oversized prologue, filled with exposition both in its dialogue and in its imagery to prepare you for the (hopefully) more in-depth approach of the second part.

With Dune , Denis Villeneuve invites us to enter a world we know nothing of and from the score and cast to the special effects and photography, everything leads us to believe in his gigantic movie. So how can such an ambitious project feels so shallow? Well, at some point, I found myself wondering what was happening. Spoiler: nothing really happens. It is just a 155 minute trailer of the second chapter. Impressive CGI aren’t enough for Dune to measure up Villeneuve’s ambitions. There’s not a single character that’s developed or just a little bit complex. We don’t know who they are, where they come from or what they really want. Scenes follow each other in the most illogical way which leads us in the wrong direction. For instance, Paul’s dreams seem to be a big deal and yet, the girl he keeps fantasizing about brings absolutely nothing to the narrative. Dune is like the promise our parents made us that Santa Claus exists. We all know how it ends: everything’s fake and there’s no magic. It’s a bad dream we’re trying to forget.

First of all, disregard all the five-star reviews, there's no way even for the biggest Dune or Villeneuve fan to seriously think this movie is a masterpiece other than to hype up their fellow fans ahead of the release (a commendable action that makes for a nevertheless dishonest rating) Talking about the movie: there's no way around it, it's pretty bland and forgettable. Almost all of its problems come from its meandering pacing—full of useless things while glossing over a lot of important and/or interesting ones that would have improved the movie—which I think comes from Villeneuve's desire to faithfully adapt the parts of the novel he likes the most clashing with its cinematic potential as a whole: e.g. we don't even see House Atreides space-travelling to Arrakis, although the movie tells us right at the beginning that the reason because the Spice—the very thing Dune revolves around—is "the most precious substance in the universe" is precisely that's so essential to space travel. Worry not, however, because we get to see instead Jessica choosing her housemaids in Arrakeen 😎😎😎 (This is to introduce the Shadout Mapes, a character from the novel which in this movie serves no purpose whatsoever other than being… a character from the novel, and makes her only other ten-second appearance later and dies) And so on, and so on... I have to say however that the faithfulness also makes for a good thing: in the 1984 adaptation, the part in the desert after Paul and Jessica escape was greatly reduced, becoming boring and uneventful, while here is not only more fleshed out, but it is straight up the best and most enjoyable section of the movie, with the flying chase scenes being almost Mad-Maxian (*high* praise right here!). It alone makes you almost wish for a sequel Black marks: Hans Zimmer's score is AWFUL and annoying to the point of effectively distracting you from what's happening on screen at times (which wasn't already that captivating on its own), the fight scenes are somehow even clumsier than the old ones, and—well—that's it: as I said before, it's just really mediocre.

This was, undeniably, epic. But not in the way Herbert probably intended. Villeneuve's Dune is told from a whole other perspective than the book. It stems from a mind craving action-packed sequences and technical grandeur, a mind keen to please a public eye trained by the likes of the MCU. Attempting to amalgamate that mindset with Herbert's text, which makes a point of avoiding wordy descriptions of fights and focusing instead on the power play and the political machinations, is all but doomed to fail. Villeneuve expands upon technicalities that Herbert skipped and instead either leaves out or dumbs down the complex net of suspicion, betrayal, loyalty, and plotting that Herbert so delicately weaved throughout his book. The result is a huge cast of characters with little to no believable intention and charm, a set of beautiful cardboard people if you will, riding fleets of various intricately designed huge vehicles and looking over incredibly vast and glorious landscapes. A feast for the eyes, but hardly more than that. It may well be that Dune is unadaptable for the big screen, probably even the small screen. So much of this book's story goes on solely in the minds of the characters and hardly ever has anything on a screen of any size managed to deal with the proper communication of an abundance of thoughts. However, when faced with that obstacle, Villeneuve does not try his hand at rising above it. He runs the other way, shifting the storyline's focus instead to the action sequences and the machinery. His film, therefore, works more as a mere visual companion to the book rather than an adaptation.

Dune wäre der richtige Stoff für das nächste “Game of Thrones”, denn was haben wir am Ende des Tages? Einen Prolog, der uns in die Welt einführt und genau da aufhört, wo es spannend wird. Bei einem 60 Minuten Pilotfilm kann man das machen, bei einem 155 Minuten Film nicht. I’m Gegensatz zu “Herr der Ringe: Die Gefährden” hat man hier da aufgehört, wo Frodo sein Dorf verlässt. Denis Villeneuve gibt uns Hoffnung auf etwas, dass es vielleicht niemals geben wird. Ansonsten matte, ausgewaschene Farben, und einem dröhnenden recycelten Zimmer Score, der jede einzelne Einstellung epochal wirken lässt, wenn Zeitlupe noch wäre, könnte man es glatt mit Snyder verwechseln. Auch ist die Gefahr der Harkonnens nie wirklich greifbar, es wird viel über ihre Grausamkeiten geredet, gezeigt leider wenig. Dennoch ist der Stoff genau für die große Leinwand gemacht, die Bildsprache ist Kinoreif auch die Darsteller trumpfen excellent auf. Nur verliert der Film oft das Pacing und zieht sich im Laufe der Zeit, jedoch ohne dabei langweilig zu werden. Dennoch ist der Film am Ende der Tages, nicht der erhoffte Durchbruch, sondern lässt einen mit der Frage zurück, was ist, wenn hier Schluss ist? Der Film kann leider nicht für sich alleine stehen, ohne das Buch zu kennen, geht hier nicht, wenn man wirklich den Inhalt verstehen will und sich nicht nur berieseln lassen will. Danke Herr Ober, aber ich hätte doch gerne das ganze 5 Gänge Menu und nicht nur die Suppe und die Vorspeise.

Frank Herbertin klassiseen tieteisromaaniin perustuva Dyyni on ehkäpä vuoden odotetuin elokuva. David Lynchin vuoden 1984 filmatisointi karahti kiville, mutta Denis Villeneuven projekti on hallitumpi kokonaisuus. Villeneuve on jo osoittanut kykynsä tehdä älyllistä suuren luokan scifiä (Arrival, Blade Runner 2049). Tällä kertaa lopputulos on kuitenkin ristiriitainen. Dyyni näyttää kaikin puolen sykähdyttävän upealta, ja siinä on vaikuttavia kohtauksia. Elokuvassa on liikaa tyhjäkäyntiä, joka ei vie tarinaa eteenpäin. Timothée Chalametin esittämä päähenkilö jää etäiseksi, eikä elokuva muutenkaan aiheuta värinöitä. Läskipukuun pukeutuneen Stellan Skarsgårdin pahishahmo on tahattoman koominen muuten kuolemanvakavassa elokuvassa. Mittakaava on eeppinen, mutta resurssit ovat menneet osittain hukkaan, kun monissa kohtauksissa vain pönötetään pimeissä sisätiloissa ja höpötellään joutavia.

Now that the DUNE discourse has begun I can say that I saw it in July. I've been released from the NDA I signed (like I was joining The Weinstein Company) and now that reviews have flowed like canal water from Venice…I liked it. It’s good, but unlike a largely self-contained LORD OF THE RINGS installment, say, this ends on a cliffhanger (not if you’ve read the book or seen a prior version, that is) so it can’t really be evaluated in its totality. (A number of things that are mentioned in passing, like the Emperor and the Spacing Guild Navigators, go unseen; a number of actors, like Javier Bardem and Zendaya, who's all over the trailer and whose voiceover kicks off the film, have only brief roles in this part.) Apparently the money and the cast are in place if this hits but, well, it's DUNE, exhaustingly dense and humorless other than for Jason Momoa's swagger, so a leap of faith and fan demand may be required. How things change: in 1984 I was given a glossary of terms before entering the theater, in 2021 I was handed earplugs, as it was “very loud.” (It is, starting with Hans Zimmer’s Middle East/GLADIATOR score, which plays and plays; I toughed it out and didn’t wear them.) And while David Lynch’s adaptation was very wet with boils and blobs and pustules this is very dry, with Stellan Skarsgard as a baron who’s more APOCALYPSE NOW (and later) Marlon Brando and muted greens and sandpaper colors, except for Paul’s acid-washed dreams. Timothée Chalamet is fine in the part, and the rest of the cast finds both dimensions in their two-dimensional characters, with Momoa, an unexpected Stephen McKinley Henderson, Chang Cheh, and Sharon Duncan-Brewster in roles filled in the past by white actors. And, yes, definitely worth leaving the house and HBO Max for, in favor of an IMAX presentation in your vicinity. (I rewatched this on HBO MAX with my family on Nov. 6. I found I liked it more; for one thing I could adjust the volume and hear more of the dialogue. I was almost amused to discover, amidst the thousands of end credits, one for Marianne Faithfull as a "background Bene Dessert vocalist" and of course she was.)

The way Dune treats its characters of color + women + Deaf culture is pretty annoying to watch, and throughout its 2 and a half hour runtime, no two women share a single bit of dialogue that isn't about a man. But if you can compartmentalize, it's an exciting theater experience. (And if you're opting for a small screen, like a laptop, it might not even be worth your time. The writing doesn't carry the film very far, beyond meandering for long stretches of lore. Instead, visuals and musical score make up the lion's share of Dune 's enjoyability.)

If there's one constant to be found in Villeneuve's movies, it's that they all look gorgeous. The cinematography was just incredible with some beautiful shot compositions that you won't find back in any other movie of this scale. Villeneuve is the one director that manages to make an epic arthouse movie. Perhaps Nolan's Dunkirk also fits to this rare form of cinema. That being said, the story was underwhelming. There's a lot of exposition that could have been handled more subtle, but that's only the tip of the iceberg. Chalamet's character is simply uncompelling. There's nothing that really drives him, except for the dreams/visions he's trying to make sense of. His desire remains bland which make the stakes feel insignificant as it's not clear whether the obstacles he faces really stop him from reaching his goal. As it turns out, this is only Part One, which could make you think that Villeneuve and Roth would have taken more time to explore the main character in a meaningful way. Unfortunately, instead the focus remained too much on the world building. A shame, because I cannot stress enough how gorgeous this movie looked, same doe the sound design and mixing. Overall, I would recommend the movie.

在近乎一張白紙，只對故事有著基礎概略的情況下進場，完全不用擔心會有不懂的情節，維勒納夫用了細水長流般的節奏鋪墊人物、地點、衝突，完全可以理解。他勾勒的厄拉克斯星球在夕陽下美極了，儘管不是看IMAX，坐在放著冷氣的影廳，卻隱約感受到荒漠上的熱浪，《沙丘》也不是有著強烈聲光效果的浩瀚爽片，像《銀翼殺手2049》在前半段緩緩講著故事，後半段用他獨有的視覺美學拍出幾場磅礡的爆破。 最佳，喔不對，唯一打開這部電影的方式，是在黑盒子，用小螢幕會完完全全體會不出電影是多麼地用心，電影院就是為了這種電影而生的，每一幀都是如此，無論你多麼期待《沙丘》，或許都不夠，我坦承對於這部電影已經賦予高度的期待，正片依然比我想像中更好。 我不太喜歡用其他的電影系列（ex魔戒、星戰）來比擬這部電影未來會是怎麼樣的發展，但身為承接接下來故事的《沙丘》，它非常紮實的打好第一步，維勒納夫的野心不過於放縱，他極有自知之明知道第一部講述的是保羅亞崔迪所要承擔的一切，他也做到了，電影收在不會過於吊胃口，也不會過於不知所措的地方。 《沙丘：第一章》，正結束，但這個故事，也正要開啟。 長文預計二刷貼上來，到時講講技術面和演員表現，週六要在美麗華IMAX看，還要等好久，好痛苦。預計三刷（或以上）。

This new incarnation of Spice World is essentially Game of Thrones in space, and threatens at every other moment to collapse under the considerable weight of its own self importance. There are impressive vistas to behold, sure, but the storytelling is leaden, and the overly heavy usage of slow motion certainly does not help alleviate the sluggish pace. Neither does Hans Zimmer's ethno-screechy soundtrack attempts at moving things along, by mostly amping up the volume and wailing to give an illusion of intensity. That said, Denis Villenueve's ultraformalist style of filmmaking is never without surface level riches - his movies look (and mostly) and sound impressive, and so it is with this adaptation of the first half of the Dune novel too. But beyond that this had little to offer me. At 2.5 hours you really need to provide more substance than this, but it doesn't, and I was mostly bored and unengaged for the duration of it. A final, technical note: I saw this in IMAX, and the constant aspect ratio changes drove me nuts. Filmmakers, if you're going to shoot in IMAX format, fucking *commit* to it! This half-hearted stuff with every other scene in a different format is pointless and annoying. If you're going to use different aspect ratios in your movie, at least have it tied to the narrative!

Три звезды — это потолок, который я могу поставить «Дюне», ведь, извините, какую оценку стоит поставить фильму, являющийся, по сути, пилотом сериала? И не факт, что продолжение вообще будет. Вильнёв в одном интервью сказал про первую часть «Дюны» следующее, цитирую: «это что-то вроде закуски. А продолжение — основное блюдо, куда мы сможем добавить ещё больше». Вильнёв говорил много раз, что будет идти строго по книге и даже на первый роман ему понадобится два полнометражных фильма. «Дюна» плохо работает как кино. Это завязка на два с половиной часа к истории, что случится когда-то потом, в других фильмах, которые ещё никто не начинал снимать. И «завязка» в данном случае — не какая-то красивая фигура речи. Фильм действительно сценарно выстроен так, будто это не эпический двухсотмиллионный блокбастер, а пилот сериала. Взять, к примеру, «Властелин колец». Первая часть тоже была, по сути, завязкой, но там была драматургия! У Вильнёва в предыдущих фильмах тоже! Я склоняюсь к тому, что «Дюна» вообще не экранизируемая. Хорошо это или плохо? Черт его знает... Хотя чего у фильма не отнять, так это его аудио и визуальную составляющую. В IMAX смотрелось все просто великолепно. Лично я дома бы не выседил, так что смотреть только в кино и только там!

I almost gave this a 2.5 rating but I couldn’t bring myself to do it. All that excitement I had for the movie after reading the book….I just couldn’t believe that I’m this disappointed in it. So idk, gave it 3 stars in hopes I’ll grow to truly feel like it deserves 3 stars.

Yes it's very pretty in the currently popular washed-out grey muddy kind of way. Villeneuve lovingly frames all the brutalist architecture and rippling sand dunes, and the cast do their best to breathe some life into it. There are some cool fight scenes too. But OMG it's long, and it only covers half the story. The first half is relatively brisk, but the last 30-40 minutes really drag. Lynch 's version was far from perfect but it managed to hit all the main plot points while also being stylish and weird. Also, for all the talk of colonial oppressors and the promise of a story updated to reflect modern sensibilities, the racially diverse Fremen are still very willing to accept a pale young man as their saviour. The Bene Gesserit politicking which forms the backbone of the story remains undeveloped so that we can spend more time on slo-mo shots of Chalamet looking pretty and angsty in the desert. Let's hope the pace picks up and some depth is added in part 2.

Somehow I didn’t know it was part 1/2. Not mad tough, I appreciate the will to take the time to tell such a story. I’ll start by saying that Dune makes you see , it does not make you feel . It is relevant in the context of the film as Herbert describes a time where men have become more computing machines than human (Mentats, Bene Gesserit…). This aloofness with the characters, especially with Paul (who is a combination of both groups) makes it hard to care for their journey and ordeals. It doesn’t help that the dialogues are inexistent or a mere tool to dump exposition. Overall Villeneuve and his team had an impossible task and they did a lot a judicious choices (the photography is amazing, the costumes look great, it’s rather faithful to the book etc.). Still it’s a high budget studio film, with (not so convincing) A-listers and not a transcendental gospel nor, for all that matter an exciting SF flick.

Si on est face à un œuvre visuellement magnifique visant la perfection, avec un réel travail de vulgarisation du lore créé de Herbert, les personnages sonnent assez creux et étirent une histoire déjà bien à rallonge.

Dune , one of the most anticipated films of this year. Partly because of Frank Herbert's influential book it is based on, partly because this may finally be the adaptation everyone's been waiting for after the first attempt . Although I think Villeneuve's version surpasses its predecessor, I can't help but feel a sort of emptiness after watching it, where I hoped it would be awe-inspiring and linger in my mind days afterwards. There are several things at work that contribute to the best and worst of this sci-fi epic, which is only the first half of Herbert's first book. This choice helps to give the story more time to develop over the course of its two-and-a-half hours, but also stretches the events out to a point where it loses its pace. The moment in the story where Part I finds its conclusion is logical, but happens quite sometime after its peak, wherefore the last half hour or so feels too much as an outstretched epilogue. About the casting choices: As much as all the actors seem to be born for their role – they all perfectly fit the description; in this film and according to the book – I couldn't help but see them apart from their other roles. That's the danger with such an all-famous cast as this. Whenever Gurney (Josh Brolin) spoke, I heard Marvel's Thanos. When Leto (Oscar Isaac) talked about wanting to be a pilot, I thought about Poe Dameron from Star Wars. Only Dave Bautista and Rebecca Ferguson seemed to accomplish totally transforming themselves in their role. That actually brings me to another point: How much this doesn't feel like a whole new world with its own rules and vibe; something that Herbert's book certainly is. Somehow, it feels too earthy. Instead of taking me to a galaxy far, far away, the oriental vibe only brought me to another place on Earth. The various space ships, costumes and interiors (wonderfully designed; I'm not gonna lie about that) seem to be the only things reminding me this is science-fiction. In any case, it needed a little more mystique, something that's only really accomplished in the 'fear-scene' where Charlotte Rampling asks Timothée Chalamet to put his hand in the box, and the famous words "Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little death that brings total obliteration" first get spoken. I admire Denis Villeneuve for being able to get such a vast and complex story off the ground, and, despite my critique, I really enjoyed it. There are multiple moments that got me really excited. But, I keep thinking about how much more creative, mystique and off-worldly this could be. Lynch's version may not be a success, but it has all of this what Villeneuve's hasn't, and is therefore closer to my heart. Of course, this is a new vision that shouldn't be blindly compared to the other, but considering the hype and Villeneuve's reputation, it's a bit of a letdown. Ranked: Denis Villeneuve - 2021 Crossed off: Hyped 2021

Το «Dune» του Ντενί Βιλνέβ, βασισμένο σε έναν φανταστικό κόσμο του μέλλοντος, όπου ισχυροί οίκοι οικογενειών εξουσιάζουν ολόκληρους πλανήτες ενώ το πιο πολύτιμο υλικό που υπάρχει είναι ένα πανάκριβο μπαχαρικό που επιτρέπει την διαπλανητική μετακίνηση, είναι πλέον εδώ: γυαλιστερό, πιστό στο πρωτότυπο υλικό, γεμάτο τάσεις μεγαλείου και μια αυθεντική αγάπη για όλα όσα αγκαλιάζει αυτό το σύμπαν, σε μια ευλαβική σχεδόν προσέγγιση. Αλλωστε ο Βιλνέβ είχε ήδη αποδείξει τις ικανότητες του και στην εικονογραφία της επιστημονικής φαντασίας («Αφιξη», «Blade Runner 2049») αλλά και στο χτίσιμο μελλοντολογικών, πολύχρωμων ή μη, κόσμων. Η ματιά του ήταν ανέκαθεν επική, η αφήγησή του πάντα έβρισκε τον άνθρωπο ανάμεσα σε όλα τα τεχνολογικά επιτεύγματα και τα κάδρα του μόνιμα αρέσκονταν στο να ανακαλύπτουν νέους τρόπους να δει κανείς τον κόσμο. Στο «Dune» ο Βιλνέβ επιμένει στα δυνατά του στοιχεία, ρίχνει φως στις ερήμους του Αράκις και τα παλάτια των Ατρειδών, βουτάει στο σκοτάδι των Χαρκόνεν και τα οράματα του Πολ με την μυστηριώδη Τσάνι που υπόσχεται μια ακόμα πιο μεσσιανική συνέχεια και παρουσιάζει κάθε χαρακτήρα με στόμφο και βαρύτητα, χορογραφώντας τις κινήσεις τους με αυστηρότητα και ντύνοντας τα λόγια τους με υφέρπουσα τραγικότητα, κλείνοντας το μάτι στην αρχαία ελληνική τραγωδία που έτσι κι αλλιώς επηρέασε (όχι μόνο λόγω «Ατρειδών») το έργο του Χέρμπερτ. Το μόνο που θα μπορούσε κανείς να προσάψει στον Βιλνέβ είναι το γεγονός ότι δεν τολμάει να ρισκάρει ή να προχωρήσει σε αιρετικές επιλογές, τουλάχιστον προς το παρόν. Από την άλλη όμως, ακριβώς αυτό είναι και το δυνατότερο σημείο της ταινίας: ένα «Dune» φτιαγμένο για τους οπαδούς του «Dune» και ένα δώρο σε όλους τους φαν που εδώ και δεκαετίες ανέμεναν μια εντυπωσιακή και επική κινηματογραφική μεταφορά αυτού του κόσμου. Και όπως λέει η Τσάνι της Ζεντάγια «Αυτό είναι μόνο η αρχή.» Πληρης κριτική της ταινίας από το 78ο Φεστιβάλ Κινηματογράφου της Βενετίας, στο Flix.

Venezia 78 #1 Dopo anni di spasmodica attesa, un posticipo doloroso ed una distribuzione controversa, Dune di Denis Villeneuve comincia a mostrarsi al pubblico e alla critica, suscitando reazioni più miste di quanto auspicabile. Vedo di iniziare con uno spirito più positivo per non dare idee sbagliate su ciò che effettivamente penso del film : è un’opera mastodontica, che spinge i limiti di ciò che può essere messo in scena in un contesto fantascientifico, che suscita un sense of wonder tolkeniano anche nei suoi momenti più bui e tenebrosi, introduce concetti accattivanti e stimolanti, utili a ribaltare la superficie già vista e già conosciuta dei ruoli e dei percorsi dei vari personaggi, portati in vita da performance sublimi e stratificate, anche se alcune sono più sprecate di altre. Però non posso fare a meno di chiedermi il perché di alcune decisioni editoriali di scioccante ingenuità da parte del regista e dello studio, che lasciano il film fondamentalmente incompleto, un eccitante inizio di un percorso che si rischia di non vedere mai. E questo inizio è davvero immenso, travolgente e a tratti inebriante nella sua immersività scenica e nella sua mitologia pregna di politica, filosofia, spiritualità e misticismi vari, ma commette il peccato originale di qualsiasi blockbuster, ovvero quello del non reggersi interamente sulle sue spalle e sprecare il suo terzo atto in promesse che rischia di non poter mantenere… 2 anni e mezzo dopo, un rewatch in sala e a due settimane dalla Parte Due, mi sento solo di chiedere umilmente scusa a Denis. Monumentale inizio, non vedo l’ora di vedere la monumentale conclusione.

Nothing can prepare you for the grand-scale epic Denis Villeneuve has in store with this instant science fiction classic, and perhaps the best first entry in a franchise since ‘The Fellowship of the Ring’ and ‘The Matrix’. Although interpreting well-known themes of environmentalism, totalitarianism and religion, that have been seen explored hundreds of times on screen since the release of Frank Herbert’s influential novel, everything feels new through the masterful lens of Villeneuve (working for the first time with great DoP Greg Fraser). The story succeeds where ‘Blade Runner 2049’ failed, simply because it is allowed time to develop organically and be fully fleshed out. Sure, there is exposition, but all information is to the point. Villeneuve focuses on spacecrafts in motion, the specificities of the different planets and the movements and bodies of the main characters, all of which seem fully formed from the get go. The result is a riveting spectacle unmatched by current Hollywood filmmaking. The worldbuilding is extraordinary, rivaling ‘Game of Thrones’ when it was still at its best. Villeneuve’s mastery is apparent from the decision to focus more on the complex power plays at hand, rather than indulge in unnecessary set pieces. This makes it all the more effecting once everything goes to shit, with some of Villeneuve’s best suspense scenes since ‘Sicario’. Timothée Chalamet is great in the lead, but Oscar Isaac really blew my mind with his deepfelt performance. From this to ‘The Card Counter’, he has solidified his position as one of the most interesting actors working right now. Please go see this on the biggest screen possible (Also Zimmer's pitchperfect score demands the loudest speakers possible). This is the kind of film that brings hope to blockbuster filmmaking. And sadly, it is not automatically guaranteed high gross and renewal like other blockbusters of this day and age (I am looking at you ‘Fast and the Furious’). Yes, I am hyped. Welcome aboard.

Samuel L. Jackson tells a story about seeing "Star Wars" for the first time on opening weekend in 1977. Everyone in the theater was smoking weed, he told "60 Minutes" a couple of years ago, and when the opening titles exploded onto the screen, it blew him back into his seat. He had never seen anything like what George Lucas had created. I saw "Dune" at a press screening in August. No one was smoking weed, everyone wore masks. But when the Hans Zimmer score boomed out of the speakers, I understood what Jackson felt. I had never read "Dune," never even seen the movies. My knowledge of the property was limited to Wikipedia, preview articles, and just general cultural osmosis. But none of that mattered: the movie enveloped me in a way no other Denis Villeneuve work has done prior. I experienced "Dune" inside the recesses of my mind, lost in the wicked sound design and bespoke production. This movie absolutely rules, building to a near anti-climax that basically dares a multi-billion dollar corporation to not make its second part. As much as I want to see how it turns out -- and see how Denis tries to pay off that truly deranged Wiki summary of the book -- I almost hope a sequel doesn't happen. "Dune" deserves to stand as this singular cinematic exhibition. I think Sam Jackson should check it out.

Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

I watched this movie right when it came out because I’m friends with this nerd who loves Dune. He’s read the books and everything, the books actually lose the plot after like the 3rd one according to him. For example the grandson of Paul (who is the main character further down the line) is actually just one of those sand worms, no human part he’s a sand worm and somehow that works I suppose. Anyways why did I give this a 2? Well there’s a few reasons. First I should mention I slammed 2 Four Lokos during the runtime of this movie, which got me pretty loko ngl. In fact I blacked out at some point during the film and spawned back in at the final fight. But before that happened I felt the movie was too slow and convoluted. My very informed opinion was backed up because my friend said the books do a much better job of explaining what’s going on and it’s hard to explain it visually which is what the movie has to do. Also he had to explain the movie to everyone we watched it with (they did not have Four Lokos, they were sober) because even they had no idea what was going on, and there were a bunch of unexplained scenes that you can only understand if you read the book. For example they’ll flash a scene with Anya Taylor Joy and you’re gonna be like wtf, but since we had a guide he told us that’s his sister and his moms race can see shit or something? Idk, I don’t remember but I think you get the point. Luckily he was our guide. You need to watch this movie with a guide or you’re just gonna be watching people hanging out in the sand. However I do not think this movie is bad, it’s well made. Very visually interesting despite the fact that it’s just sand, and the characters are interesting, the mystery is interesting. It’s also not poorly paced, it just felt slow for my taste. What brings it down to a 2 is that you basically either have to read the books or watch a YouTube video to understand what’s going on and in my opinion that is a film that doesn’t do its job well. If you can’t understand the story from watching the movie then it failed. I believe it has failed a bit as a film, but it’s quality saves it hence the slightly below average rating. TLDR: Watch it off of 2 Four Lokos because you’re not gonna understand what’s going on anyways.

Dune annoyed me during this viewing, and it falls off each time I watch it. Let's call this the " Endgame paradigm", and blame my excising liberalism. I'd like to make three points, or point out three categories which I see as quite deficient. Firstly: Fremen Denis elects for a blankly Afro-Asiatic look for the Fremen, making them a simultaneously sub-Saharan, Middle-eastern, and North African people. Nevermind that they have been an isolated population with nye-on zero outside inter-mingling possible. He also chooses to include death wailing in the grieving of Jamis. This genero-ethnic mix betrays the desire to vaguely represent all of the (virtuous) third world in the Fremen, and to marry this minted people with Islam. It berays the portrayal into a more favourable framing than that of Frank Herbert, and complicates the story with a more cosmopolitan, pluralist appearance than was given them by their creator. Denis wants the residents of Arrakis to be somewhat blameless in their behaviour and sympathetic in their desires, even if they are implied to be stupid by following Paul. Yes, this is a backwards culture, but it is one that Denis seems to simultaneously revere and chide. This is a problem for many modern liberals, who would love to totally embrace Islam and Islamists, but can’t quite get over their pesky superstition. Attila and the witch doctor. Second: Method As has become an assumption of modern production, handheld, mid-close shots with a shallow depth-of-field obfuscate the production elements in the background. The reflecting pool with Stilgar and Jessica is a good example. What is the point of all of the beautiful and very detailed work of set production if we cannot see it? This method also subverts the style of the sci-fi/warfare epic we know - work of the likes of David Lean - which is a fine stylistic choice in a vacuum, surely, but aggravating when it seems to genuinely lessen the feature. Where are our grand wide shots in 65mm? They disappeared by taste, and have not returned because of our self-importance and our view of method as a continuum from which we would be foolish to get off. As a result, I dislike much of how the film was shot. Opening with such a stylized eclipse scene does the rest of the film no favours. "Realism" apparently means no lighting or blocking work in most shots. That might also have something to do with the fact that most shots are CG, or contain CG composites. The very effective scenes (like hunting Harkonnen in the sandstorm ) make you wonder how much more effective they might have been with better lighting. And there are tons of lens flares here like would get Zach Snyder made fun of, but I have heard nothing of them. So I don't think I like Greig Fraser. Third: Meaning The movie thematically leans deeper into the commentary and critique of the novel, and does so inelegantly. With every modern auteur who claims themselves a "realist" whose joy it is to approximate reality, there is this kind of inelegance and incoherency which pervades their films. (For example: in fidelity to the faith, all Hollywood productions are now pluralist and cosmopolitan after the manner of the creators' experience walking down the street, regardless of their diegetic setting.) Despite Frank Herbert’s principal antagonist in this analogy, Dune the Movie's religious critique is more directed at Christianity than it is Islam. The local religion of the Arrakeans (more analogous of Islam, and more sympathetic) is subservient to the misanthropic political calculation of the Bene Gesserit, who themselves firmly believe in a messiah figure, but one of their own making; they believe that they can conjure his coming. Ultimately, his arrival is so great and terrible as none of them could have foreseen, and though the religious leaders are put off of his upending and (yet) fulfilling their prophecy, they are eventually powerless to do anything about the rise of the faith of Lisan al Ga'ib, or of the number of his adherents. We the audience are given an anachronism in Chani and the disbelieving secularists for our point-of-view character, and Denis ensures that they make all the right assertions. Excepting, of course, that assertive question or two which could cause Paul pause... From whence are these dreams coming? Obviously, the story parallels better with the advent of Christ to the upheaval of the Jewish legalists and fulfillment of their prophecy, and so this portion of the film plays a bit like historical fan fiction, wherein the atheist of today gets to go back and ask his brilliant and cutting questions of Jesus of Nazareth. He, of course, can see right through the religious deception. From all of this modernist compulsion to the "realism" of our day, and a compunction against representing women, minorities, or, indeed, rational (unreligious) people badly (or at least, without excusing them by trauma or manipulation from their bad behaviour), the film's immersion strains. The anachronism of a complete lack of belief from Chani and the secularists is one of the first inflection points. (The secular Fremen are a somewhat large and vocal number in the film, enough to make the distinction of the "southern fundamentalists" a relevant one, even if not subtle.) Chani will talk both in the novel and these movies as a believer of something. Across the mediums, one can hear her - say that Shai-hulud is sacred, especially in his role in the production of spice, - assert that water and the burial rites are important in a spiritual, and not just practical sense, - say that spice is her people's birthright, and - talk of her son, and of her husband's prodigious sister providentially (as though some force brought each to them). Chani's assassination in this film (a wholly different character than the novel, and self-contradictory in the movies themselves) happens to bring her from adapted character, to one with the same thoroughly modern opinion of religion as the writers. Imagine that. And so, with this self-portrait of Denis, we are left to conclude that more than an audience-insert with whom we are meant to sympathize (and by whom we transpose ourselves into the story), Chani is intended as a theme and message delivering bullhorn -- a manner by which the writers might tell you what the story is about. Which is how we get lines like, "You wanna control people? You tell them a messiah will come, then they wait for centuries." More than just a thematic narrator, she is the writer’s holy self-insert, for where Paul is in agreement with Chani, deriving his understanding of the world through her, he is in the right. Only when he begins to reject her framing, making use of his power and of the religious fervour of the Fremen, does he begin to be wrong. "What your people did to this world is heartbreaking." - "We gave them something to hope for." - "That's not hope!" contrasted with “I am pointing the way! (…) God be my witness: I am the Lisan al-Gaib. I will lead you to paradise!” In Denis’ movie, a character's proximity to the masculine political tendencies (exercising direct authority, reacting aggressively when faced with hostility, viewing war as a political solution, et al.), and, more crucially, their proximity to the religious determines their quality. The feminist and anti-Christian sentiment in the film was inevitable, the outworking of Herbert’s own framing, and of Denis and the writers writing what they know: they weigh every (white) man, colonial effort, and every Christian, and find them wanting. It makes their job easier that conflating these is something that we already do, as history’s colonial efforts were often white and Christian. And Herbert gives the modern creator many excuses for woman worship in particular. Setting quite the bar for inelegance already, the Chani character being made a cudgel for the writer to beat the viewer about the ears with the right interpretation of things is somehow not an assassination so severe as that of Stilgar. His character turned into a joke as he was is not appropriate to the tone, nor useful to the theme. In so doing, the writers sabotage his contributions to Paul's own "conversion" to his myth. It takes the teeth out of the line, "I don't care what you believe! I believe!" if we are constantly jeering at the silliness of faith. A driving component of Frank Herbert’s work was to show the signs and wonders of Paul as a genuinely compelling, insidious deception. Gawking at the silliness of faith and prophecy constantly does not help us to find the myth compelling, especially when the character who is meant to represent sincere faith to us as a cautionary warning is the one at whom we have been laughing. Additionally, Denis in his secular modernism cannot resist giving everything a science-y explanation, leaving nothing but the visions to the spiritual, with even those receiving a handwave as, "planted by the Bene Gesserit." (That is the best explanation as given by the book, near as I can remember, but the impression is given in the film that it is some kind of device – whether psychological or technological – that has achieved this, and that this inception is not even done by a spiritual means. Meaning that the Bene Gesserit have a closer relation in Villeneuve to Scientology and hypnotists than they do any of the Christian tradition.) The mystery of the spiritual force at work in the events of this universe is part of the compelling nature of the narrative. Who or what force is at work in these events? Is this messiah who can see the future really possible, and is it really Paul? Even if we rug-pull all of the spiritual elements at the last minute for the big reveal that it was the Order all along, there would be a more convincing conniving and malevolent quality to Paul’s works, which better sells the theme. We are meant to come away from this tale feeling cautiously inward, wondering where we have been the victim of religious propaganda, or how we might have been carried off by soaring rhetoric and religious zealotry. Did anyone walk away from the movie Dune: Part Two thinking that they had seen a serious critique of religion? Did anyone walk out with that worry that they too would have been swept up in Paul’s ascendency if they were one of the Fremen? In all the confusing rhetoric of the film, the point is that you, audience member, would have something to latch on to. The strategy is shotgun vagary: there’s something in it for everyone. Just as the casting means there's someone in it for everyone. With the first Dune , I had a hope that there was a resurgence of questions about faith and fate in film. Blade Runner 's moral clarity made me even more hopeful as to Villeneuve's chances with Paul. Unfortunately, he is evidently still an atheist. Dune: Part Two is, however (as I often caveat movies, and for your sake, dear reader), in portions, very fun to watch. While I have more to say about the technique of the film, I have probably reached your limit, haven't I? I know I have reached my own. 50/100

(Written in 2026) So, after 2 years of reflection (more like 10 months but shhhh), I've come to the realization that Dune: Part Two is overrated. This film contains very little of what I enjoyed about the first film, and it's so generally unimpressive that its flimsy narrative takes center stage. Gone are the complex politics of Dune and its varied and complex scenery, insert a rehash of the already lackluster score of the first film, and a lack of technical flair from every department, and you get this film. The cast is fine, although generally weaker than in the first film. The cinematography and sound are still good (although less impressive than Dune ), but the production design is too bland, and Fraser's insistence on using mostly wide/extra wide shots showing mostly empty scenery doesn't hide the production design flaws. The editing is also notably worse here, Denis Villeneuve/Joe Walker remain insistent to linger on certain shots for too long, once again grinding the pace to a complete halt, and wringing out whatever energy the viewer has left. Back to the cast, Austin Butler is a very disappointing Feyd-Rautha. He does a uniquely awful job at instilling fear (what with his on-again/off-again Elvis accent ruining whatever was left of the dialogue), which betrays the work he put in on the combat choreography. He also lacks any real skill physicality-wise, all of the random yells, spasms, and "quirks" of his performance come off as comedic and are totally unfit for the character's role in the film. The action sequences in the film are also no longer the strength they were in the first film, with Villeneuve's staging and Frasier's cinematography becoming progressively less interesting throughout the film.

Visuellement bluffant, émotionnellement creux. Aie Aie Aie. Je m'attendais à BEAUCOUP mieux que la partie 1, mais à peine. Toutefois, les raisons de mon retrait sont différentes entre la partie 1 et la partie 2. À de nombreuses reprises, j'ai trouvé le film austère et glacial avec un manque de liens émotionnels avec les personnages. Par exemple, j'aurais aimé voir comment Chani et Paul se sont rapprochés car au départ elle avait quand même des doutes et lui avait ses visions prémonitoires la concernant. Enfaite, j'ai trouvé leur rapprochement hyper soudain comme précipité tout en étant assumé et c'est pas pour moi. De manière générale, je sens une certaine précipitation des évènements de la part de Villeneuve, ce qui m'a fait décroché. Des années ont l'air de passer comme des semaines là où, je peux le sentir, les livres doivent probablement bien nous le faire sentir ce temps qui passe. Autre remarque, l'expansion et la croissance de la "religion" de la mère de Paul qui est fourré au 1000e plan du film. J'aurais aimé un focus dessus parce qu'une parole de la mère qui dit "il faut commencer par ceux qui ont peurs" et puis "on a fini avec le nord, passons au sud"... mouais Denis steuplait hein. Des révélations chocs comme le fait que la mère de Paul soit la fille du baron et la mort symbolique de celui-ci part la main de son petit-fils m'ont laissé de marbre. Je soupçonne que cela s'explique par, pour moi encore une fois, un retrait de l'intrigue politique au second plan afin de polluer le premier plan du film sur le fait que tout indique que Paul est le Lisan Al-Ghaib (jeu de mot qui m'a fait croire à autre chose et je pense que c'était totalement le but). Je ne dis pas qu'il n'y a aucune intrigue politique, ce serait mentir sans vergogne. Je dis plutôt que sa place est hybride là où elle devrait être centrale. Toutefois, je comprendrais que d'autres ne pensent la même chose, et c'est OK. On retrouve des personnages qui se veulent être impactant retirer de tout leur éclat dû à un manque de place affligeant (ex: Empereur, Rautha). J'ai également du mal à croire en la relation entre Paul et sa mère. Leurs interactions me font plus penser à un frère et sa soeur plutôt qu'à un fils et sa mère. Vers la fin elle se reprend mais bon. Si on recentre notre attention sur Paul, j'ai pas compris en quoi c'était évident qu'il aille chercher la potion bleue. Pour moi c'est un peu sorti de nulle part. Oui oui sa prescience etc mais je suis pas convaincu par ce que je vois, justement parce que tout va vite et de manière très déconnecté. Et son shift ne s'explique pas tant que ça, on peut le comprendre en l'imaginant mais ce n'est jamais rien de factuel là où on comprenait celui d'Anakin par exemple. D'ailleurs, on sent que ce film est un film qui prépare le prochain. Ça m'a un peu dérangé. mais ça reste minime. Passons au positif, c'est déprimant sinon. J'ai beaucoup aimé le choix visuel de passer de la couleur au noir et blanc dans l'arène. Je n'ai pas d'explication au phénomène mais c'était sympa. De plus, les éléments du film sont présents mais mal intégré à mon avis, c'est dommage. (pff j'étais censé virer au positif) L'amourette bien que rapide est mignonne. On peut imaginer que Paul et Chani tienne énormément l'un à l'autre. De plus, j'ai bien aimé la première traversée du désert de Paul avec Chani. Les plans étaient beaux, l'ambiance était chic, les chorégraphies étaient apaisantes par leur synchronicité. Bref c'était chouette. Enfin, j'aime bien l'idée d'un faux saveur qui s'approprie les mythes pour parvenir à ses fins. C'est intéressant. On en vient même à se demander si le mythe est réellement faux ou s'il est devenu réel à force de le propager ou s'il a toujours été réel. Notre avis peut néanmoins se trouver biaisé par la mise en scène et le pdv de Paul (visions etc). Bref, c'est sympa ça. PS: Voir les idées des adaptations m'a donné envie de débuter les livres un jour. J'pense que j'apprécierai plus. Ou bien pas du tout et ça conclura ma tentative désespérée :( PS2: Niveau religion, et ce que traduit cette oeuvre, je préfère me taire sinon j'vais écrire 3 pavés supplémentaires. Pas content. Frank Herbert est un cas mais Denis Villeneuve est tout aussi en faute pour l'image qu'il renvoie. PS3: Je pense sincèrement qu'une série aurait été plus adaptée pour cette oeuvre.

3 stars only because I love the book so much and enjoy watching it come to screen. Too many things have been squeezed into this film, it covers such a large period of time as well as squeezing in the details about the Harkonens that happen in the first part of the story in the book that aren't included in the first film. Consequently, this film feels like a series of events strung together with little impact when major items happen. Many of the character motivations and personalities are also changed, some for the better (like Chani who frankly has no personality in the books) and some for the worse (Stilgar and Lady Jessica). Because of all of this, I also don't really believe in Chani and Paul's romance in this film, we're given no time to see an actual relationship blossom, we're just told through a montage and time jump that they're together. And Timothee Chalamet and Zendaya have no chemistry. Highlights of the film include Austin Butler's Feyd-Rauther, which he plays brilliantly, and the amazing cinematography (which at times feels a little excessively self-indulgent and doesn't necessarily blend with the rest of the film (Geidi Primes)).

Interested to see what happens with Paul’s character in the third movie, but I assume it’ll follow the book and he becomes somewhat of an evil character. If so, it will be realistic but obviously not the happy ending people would want.

I recognise your footsteps, old man. Absolutely monumental. Outstanding in every way. My favourite film of the decade and maybe all time. I love every second of it. The big three, Baron , Rabban and Feyd-Rauth motivate the picture with their spotless greed and pure soulessness. They will be missed in Part Three . The progression of the story in Part Two had me so concentrated in absorbing every detail that I felt like I was the Emperor himself receiving updates on Arrakis . The moments of Chani in Part One , lead so well into her role as Paul’s reality anchor in Part Two she is the life of the story and the heart of the Fremen. Zendaya’s best. The revelation of Paul’s family history is still a shock. I knew he was a genetic sight to be hold but being the heir to the Atreides thrown, the Son of a Bene Gesserit with Harkonnen blood leaves no room for surprise at what he accomplishes as a leader. This film being so much better visually than Part One is sooooo pleasing. There is spice in every frame and crack in Hans Zimmers score. I can’t wait for the third of the trilogy and WILL be seated the day of release, and WILL be rewatching the first two before we get blessed by Denis. I will always remember my first watch and will always love the story of Dune. Modern Masterpiece, timeless story. Thank you Frank Herbert , Thank you Denis Villeneuve. Long Live the Fighters.

Dune 2; Harkonnen Boogaloo The production on these movies continues to blow me away.  It feels like watching something from Moebius or Druillet in live action.  The costumes, the music, the differences in the worlds, heck even the language is all so well done that it feels both alien and completely natural all at the same time. I also really loved the looks of all of the Harkonnen machines.  One of the things that Villeneuve and the crew here have done very well across both films is give a sense of the weight and physics of these things.  The giant worms, the miners, the crashed ornithopters.  They all have very believable weight to them.  I've seen several bad sci-fi films where they forget about that in the fx.  They'll have these giant machines that look like they are walking across rice paper without damaging it. Watching these movies gives me the same sort of feeling that I got when I was watching The Lord of the Rings for the first time.

Denis Villeneuve en su máximo esplendor. La película es una obra maestra. Realmente magistral. Es de esas películas en las que cuesta encontrar algo que no esté a la altura: el guion, la dirección, la fotografía, los efectos visuales, las actuaciones y, por supuesto, la apoteósica banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Absolutamente todo funciona. La primera vez que la vi en el cine, en IMAX, salí completamente alucinado. La amé de principio a fin. Pero después de haber leído Dune, la experiencia fue todavía mejor. Amé el libro de Frank Herbert y, precisamente por eso, una de las cosas que más me impresionó de la primera película fue su enorme fidelidad a la obra original. Sin embargo, al leer el libro y volver a Dune: Part Two, entendí que Denis Villeneuve tomó muchas más libertades para llevar la historia hacia una dirección diferente. Y, lejos de molestarme, me pareció maravilloso. Porque eso demuestra que Villeneuve no buscó simplemente trasladar el libro página por página a la pantalla. Entendió su esencia, tomó decisiones propias y construyó su propia visión de Dune. Y eso, para mí, es precisamente lo que hacen los grandes directores. Volver a ver esta película una y otra vez es un verdadero lujo. Cada visionado permite apreciar algo nuevo: la composición de cada plano, los colores, la fotografía, los detalles de los escenarios, la magnitud de Arrakis y el nivel técnico de una producción que visualmente es simplemente impresionante. Y si hablamos de sus grandes virtudes, es imposible no detenerse en la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Personalmente, es mi compositor favorito de música para cine y aquí vuelve a entregar un trabajo extraordinario, completamente diferente al de la primera película. Hay momentos en los que basta con cerrar los ojos para sentir el desierto de Arrakis, la inmensidad del planeta y, sobre todo, cómo la tensión va aumentando poco a poco hasta convertir la historia en la promesa de una guerra santa. Las actuaciones también están a un nivel extraordinario. Era algo que podía esperarse después de una primera película con un elenco tan sólido, pero las nuevas incorporaciones elevan todavía más el conjunto. Austin Butler como Feyd-Rautha y Florence Pugh como Irulan son excelentes, pero para mí hay dos que se roban absolutamente la película: Javier Bardem como Stilgar y Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides. Chalamet, especialmente, entrega una de las mejores actuaciones de su carrera. Se puede ver en su rostro el tormento, el miedo y el dolor de un hombre que sabe perfectamente hacia dónde lo está llevando el camino que ha elegido, pero que también entiende que cada paso que da puede acercarlo cada vez más al caos que intentaba evitar. Dune: Part Two es una película maravillosa, épica y técnicamente impresionante. Una obra que consiguió conquistar tanto al público como a la crítica y que, en mi opinión, tiene absolutamente merecidos todos los elogios que recibió. Denis Villeneuve tomó una de las obras más importantes de la ciencia ficción, la llevó a la pantalla grande con una visión propia y consiguió convertirla en una experiencia cinematográfica monumental. Una verdadera obra de arte moderna.

this was the film that really helped me out a ton when I first started doing production design- watching interviews with Sam Lisenco (the p.d) introduced me to a new world of film production, and I'm forever thankful for it. finally, after some years, I've come around to see the film that had a huge impact on my aspiring career and deepened my understanding and appreciation of film as a whole. it's a given that what makes this film feel very special is the world and setting of this middle school, the use of intertextuality, and fantastic direction from the character acting, the specific style of cinematography, and the outstanding art direction. This is a very charming coming-of-age story that feels very magical for its modern and internet-age depiction of middle school. I was going into my senior year of high school when this came out, but youth-hood is a timeless experience all the same. In all honesty it would be unfair to compare this to a show like PEN15 because of its lack of social commentary, yes obviously they are both coming of age stories with awkward and anxious preteens, but both pieces of media are accomplishing two different goals. PEN15 has its two female leads, Maya and Anna, who bring a lot of interesting dialogue to be said about race and class in television. Usually I would label a film like this as “white people: the movie” but it would rub me the wrong way doing so as such, so I’ll make a one time exception for this film.

"Growing up can be a little bit scary and weird." — Kayla Day Eighth Grade follows a young person who struggles to express themselves and turns to internet video to build self-confidence. Bo Burnham is recognised for his realistic depiction of the internet, effectively illustrating what motivates people to create content. He presents the internet as a space for self-expression, reflection, and performance, often without an audience, particularly in unwatched vlogs. To ensure authenticity, Burnham cast real eighth graders and addressed mature topics relevant to their age group. The MPAA assigned the film an R rating, which sparked controversy by restricting access for actual eighth graders. In response, A24 organised free, unrated screenings across the United States. This film serves as Generation Z's counterpart to "Thirteen" (2003), though "Thirteen" used lighting to convey its darker themes. In Eighth Grade, students are often absorbed in their phones. Modern mean girls rarely make direct, passive-aggressive remarks, since that would require personal interaction. Instead, they exclude others by ignoring those they consider uncool. While this behaviour is harsh, the film does not portray these popular students as villains. Instead, it shows them coping with their own insecurities. Ultimately, there are no villains in Eighth Grade; the characters are young people trying to understand themselves and their lives. I would love to see another film that is both an interesting social commentary for teens and a generally good film with deep emotional ties that people can relate to.

As an educator, I can't express how "right" Bo Burnham's coming-of-age, anxiety-inducing drama Eighth Grade is to anyone outside the field who has forgotten what middle school was like. Stellar lead performances and horrifying tension propel this to classic " every teen should watch this "–status. Once again, I wish middle school me could've seen something like this—maybe even high school or college me—and find more about himself to love and be grateful for.

Oh to be the only girl at the pool party in a one-piece. Kayla, you are everything to me. Putting on makeup before taking a "just woke up like this" selfie. Spending hours trying to engineer the perfect Instagram post like it might somehow engineer a better version of yourself. Every Snapchat story felt like evidence in the case for whether or not you of all people were worth noticing. Eighth Grade understands that before you know who you are, you're already performing as someone else. Every hallway feels like an audience. The boys are impossibly dreamy, the girls impossibly cruel, your parents impossibly embarrassing, and adulthood seems like the cure for it, a glimmer of hope through it all. What a beautiful tragedy it is to be thirteen; how special it is that a movie can almost let us do it all over again.

Wanted to cry for most of this movie. Did cry at several scenes. I love her dad. His monologues are unbelievable. I adore Bo Burnham and his screenwriting. It's incredible how he goes from viscerally cringe dialogue to randomly inserting these subtly beautiful, understated lines. "It's dumb in a way that it's fun to play when it's raining outside" stood out to me for this reason. There's something to be said about how this movie does not use gratuitous violence. I knew what was coming from having shadowed my colleague's film class when this was being covered, but the "bad" scenes still made me nauseous and unsettled. I kept awaiting an escalation, as other popular films have conditioned me to anticipate, and yet the escalation never came. I like that Bo Burnham rejects the spectacle of violence in this respect. Culturally and artistically, we've overly normalized the use of unnecessary violence and brutality in the arts. I'm talking specifically about violence that isn't necessary to plot development. Violence in this respect is used to replace screen-writing that is a) legitimately good and b) trusts the audience's intelligence by instead choosing to depict implied violence. Sure, media literacy is abysmal nowadays, but that's no reason to make art that essentially hinges on the audience's willingness to actively participate in the degradation and oppression of vulnerable, marginalized people (which, for the record, many of the "greats" necessitate we do). Incredibly symptomatic of its time, almost like a time capsule. Missing Bo Burnham's screenwriting a little extra today. Great work.

i don't think anyone will ever understand what this film means to me. i watched it for the first time at 17, when i had already grown out of my preteen awkward phase and somehow considered myself at that point to be a full-fledged adult. but as i watch this film again as a girl in my mid-20s, this stirred something in me i didn’t expect. when i was 17 i saw my younger self in kayla. awkward, anxious, always wanting to be chosen, too shy to talk to the cool kids, and feeling so uncomfortable in my own skin. but at that time of viewing the movie, all i could think was, “thank god that phase is over.” and yes, most of us do not miss that age. but now at 25, i found myself crying with love for this character. that version of ourselves that feels so overdramatic and inexperienced and terrified of growing up, who only a couple of years prior to puberty couldn’t care less if other kids thought she was cool enough. kayla stares at her 6th grade time capsule, addressed on the front “to the coolest girl in the world.” she somehow is depressed and embarrassed that her 11 year old self had that much confidence that her older self would be just that. but it’s that exact kind of confidence that allows us to not only stop judging the awkward versions of ourselves, but to embrace them with our whole hearts. every phase of life is a stepping stone to the next, but every version of ourselves is a part of us. be kind to every age you find yourself in, and cherish it. you grow every day from who you were yesterday, but you don’t forget that awkward girl that got you to where you are today. bo burnham i adore you so much. thank you for this film

Quando comecei o filme, a primeira sensação que tive foi a de estar assistindo a uma versão alternativa de algum filme da Marvel, principalmente uma espécie de Doutor Estranho no Multiverso da Loucura com uma abordagem diferente. Talvez por eu não estar tão acostumado a ver o conceito de multiverso sendo explorado fora do universo dos super-heróis, Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo parecia uma ótima oportunidade de enxergar essa ideia por uma perspectiva mais autoral e menos limitada pelas regras de uma franquia. E é curioso porque o conceito de multiverso aqui é muito mais amplo do que simplesmente mostrar versões alternativas dos personagens ou brincar com realidades diferentes. O filme usa essa ideia quase como uma representação das infinitas possibilidades da vida, das escolhas que fazemos e de todos os caminhos que poderiam ter sido seguidos. Essa é uma proposta interessante, e eu gostei da forma como o filme tenta enxergar o multiverso por um lado mais humano e existencial. O problema, para mim, está na forma como essa ideia é apresentada. Em muitos momentos, o filme parece querer ser mais inteligente do que realmente é, como se precisasse constantemente provar sua própria genialidade. A mistura de estilos, o exagero visual e a quantidade absurda de ideias fazem parte da identidade da obra, mas às vezes a sensação é de que o filme força tanto a sua criatividade que acaba perdendo um pouco da naturalidade. Ele quer ser caótico, profundo, engraçado e emocionante ao mesmo tempo, mas em alguns momentos parece mais preocupado em mostrar o quanto consegue ser diferente do que realmente desenvolver tudo aquilo que propõe. Eu gostei mais do ato final justamente porque é o momento em que o filme finalmente parece entender a própria força. Depois de passar boa parte da duração mergulhado em um caos constante, entre cortes frenéticos, exageros visuais e uma tentativa quase desesperada de ser irreverente, ele finalmente desacelera e permite que seus personagens existam de verdade. É quando Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo deixa de tentar provar o tempo todo o quanto é criativo e começa a explorar aquilo que realmente tinha de mais interessante: as relações humanas por trás de todo aquele espetáculo. Antes disso, porém, eu tive muita dificuldade de me conectar com a proposta. Não é pelo fato de o filme ser absurdo ou querer ser engraçado, porque essa é claramente a identidade dele, mas pela forma como ele constantemente interrompe os próprios momentos de profundidade. Sempre que surge uma oportunidade de desenvolver melhor suas ideias sobre arrependimentos, escolhas e a sensação de insignificância diante de infinitas possibilidades, o filme parece escolher quebrar a atmosfera com uma piada que muitas vezes não funciona e acaba tirando todo o peso daquilo que estava sendo construído. E isso acaba prejudicando justamente a profundidade que ele tenta alcançar. Algumas cenas são tão forçadas e constrangedoras que, ao invés de aproximarem o espectador dos personagens, criam uma distância. O filme quer ser caótico, divertido e emocionante, mas em muitos momentos o caos domina tanto que a parte humana fica escondida. Só quando ele finalmente abandona um pouco essa necessidade de transformar tudo em uma grande piada é que a mensagem começa a encontrar espaço para respirar. Eu realmente acredito que a campanha desse filme no Oscar foi um delírio coletivo. Sinceramente, não consigo enxergar uma obra digna de sete estatuetas aqui. Para mim, o único prêmio realmente justificável é o de Melhor Montagem. Todo o restante parece premiar mais a ideia do filme do que a sua execução. É uma obra que força a própria genialidade, insiste em uma profundidade que raramente alcança e, justamente quando parece prestes a dizer algo verdadeiramente significativo, escolhe sabotar o momento com um humor que, para mim, soa artificial e deslocado. E no fim, eu continuo com a sensação de que assistir a Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo não foi uma experiência tão distante de assistir a um filme da fase 4 da Marvel. Talvez exista mais criatividade na forma, uma identidade visual mais autoral e uma ambição maior nas ideias, mas a essência ainda me parece muito semelhante. O multiverso continua sendo tratado como um grande espetáculo, onde tudo precisa ser maior, mais caótico e mais excêntrico do que o anterior. Se a Academia decidiu premiar justamente esse tipo de proposta com o maior prêmio da noite, então talvez fosse mais coerente ter reconhecido um dos próprios filmes da Marvel, que, gostando ou não, sempre assumiram esse espetáculo sem a necessidade de revesti-lo com uma profundidade que, para mim, aqui nunca se concretiza.

I think there's a very sincere 80 minute movie in here that would work like gangbusters. Unfortunately, this thing is nearly 2.5 hours long and undercuts so much of its tenderness with sub-Edgar Wright sophomoric hijinks, and somehow even throughout this bloated running time, one of the key leads is still utterly two-dimensional. Honestly, it made me wonder if I could even revisit those old Wright movies either at this age, maybe the problem is me...but so it goes. I liked the Ratatouille joke. And the WKW visual reference. And Yeoh's delivery of the hotdog line.

It’s easy to see what people are responding to - A24 finally made it’s own version of a Marvel movie - pure spectacle with a hollow and sentimental core. Everything… shares the same theme as both Encanto and Turning Red and considering it’s a movie for adults, lands pretty much at the same place, with somehow less grace and sophistication. Let’s start with the rock bit - it’s been done already in I Heart Huckabees with less google eyes. Additionally, like many other LB reviewers, it’s hard not to see some heavy lifting from the most notorious episode of Rick and Morty . Do I even need to highlight recent movies about generational trauma or multiverses? Truly, other than the throw everything at the wall visuals, Everything… generates no new thematic or intellectual ideas whatsoever - the universe is large, be nice to your kids, it’s all about love, zzz. None of these would be bad on their face if they were inferred through the story - but most of them are dumped as platitudes in the final exhausting 30 minutes. The word “messy” keeps coming up in reviews as an almost compliment. I would say it’s more “sloppy” - jokes are beat into the ground - even ones I liked - and most of the “weirdness” is that icky brand of “that’s crazy” without any meaningful symbolism. Weird for the sake of seeming interesting. Cut away the smoke and mirrors and what’s left? A husk of a film spewing broad pandering schmaltz. The thread I thought the movie would follow was exploring the different types of relationships the mom may have had with the dad, as well as her father that illuminates more about her inner workings. Movies about older people are rare, especially women. While the directors want to frame the movie that way, by the end this seemed like another millenial movie complaining about boomers. The pyschology of this movie is basically Greenberg ’s “hurt people hurt people”. It all feels so slight for a movie nominally about the human condition and other “big” ideas. Ok so the visuals are compelling but it’s nothing Gasper Noe and Leos Carax haven’t done for years. The saving graces for me, if they exist at all, are the perfomances and the costumes. Especially the costumes.

I'm so happy that Asian-American cinema is a legit real thing now, and that we have roles like these for Michelle Yeoh and Ke Huy Quan. But I'm less happy about how pastiche cinema has become a substitute for genuine invention—I'm not sure I need another genre mashup exercise where the directors wear their influences as conspicuously on their sleeves as this. This movie doesn't even feel like sub-Tarantino fare to me; it's sub-Edgar Wright-ian, really, and that's not a compliment. I went in pumped for a good time but felt overwhelmed by the self-satisfaction and an over abundance of exposition. There are those who would argue that those encumbrances are balanced out by the family drama underpinning this whole affair, but the contours of that story are so maudlin that its sum total is basically just Disney-isms with a mildly indie sensibility.

I appreciate the range of style it allows itself, and it was nice to see faces I haven’t seen in movies for a while, and some of this should should be right up my alley—but man did I feel nothing. Might be too “gen z” for me
