روایت بین دو خط سیاسی و بازنمایی زندگی و جهان فراغ از آن گیر افتاده است به همین دلیل نه میتواند جامعه ای تحت سلطه استبداد بسازد و نه میتواند خانواده بسازدد، به خصوص خانواده متاثر از آسیب چنین جامعه ای! فیلم با جهان خانواده و با محوریت شخصیت اصلی یعنی (مادر خانه) آغاز میشود، جهانی که گه گاه اشاراتی به فضای سیاسی جامعه برزیل دارد اما تکیه بر خانواده ای و پرجمعیت که احتمالا قرار است اتفاقی باعث از هم پاشیدگی یا اسیب به ان میشود. اتفاقا نقطه عطف داستان یعنی گرفتار شدن روبنس سبب میشود که کارگردان به دلیل عدم انتخاب در زاویه نسبت به روایت خود باعث میگردد که روایت بلاتکلیف بماند و خانواداه ای که در ابتدای روایت به کشل نسبتاً خوبی در حال شکلگیری بود، شخصیت‌هایش تبدیل به جزیره‌هایی میگردند که تا پایان روایت نقطه اتصالی در آنها نمیتوان یافت. البته در نقطه عطف بزرگ یعنی در زمان که دستگیر شدن روبنس و به طبع آن اونیسی و دخترشان اندکی فضای فیلم که نگاه سیاسی در آن غالب است سعی دارد آن رعب و وحشت و بی‌منطقی حاکم را بسازد اما در آن موفق نیست. بعد از این است که روایت دچار افت معنا و فرم میشود و شخصیت‌های سرگردان (به خصوص فرعی مانند وکیل یا روزنامه‌نگاران و دوستان روبنس) باعث میگردد که اثرات سنگینی که میتواند چنین اتفاقی بر خانواده بگذارد مشاهده ننماییم. در نهایت روایت داستان در جایی که خانواده تصمیم به ترک و رفتن به سائوپائولو میگیرند پایان میپذیرد که همین نقطه نیز توانایی ساخت یک روایت تمام کمال را ندارد اما از نظر پایان بندی میتوانست نقطه مناسبی باشد. اما به دلیل وفادار بودن کارگردان به روایت اصلی که فیلم بر اساس آن ساخته شده فیلم ادامه میابد و از اینجاست که فیلم به شدت ضعیف و کاریکاتوری پیش میرود. ما ناگهان به 25 سال بعد منتقل میشویم، نه برای دیدن خانواده ای که اثرات این ماجرا را متحمل است، بلکه برای اینکه نامه گواهی فوت روبنس به دست اونیسی برسد و در فیلم ثبت گردد. عجیبتر اینکه باز هم 18 سال پیش میرویم و یک خانواده را میبینیم که هیچ بازتاب دراماتیک ندارند و تنها برای اینکه ما ناگهان اونیسی را در حال دیدن گزارشی از قهرمان بودن روبنس ببیند. این مخ آخر به این روایت ناقص و ضعیف است. البته نمی‌توان از سکانس‌های خوبی در ابتدای فیلم که مربوط به خانواده است صرفه نظر کرد، هرچند که نمی‌توان به فرزندان نزدیک شد به این دلیل که فیلم بیش از حد متکی به شخصیت اصلی (اونیسی) است و همان را هم ناقص می‌سازد. همچنین بازی خوب .. در نقش اونیسی نیز باعث شده که فیلم تحمل‌پذیرتر باشد. در مجموع روایتی ناقص و بی‌هدف که تکلیفش با خودش مشخص نیست، باعث می‌شود فیلم به یک فیلم متوسط تنزل پیدا کند.

Dieser Film hat mich an manchen Stellen tief berührt. Doch mein Rating variiert zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten stark. Die Hauptdarstellerin und die Figur der Mutter sind für mich das Schönste gewesen - man sieht sie nicht in Selbstmitleid verfallen, sie ist unerschütterlich tapfer, radikal pragmatisch, strahlt Besonnenheit aus und dann diese rührende Zärtlichkeit ihrer Familie gegenüber - und zeitgleich sieht man ihr an, wie sie der Verlust des Mannes und dessen Umstände unwiderruflich gebrochen haben. Sie strahlt zum einen leise Hoffnung, Resilienz, aber zum anderen endlose Melancholie aus. Dieses Schauspiel verdient wirklich Aufmerksamkeit, Fernanda Torres ist unglaublich charismatisch. Zum Ende des zweiten Akts möchte ich dem Film somit gern vier Sterne geben. Aber in anderen Momenten verfällt der Film in Kitsch, wie im letzten Akt - das ist wirklich ärgerlich. Außerdem kratzt mir der Film zu sehr an der Oberfläche, ist unpolitisch und fokussiert sich zu sehr auf die Biografie des Einzelnen. Da würde ich doch am liebsten nur 2 1/2 Sterne geben aus reinem Trotz. So fühlt sich mein Fazit nicht ganz authentisch an. Dem hohem Averagerating kann ich mich nicht anschließen, für ein Meisterwerk halte ich den Film bei Weitem nicht. Da er trotz Laufzeit erstaunlich kurzweilig und unanstrengend ist, bin ich milde gestimmt.

Very gripping true story! Very sickening too if I’m honest - dictatorships like that in Brazil are just disgusting the way they treat their people. Scary. Honestly thought this was heavily emotional - the acting across the board was top notch, and helped me feel every emotion on the board. Fernanda Torres shines in her role as Eunice; an absolute powerhouse performance. Loved Mikey Maddison in Anora, but this was the performance of the year for me. No doubts there. Shame she didn’t take it. Critics’ tastes never fail to baffle me. The first half of this film is one of the most gripping of 2024. Eyes glued to the screen, incredibly tight screenplay keeping me utterly hooked and invested in the characters, and a filmmaking style to invokes a proper real-life, yet nostalgic feeling in the first 30 minutes. I thought it was so important to showcase their day to day family life in the beginning of the film - it helps make the devastation feel all that more sudden and shocking! Unfortunately after the capture situation, i feel like the film loses its way a bit, the pacing slows down quite a bit, and the interesting plot slowly fizzles out, which is a shame, because the first half of the film was incredibly written and paced. That’s the problem with real life stories - they can only be as interesting as the actual story, unless you want to manipulate events that happen, which is never a good idea. So it’s almost hard to criticise the filmmaker for this, when there’s a lack of creative freedom when adapting a true story. This was a great film though - a must watch emotional tale of grief and heartbreak. It’s not without its fun opening half hour, but don’t expect thrills and joy after that mark, it’s all depressing from there. Truly harrowing story.

While it didn’t quite hit me as hard emotionally, I understand why this would be so devastating to so many people. Especially considering this all being real. As far as just as a film goes, I have 1 or 2 nitpicks that prevent me from loving it but it’s still great.

Goodness gracious, I get existential about the ability to authentically portray period in films as time, technology, and civilization moves on but movies like I'm Still Here give so much reassurance and strength whilst bravely dealing with crises of their own. To process an entire generation's worth of grief under dictatorial rule is not the goal of this film, but through a somewhat high-profile example that speaks to thousands of personal histories, this film is pretty exemplary. It shows how stark and banal the backslide into this type of brutal rule can and will look like. A nation always outnumbers its government but a combination of shocking brutality, public grandstanding, collusion with corporate interests, and hoarding of resources will depress the power of any individual or small group. It's quite scary to lose the power of criticism, the gumption to inspire change in your country, or the relative simplicity of alternate viewpoints under threat of sanction, capture, and/or murder. I'm Still Here explores these consequences mostly offscreen, putting in its place the shattering of an idealized household. This property on the beach becomes a visual metaphor for Brazil in microcosm as the tumult plays out. Incredibly dark forces threaten to ruin and re-contextualize the beautiful lands you call home and yet, there's nowhere else you'd rather be, with nothing to do but try and find peace. It is noble to stand up in face of these inhumane challenges but life can be so unfair. There is no guarantee of reward or recompense. If anything, the point of a journey like this is not to be persuaded, but to be well and truly broken. Everyone possesses a personal tolerance for such things. Bravery is taking yourself over the edge without much care as to the outcome, only that there is one. Dense, deep, emotional, I'm Still Here is no easy watch per se but it is a deeply informing and affecting one, driven by Fernanda Torres's incredible performance, as well as the film's immaculate capture of Brazil's view of the coup.

Not every tragedy has to be told on the biggest scale it can be. While hundreds were killed and disappeared during Brazil's military dictatorship, choosing to focus on one specific instance so that we can really come to love this family before it gets told apart makes it hit much harder. Stunning performances all around with a really great cameo by the legendary Fernanda Montenegro (best nonagenarian performance ever?). For whatever reason, I don't always love how it looks, especially the grittier second half, and thought the script sometimes could have done more showing less telling, but these are minor nitpicks. Powerful and important movie.

The film requires a fair amount of patience, especially at the beginning, as the story unfolds slowly. But the longer it goes on, the more it pays off. It’s honest, harsh, and refuses to comfort the audience with feel good moments. Felt it necessary to rewatch since it’d been a decade. Despite its best efforts to conform to a more transcendent cinematic language, drawing from 2001 and other monuments of modernist cinema, the film is fundamentally incapable of embodying that language because of its ideological hostility to the very nature of art. Where 2001 embraces mystery, ambiguity, and the limits of human understanding, Interstellar cannot help but reduce everything to a problem awaiting calculation. The film reeks of the resurgent scientific arrogance that defined much of the 2010s, the kind embodied by Dawkins and his contemporaries. And Elon Musk now a testament of its logical conclusion. It carries the self-assured belief that scientific reasoning and human computation alone are sufficient to save humanity from the very crises those same forces helped create. Even the film’s apparent concession to the irrational, love, is ultimately folded back into the logic of quantification. And thus, even the very medium used to tell this story becomes a means to a self-defeating end. The older I get, the more deeply I believe that the arts are our greatest means of approaching transcendence. Art is how we encounter the sacred, how we gesture toward truths that words, logic, and reason can only circle. To use cinema in service of an ideology that insists every mystery must ultimately be rendered calculable is to undermine the very essence of the art form itself. A truly evil film.

I feel that the writing in this film drags this film down heavily and the conclusion to this film made no sense- Cooper spends the whole movie trying to get back to his daughter just for him to leave again within 30 seconds of finally reuniting. I get that he wanted to save his family, but it ultimately seemed like a selfish decision to get to leave the planet you know is dying & your kids behind with it. It's like he only cared about his daughter towards the end of the film. I wished that during the end they would show Murph at different ages trying to figure out what the gravity meant, but they clearly didn't want to hire another actor (lazy). Boasts itself as both the most popular and most viewed film on this very platform as of this writing; I was likely going to stumble into it sooner or later, but of course since The Odyssey is the current hot (and somewhat contested despite what scores on here and IMDB would indicate otherwise) new thing, I just had to dive back into Christopher Nolan once more. Do I think this is any good? …Sort of? The production design is well crafted, colour grading is decent, the space stuff itself seems to have been thoroughly researched, and I can’t deny the score is well composed. However, like plenty of these Nolen directed flicks, it’s the story which I struggle to emotionally connect with. Not for lack of trying however, I just don’t feel that emotional spark others seem to with this guy’s works. Also, I think I just prefer 2002: A Space Odyseey as far as space travel films go, that one got weirder with it decades earlier and leaves further unanswered questions in its wake. Also, the World of Tomorrow shorts emotionally connect with me way more while also balancing a combination of weirdness and absurdity for that matter. I think I know what I’m looking for in Sci Fi at this point, and I don’t think this film is quite it with its attempts to be sentimental and tear jerking. This has its moments, don’t get me wrong, but they’re a bit too spread out for me across the almost three hour runtime for me to get into it fully. At least I can say I watched it and got something out of it.

It's a great narrative, and the emotional arc really hit me. At the same time, it shows Nolan's biggest weakness: exposition. It's a tell-more-than-show kind of thing. But because of how good it looks, I'm inclined to let most of it slide. I just wish Nolan would have allowed for some of the stuff to have an ambiguous element. Still, such a great film though and definitely worth the watch.

Interstellar is one of those movies where you completely lose your sense of space and time while watching it. It’s also one of those movies you have to watch twice because you never fully understand it the first time. Sometimes even a third time. After that, the rewatches are just because you genuinely enjoy it. Once you finally understand everything, you just sit there thinking, “Wow, this is such a great movie.” It’s incredibly well made. The cinematography is beautiful, and everything feels so carefully and precisely done. What makes it even more incredible is that, for the most part, the movie tried to stay as scientifically realistic as possible, based on what was known or could actually be proven. And that just makes it even more amazing.

Uff, qué puedo decir de esta película que no se haya dicho ya. La amo y me rompe el corazón cada vez que la veo. Es una obra maestra absoluta del cine de ciencia ficción y de la vida misma loco. Al principio confieso que me costó un poco enganchar por toda su avanzada filosofía, me parecía demasiado compleja para mi humilde cerebro pero a medida que avanzaba me fui metiendo en la historia y en los personajes. La parte que más me destrozó fue cuando Cooper se reencuentra con su hija, Murph, que ya es una viejita. No paré de llorar. Es desgarrador ver cómo el tiempo ha pasado y cómo él se ha perdido toda su vida. Es una escena tan potente y emotiva que es imposible no conmoverse. Y esa frase que dice: " El amor es la única cosa que trasciende el tiempo y el espacio ". Es tan real y tan doloroso a la vez. Creo que todos tenemos que ver esta película mínimo 1 vez por año hasta morirnos.

One of the greatest films ever made, periodt. Every single time Hans Zimmer’s organ music swells in Interstellar, I get chills. Christopher Nolan created a visual marvel that is one of the greatest I've ever seen, but what makes this movie an absolute masterpiece to me is how deeply emotional it is. A lot of sci-fi movies get so caught up in quantum mechanics and space travel that they feel cold and robotic. Interstellar does the exact opposite. It uses terrifying concepts like time dilation where a single hour on a water planet costs Cooper years of his daughter’s life back on Earth to create an unbearable sense of stakes and grief. No idea how he managed to fit wormholes, black holes, grief, promises, love, cold space, the bond of a father & child all at the same time. Nolan is undoubtedly goated. It’s ambitious, loud, visually flawless, and aggressively sentimental in the best way possible. A true Christopher Nolan classic. 🎬🚀

I did notice that while Nolan is quite visionary when it comes to production design and set pieces and the background score, he is quite conventional, sometimes even a bit simple in his writing of dialogues. Some dialogue seemed quite a bit cheesy if I'm being honest. Nonetheless, watching it tonight reminded me of the first time I watched it back in 2014 in the midst of my first semester of engineering. I was so enamored by this movie that I spend the next few days reading up about the movie, wormholes, blackholes and other fun stuff instead of studying for my exam for Mechanics, which caused me to fail the subject. In the 12 years since, I have no regrets about it. This is probably enough to describe how much I like this film.

Joker: Folie a Deux Review: Da Vinci pissing on the Mona Lisa ____________________________________________ "Arthur Fleck is dead.       Long live the Joker." ____________________________________________ 👍: Soundtrack/Sounds: 10/10 Plot/Concept: 6.2/10 Pacing: 7.1/10 Characters: 6.3/10 Emotion: 7.2/10 Cinematography: 10/10 Casting: 9/10 Acting: 9.5/10 Ending: 9.3/10 Overall: 🍿74/90🍿 Joker: Folie à Deux has a lot more good things than people give it credit for. Joaquin Phoenix gives another incredible performance and carries every scene with intensity. I also enjoyed all of the songs , and the soundtrack and sound design create a unique mood. The visuals are beautiful , with grey but yet bright colours that make Gotham look perfect. The scene where Two-Face is born was one of my favourites . And the overall court sequence is excellent. I also liked the ending . I know most people hate it, but I thought it fit the story well. In my opinion, this film is still very overhated. The Message: Joker: Folie à Deux shows how society can turn a broken person into a symbol they never wanted to become. Arthur is no longer seen as a human being with fears, but as the Joker , an idea that people project their own anger onto. The film questions whether people truly care about justice or if they simply enjoy watching chaos. Do we become who we really are or who everyone expects us to be. Arthur struggles between being himself and living up to the Joker . The ending suggests that ideas can survive even when the people cannot. symbols are often more powerful than people, and once society creates a legend , it becomes almost impossible to forget, no matter how much someone changes. ____________________________________________ 👎: Joker: Folie à Deux has a lot of problems. The biggest one is that almost nothing happens. The story barely moves forward , and around 70% of the film feels wasted because there is almost no real progress from beginning to end. The direction is bland, and the overall screenplay is weak. I enjoyed the songs themselves, but the musical numbers often don't fit the story and become exhausting after a while. Good music alone isn't enough to carry such a thin plot. Harley Quinn was also disappointing because she barely does anything important. She had a lot of potential , but the screenplay gives her very little to give , making her feel completely unnecessary. I know the film is overhated , but it's still a pretty mid film . To make things even worse, I watched it at 2 a.m. , so I even lost sleep for it. ____________________________________________ Overall: Joker: Folie à Deux is a weak ass film , but it's still massively overhated. It has some genuinely great aspects , especially the acting, visuals, and music, but they're overshadowed by an unfocused story, bland direction, and wasted potential. The flaws are simply much bigger than the strengths, making it an average experience. Rating by Greatness: ⭐✨ Rating: ⭐⭐ ```````````````

Coringa: Delírio a Dois foi um filme de interpretação dúbia. Não é uma obra que odiei, muito pelo contrário, minhas expectativas eram extremamente altas por gostar muito do personagem Coringa, e talvez tenha sido justamente isso que tornou a decepção maior. Gosto da proposta do diretor de explorar o Arthur Fleck, aprofundando seus conflitos internos e mostrando o ser humano por trás do símbolo. As reflexões sobre identidade, solidão, julgamento e a forma como a sociedade constrói e destrói figuras públicas são interessantes e, em muitos momentos, muito bem executadas, o problema é que essa proposta entra em conflito com aquilo que o próprio filme promete, pois ao assistir a uma continuação de Coringa, é natural esperar o desenvolvimento do personagem que conhecemos, mas a narrativa permanece centrada quase exclusivamente em Arthur. Para outro filme, essa abordagem talvez funcionasse ainda melhor, mas, para uma sequência de Coringa, ela me pareceu uma escolha equivocada. Outro ponto que prejudicou bastante minha experiência foi o excesso de números musicais, que em diversos momentos tornaram o filme cansativo e quebraram completamente o ritmo da narrativa. Por fim, o desfecho também me dividiu, embora eu compreenda a intenção simbólica do diretor, a forma como Arthur morre me pareceu simples demais para um personagem tão marcante, portanto esperava um encerramento que desse mais grandeza à sua trajetória, e não um fim causado por alguém praticamente irrelevante para toda a construção da história. Ainda assim, reconheço que é um filme corajoso por fugir do convencional e propor discussões interessantes, minha decepção não veio da qualidade das reflexões, mas da sensação de que elas pertenciam a um filme sobre Arthur Fleck, e não à continuação do Coringa que eu esperava.

Coringa 2 é um filme que não consegue se sustentar sozinho. Ele vive inteiramente à sombra do primeiro. A nova proposta de transformar a narrativa em um musical é, na teoria, interessante. Ela até combina com a leitura psicológica e frágil que esse universo fez do Coringa. O problema é que, na prática, a execução falha completamente. O longa não consegue decidir o que quer ser. Ele não funciona como musical, porque as músicas não impulsionam a história nem revelam nada novo sobre os personagens. E também não funciona como um drama de tribunal, porque o roteiro jurídico é fraco, arrastado e não constrói tensão real. No fim das contas, o que resta são dois pilares: as atuações, que continuam sendo impecáveis, especialmente de Joaquin Phoenix e Lady Gaga, e a fotografia, que segue linda e atmosférica. Mas tirando isso, o filme se esvazia. Não sobra substância, não sobra tema, não sobra impacto. Me parece que Todd Phillips gastou o filme inteiro tentando responder aos fãs que idolatraram o primeiro Coringa e transformaram aquele personagem em um ícone a ser seguido. Ele quis dizer: "olha, esse cara não é um símbolo, ele é só um doente". E tudo bem querer desconstruir isso. O problema é a forma. Ele mesmo criou essa versão do Coringa. Ele mesmo construiu um protagonista magnético, caótico e sedutor no primeiro filme. E agora parece arrependido disso. Em vez de aprofundar ou amadurecer essa ideia, ele optou pelo caminho mais raso e mais medíocre: desconstruir por desconstruir, chocar por chocar. O resultado é um filme que trai a própria proposta que o consagrou.

بعد ما خلصت Joker: Folie à Deux، للأسف طلع بالنسبة لي من أكبر خيبات الأمل. الجزء الأول كان تحفة بكل معنى الكلمة، قدّم شخصية آرثر فليك بطريقة واقعية ومؤلمة، وخلاك تتفهم كيف وصل إلى مرحلة التحول للجوكر. أما الجزء الثاني، فحسيت أنه ضيّع كل اللي بناه الفيلم الأول. أكبر مشكلة عندي أن الفيلم ما كان يركز على قصة الجوكر نفسها. كنت داخل وأنا متحمس أشوف تطور الشخصية بعد نهاية الجزء الأول، لكن اللي حصل أن أغلب وقت الفيلم كان عبارة عن أغاني ورقص واستعراضات موسيقية. فكرة الفيلم الموسيقي ممكن تعجب بعض الناس، لكن بالنسبة لي ما خدمت القصة، بالعكس كانت تقطع الأحداث وتخلي الإيقاع بطيئًا بشكل مزعج. حسيت أني أشاهد فيلمًا موسيقيًا أكثر من كوني أشاهد فيلمًا عن الجوكر. حتى على مستوى القصة، ما كان فيه تقدم حقيقي للشخصية. كثير من الأحداث كانت تدور في نفس المكان وبنفس الفكرة، ومع الوقت صار الفيلم مكرر وما فيه ذلك التصاعد النفسي اللي ميّز الجزء الأول. التوتر، الغموض، والشعور بأن آرثر يتغير تدريجيًا… كلها أشياء كانت شبه غائبة هنا. أما النهاية… فكانت بالنسبة لي سيئة لدرجة ما أقدر أوصفها. بدل ما تعطيني نهاية قوية أو مرضية، حسيت أنها أضعفت كل اللي صار في الفيلم الأول، وتركتني مستغرب أكثر من كوني منبهر. كانت نهاية ما عطت الشخصية ولا الجمهور المكافأة اللي كانوا ينتظرونها. مع ذلك، ما أقدر أنكر أن عنده بعض الإيجابيات. تمثيل خواكين فينيكس كان ممتاز كعادته، وقدر يقدم أداءً قويًا حتى لو المادة اللي عنده ما كانت بنفس جودة الجزء الأول. وليدي غاغا أيضًا قدمت حضورًا جيدًا، والتصوير السينمائي والإضاءة والألوان كانت جميلة جدًا، وكذلك الموسيقى التصويرية في المشاهد الدرامية كانت ممتازة من ناحية الجودة. لكن بالنسبة لي، هذه الإيجابيات ما كانت كافية تنقذ الفيلم. لما يكون عندك جزء أول بهذا المستوى الاستثنائي، طبيعي تكون التوقعات مرتفعة، لكن الجزء الثاني ما قدر يحققها، بل ابتعد عن الشيء اللي أحببناه في الأصل. كنت أبغى أشوف فيلم عن الجوكر، عن عقليته وتطوره، مو فيلم يعتمد أغلب وقته على الرقص والأغاني. تقييمي: 4/10. فيلم جميل بصريًا وممثلوه قدموا كل اللي يقدرون عليه، لكن القصة، الإيقاع، وطريقة تقديمها خلت الفيلم بالنسبة لي خيبة أمل كبيرة، خصوصًا إذا قارنته بعظمة الجزء الأول.

Joker: Folie à Deux nos envuelve ya no en un descenso a la locura, como lo fue la primera, sino en un acompañamiento de este personaje durante su estancia en el reclusorio y en el juicio por los crímenes que vimos en la cinta anterior. Personalmente, considero que esta película, o al menos la historia elegida para contar esta secuela, es innecesaria. No aporta nada realmente nuevo, no desarrolla al personaje —que ya estaba perfectamente construido en la primera entrega— y la coprotagonista, que debería tener mucho peso al tratarse de Harley Quinn, no alimenta la historia como se esperaba. La elección del género musical para esta entrega creo que tenía mucho potencial. La forma en que los números musicales se integran a la cinta, como una representación de la locura dentro de la mente del Joker, funciona bastante bien. Sin embargo, la falta de un guion sólido termina afectando considerablemente esta decisión de género. En general, es una película que, si nunca hubiera existido, no habría pasado absolutamente nada. Incluso creo que mucha gente habría preferido que jamás se hiciera antes que ver cómo fueron desdibujando poco a poco todo lo que construyeron con tanta fuerza en la primera. Aun así, rescato su banda sonora y una fotografía muy cuidada e inteligentemente realizada. Visto En HBO Max

It’s a little too experimental, but I have to respect the boldness of dropping this after the first one blew up. By refusing to glamorize the violence and making it obvious that the Joker should never have been idolized, the film held up a mirror and it hit way too close to home. The ending is bold, it delivers the point and it’s perfectly in line with Arthur’s arc from film one. He’s not the Joker. He just used the Joker persona to act on his impulses, and now he has to face the real consequences. Turning it into a musical was a wonderful move by Todd Phillips. Todd Philips concebeu ao mundo uma sequência que muitos acreditavam que era desnecessária e um erro, mas ainda assim havia expectativa de que se no final do primeiro filme ele termina como algo maior, um símbolo de revolução em gotham, nesse segundo poderíamos ver o Coringa sendo esse líder revolucionário juntamente com a sua Arlequina, mas Todd pensou diferente e buscou trazer exatamente o contrário disso, e esse é um dos motivos de porquê esse filme foi tão odiado, por ser um filme totalmente Anti-Coringa, focado em descontruir tudo o que o primeiro fez, mostrar que Arthur não é um líder revolucionário, mas sim um homem deprimente, com disturbios mentais, que teve um dia ruim e transpareceu para Gotham o seu caos e sua violência reprimida, matando aqueles homens no metrô, inspirando que eles não deviam temer a elite e criar essa revolta, mas nesta sequência, isso é desconstruído à medida em que percebemos que os que idolatram o Coringa, não idolatram Arthur Fleck, idolatram aquilo que ele criou, aquela persona caótica que matou Murray Franklin na noite do dia 18 de novembro ao vivo na TV, e no momento chave do filme ele percebe, ele começa a enxergar que o Coringa traz morte por onde passa, atiça esse ódio nas pessoas, tanto de quem o apoia, tanto de quem não o apoia, e a partir dali, ele vai contra tudo aquilo que o Coringa representa, tudo aquilo que os fãs dele apoiam, desiste da imagem do Coringa, renuncia a identidade do Coringa, mas ali já era tarde demais, Arthur havia plantado a semente do caos em Gotham e não tinha como ser desfeito, Arthur é morto pela sua própria criação, por aquilo que ele criou para fugir da sua realidade, quando Arthur mostra quem realmente é ninguém liga, ninguém nunca se importou, as pessoas apenas queriam ter algo pra seguir, algo que as libertassem de si mesmas, ironicamente, o Coringa que nasceu dele mesmo o matou, não restando mais o homem por trás da máscara, apenas o Coringa.

The musical numbers carry genuine ambition even when they don't always fully land throughout. This remains a genuinely divisive but interesting artistic risk, confident enough in its own considerable unconventional ambition throughout. A sequel wasn't necessary and it seems as though the box office results proved that. I'm not upset that the sequel happened, but they waited a bit too long to make it. Probably would have faired better in 2022 or so... especially if they had released it a few months after The Batman . However, Hollywood tends to never do what we'd expect. That applies to Warners tenfold. I love bitching about their mishandling of DC in the past 10 years or so. WB deserves to fail, and DC should be in better hands. (End of tangent) Anywho, this Joker sequel is nowhere near as bad as many people made it out to be. I'd argue it's rather brilliant. We see the inner workings of Arthur's fantasies on full display. The tone is even bleaker than the first film; it's riddled with despondency, and oozes onto the viewers. I could quite literally feel the life force being sucked out of me. I swear I couldn't break out of my slump for hours afterward. There's something profound about the musical sequences. Every bit built up to a crescendo of sadness. When the world is so dire, cruel, and unjust – some people who were dealt a bad hand in life, turn into monsters who reflect the state of society. Joker is the persona and mirror image of our corrupt and inverted world. The weight of being the people's conduit for their frustrations in the world eventually broke Arthur, and he was no longer Joker. As he stated, "I can't do this anymore." To make matters extremely worse – Lee didn't truly love the man behind the mask. Only what he managed to stand for. The funny yet sad truth is that oftentimes people do this; they love an idea or aspect about somebody but if it crumbles, they abandon you. Joker 2 is a testament to abandonment. Arthur is the ultimate outcast. A misunderstood man, who knew nothing but trauma and pain most of his life. A mind that attempted to shelter itself from the harsh realities of human nature, and after all that he managed to stand for, during his brief moment in the sun – the world still swallowed him whole.

Shut up all of you. This movie, while definitely not as impactful as the first one, is straight genius 1. The idea of the Joker Arthur Fleck’s death at the end definitely shocked me, but its such a clever take on it. The Joker isnt one singular person, its an idea, a concept, a shared belief. So many people take roles playing the Joker because its not just one person theyre representing. They all have different takes on his quirks, his behaviour, his mental state because theyre taking this concept of the Joker and making it their own. And making this apart of the film’s themes had me gobsmacked 2. The lighting The lighting in both movies is incredible. Unfortunately, i began to conjure up this idea because of a tiktok, but it makes so much sense. Arthur is blue, Joker is yellow… together they make green. Lee is often dressed in yellow, pulling him into the fantasy of “the joker”. And when these different “sides” of him connect (or when he doesnt know which side to believe, the lighting is green. Its so cool and so clever. It’s subtle, but so intentional. 3. The singing Dancing has always been such a crucial idea attached to the Joker’s character—he loves music. Thus, it makes complete sense to make it part musical, especially when he’s in his delusional episodes where he’s imagining himself on a stage, being “the joker”. It can feel jarring at times, like it snaps you out of the plot sometimes, but I think thats the point. It’s supposed to shed some more insight into Arthur’s hurt and twisted mind. I can understand why some think it detracts from the film, but I personally don’t. I think it adds 4. Action movies Not all superhero/villian stories need to be straight up action. Now that is a waste of a film and such a incredibly complex character. Action and gore is straight up BORING if it doesn’t have proper reason or if it doesnt add anything to the movie. The Joker doesnt need action all the time in his origin story, and you think the movie does, you don’t understand the movie’s intention + the character AT ALL 5. CONNOR STORIE??! What are you doing here??

Co written by Scott Silver (The Mod Squad, 8 Mile, The Fighter, Joker, The Finest Hours)  and Todd Phillips and directed by Todd Phillips (Joker, Road Trip, Starsky & Hutch (2004), The Hangover, The Hangover Part II, The Hangover Part III, War Dogs, A Star is Born, Due Date), 'Joker: Folie à Deux' explores the genesis of an ideology born from the violence of a world fuelled by disdain. Phillips continues painting a viscerally dark, painful picture of a man seemingly dismantled by the machinery of law, order and social justice, yet reassembled by the flickering embers of love for a woman captivated by his public enigma. Although 'Joker: File à Deux' weaves musicality into the narrative, this film loses nothing when leading viewers through the protagonists inner workings, and with some excellent performances producing a memorable experience, this is a sequel to be embraced, not disregarded. In closing, 'Joker: Folie à Deux' rests comfortably beside its predecessor, and while a sad, and at times, harrowing portrayal of a truly "tortured" soul, this title will endure multiple, impactful rewatches, which says far more than the critics and naysayer’s who rejected and reviled it's message upon release.

It has finally happened, dear reader. We have stumbled upon a movie I may find irredeemable, and you're about to find out how bitchy-catty-gay-west-coast-elitist I can get. As a child in grade school, I'd get tested every year for the gifted and talented education program (or GATE). And every year, I'd stare at these sequences of interwoven pentagons and triangles and be asked to predict what came next. To my chagrin, I was never selected and was relegated as the most gifted among the average-intelligence kids. IMAGINE MY HORROR when I find out gate was being used to identify kids with prescience! I can predict the future! I'm Special!  (i can't and im not, i had an undiagnosed anxiety disorder and adhd). I bet Special Agent Harker was in Gate.... humpf. THE MOVIE: As an avid follower of true crime myself and an outlier fan of the horror genre, I fought hard to find value in this film.  Sadly, I drew blanks here. The writing was not something I'd classify as "good" or even "serviceable". In the spirit of fairness, I'd say I think there's a nugget of a good idea here. The scene where they're testing Agent Harker for telepathy was really well done and captured the eerie "government is after all of us" vibe that I think is particularly compelling. All the rest of it fell flat. The connective tissue between the Christian faith and the deal-with-the-devil plot never held water because the viewer was never given any insight into Harkin's mother's thought process. My understanding of the Christian faith is that they would resist satan, not get into business with him. And especially not to that level.  this felt more like a creepypasta that was given a budget and distribution. I guess in the end I'll allow Harker to be special in her way as I don't have the bandwidth to  deal with any of that mess. A footnote: I was very sleepy watching this, and I did need to rewind a few times to catch some dialogue.

J'aime beaucoup le jeu d'acteur de Maika Monroe (Lee) dans ce film. Elle campe à merveille ce personnage d'introvertie, constamment mal dans sa peau et épuisée par l'affaire. Dès les premières scènes on voit qu'elle ne se sent pas bien, et plus ça avance, plus ça empire. Le film ne lui donne jamais de vraie catharsis, ce que j'aurais bien aimé voir, mais je suppose que c'est par choix. (Bon, il y a eu le cri dans la voiture vers la fin, mais pas assez cathartique à mon goût vu tout ce que la pauvre a vécu !) Le meilleur acte reste selon moi le premier : mention spéciale à toute la scène où Lee rentre chez elle, particulièrement réussie, exemplaire en terme de tension. On a, de plus, le droit à une photo hyper léchée (la palette de couleurs du film, les ombres et les cadrages avec ces plans larges, vraiment un plaisir pour les yeux), une bande son qui fait bien le taf (même si peu mémorable), et une belle atmosphère. Le film ne cache pas ses influences, notamment du côté de Fincher, avec Seven et Zodiac , néanmoins ça ne le dessert pas à mon sens. Mais Cage cabotine . Et ça m'emmerde que ce soit le cas. Je sais pas, c'est peut-être moi, mais je ne trouve pas les scènes avec lui particulièrement intéressantes, la faute à des répliques peu inspirées et au manque d'idées de mise en scène lorsqu'il apparaît à l'écran. Pourtant, il y avait quelque chose à faire avec un Cage qui en fait des caisses, mais là y a aucune aura, le personnage ne dit rien ou ne fait rien qui n'ait été fait ailleurs en mieux, même le maquillage est assez bof. Sa performance est clairement plombée par l'incapacité du film à lui donner des répliques et des motivations qui soient suffisamment marquées (à part le "UNMAKE MEEE!" qui était chouette) et faisant un minimum froid dans le dos. C'est là où le film pêche à mon sens le plus : il peine à faire du personnage de Cage l'entité glauque et malsaine que le mystère mérite.

plot aside, but this is a pure aesthetic masterclass. Even if you find the narrative a bit mid, you cannot deny that Longlegs is an absolute art object. Osgood Perkins and DP Andrés Arochi crafted a visual nightmare that feels less like a standard horror movie and more like a meticulously curated, deeply unsettling painting. The way they weaponize the image composition is insane. Switching from those grainy, claustrophobic 4:3 35mm flashbacks to the ultra-wide 2.39:1 digital present creates this massive, yawning negative space. Arochi uses extreme wide-angle lenses even for close-ups, which slightly distorts the world and leaves so much empty air around Maika Monroe. The dread doesn't come from jumpscares but rather lives right there in the empty corners of the frame, waiting. I also loved the color palette. You're constantly trapped between the freezing, desaturated blues of the Oregon winters and the sickly, feverish ochre/orange tones leaking through the windows of the interior scenes. Then, the sudden, sharp slashes of devilish red just cut right through the monochrome sadness. It's visually rigid, perfectly symmetrical and deeply atmospheric. Even if the script didn't fully work for many, the sheer craftsmanship on display here is undeniable.

GENRE ET CONSTRUCTION HISTOIRE Le film est un mélange entre enquête et un peu d'horreur par la suite, c'est étrange. L'histoire est dévoilée petit à petit, mystère après mystère. MISE EN SCÈNE On est souvent ramené de force dans l'histoire grâce à la façon dont le film est filmé. Dans la grande majorité les personages sont tes projets de la caméra. Le film partagera par moment 2 temporalités, on les reconnaît avec les couleurs : Le présent sera les couleurs grise. Pour le passé, les couleur seront plus orange chaleureuse et/ou changement de résolution de caméra (Polaroid). Lorsque le film utilisera les couleurs chaleureuse, IRONIQUEMENT l'endroit sera tous l'inverse. Le film partagera donc des couleurs diamétralement opposées, tantôt chaleureuses, tantôt glaciales, même si la grosse majorité sera plutôt grisâtre. Petit reproche tout de même pour les plans qui sont majoritairement trop sombres (normal pour un thriller MAIS lorsqu'on ne voit rien du tout, c'est un peu dommage). THRILLER Le film est angoissant et nous tient en haleine constamment (mention spéciale aux génériques de début et de fin qui ont des musiques plutôt joyeuses, étonnant pour le type de film que l'on vient de voir juste avant, j'aime bien😅). JEU D'ACTEUR Les acteurs sont vraiment bon (Maika Monroe et Nicolas Cage). CONCLUSION Bref, le film dégage une ambiance spéciale et surtout UNIQUE, je le trouve VRAIMENT TRES TRES BIEN !!!!

Longlegs is still terrifying to me on a rewatch. The opening feels like some fever-dream nightmare I somehow never had as a kid: hazy, surreal, and deeply unsettling in a way that immediately gets under your skin. Maika Monroe devours every scene, completely disappearing into an emotionally exhausting performance that feels both vulnerable and haunted. She’s phenomenal here, and the role firmly cements her as one of modern horror’s great scream queens. And Nicolas Cage is simply unmatched. There’s something so grotesque and unnerving about his performance that even his presence alone feels like a threat. Longlegs’ mostly grounded and disturbingly plausible storytelling fills nearly the entire film. It unfolds like a grim procedural wrapped in a tightening nightmare, constantly feeding you fragments of a mystery without letting you see the full bloody picture. Every frame feels ominous. Every silence feels loaded. There’s this persistent sense that you’re witnessing something you were never meant to see. Then, when those final pieces finally click into place, the mystery reveals itself with a horrifying inevitability. It’s entirely engrossing, relentlessly foreboding, and tensely scary in a way that lingers, leaving me second glancing shadows in the corner. Even knowing exactly where it’s going, Longlegs still manages to make me feel like I’m watching something I shouldn’t be. And that’s a helluva feat. 🩸

Day 1 of surviving my bsf favorite movies @ruyaarchive… I understand what this movie is trying to say. I understand the biblical allegory, the symbolism of Mother Nature, creation, worship, humanity, destruction, the cycle of creation and destruction, and all of that. I genuinely do. But understanding what a movie is trying to communicate doesn’t mean I have to enjoy watching it. Because honestly, for most of this movie, all I could think was: why the fuck is this man incapable of respecting his wife’s boundaries? From the very beginning, Mother is uncomfortable with these people invading her home. This is their house. Her safe space. The place she has been rebuilding and caring for. Yet Him constantly welcomes more and more people inside because he enjoys being admired. He doesn’t care that she’s uncomfortable. He doesn’t care that her privacy is being invaded. He doesn’t care that the people he’s invited are destroying the very home she has worked so hard to create. And that was the most frustrating part of the entire movie for me. I didn’t see some mysterious, fascinating, all-powerful Creator. I saw an incredibly self-absorbed man who desperately needs to be worshipped and praised by everyone around him, to the point where he is willing to sacrifice the person closest to him for it. And then the movie just keeps escalating. The guests become increasingly obsessive. The worship becomes increasingly disturbing. The house turns into complete chaos. And somehow, through all of this, Him continues to let them in. At some point I genuinely felt like I was watching a cult form around this man. People aren’t simply admiring him anymore—they’re worshipping him. They’re willing to destroy everything around them for him. And Mother? She is the one who actually creates. She is the one who gives life. She is the one who builds and nurtures. Yet she is ultimately valued for what she can provide, not for who she is. Her existence is treated as something useful because she can create life, while her own needs and boundaries are repeatedly ignored. The most disturbing thing to me is that the people who worship Him don’t even truly care about what they destroy. They can adore him while simultaneously destroying the very thing that makes his creation possible. And he allows it because their love and worship matter more to him than protecting Mother. Which brings me to the ending, where I just sat there thinking: What the actual fuck? Mother gives everything. She is destroyed. The house is destroyed. The cycle ends in complete devastation. And Him? He survives. He takes what remains and starts again. So we’re essentially watching a cycle where Mother is repeatedly created, used, worshipped only for what she can give, destroyed by the people who claim to love the Creator, and then replaced by another Mother so the cycle can continue. I understand that this is supposed to represent something much larger. I understand the biblical parallels. I understand the commentary on humanity, religion, creation, environmental destruction, and the endless cycle of worship and destruction. I still fucking hated it. I spent the entire movie waiting for someone to simply tell these people to leave the house. 😭 Maybe the allegory is brilliant. Maybe the symbolism is layered and intentional. Maybe there are dozens of things I could analyze about this movie. But as an actual viewing experience? I was miserable. I didn’t feel scared. I didn’t feel emotionally connected. I felt increasingly irritated at a man who couldn’t respect his wife’s privacy, increasingly uncomfortable watching a group of people turn into a cult around him, and increasingly horrified by the realization that nobody seemed to care about Mother as a person. One & half stars. I understand you, mother!. I just don’t like you. 💀

Dans la catégorie des films que j’aurais jamais regardés de moi même mais que j’ai vus parce qu’ils passaient à la télé, Mother! c’est celui auquel je pense le plus. Je le prends comme un film d’auteur qui cherche à dire un truc de très vrai mais qui le fait par la recherche d’impact tellement dérangeant que ça dessert l’œuvre. Au fond, c’est l’histoire d’un écrivain qui voue sa vie à l’écriture de son livre, et qui une fois publié le regarde être disséqué, analysé, jugé par le public qui ne connaît pas la personne qui l’a écrit, seulement le produit fini. La mère qui donne naissance à son bébé, et qui invite des parfaits inconnus pour célébrer sa naissance, et les inconnus se mettent à fouiller les placards, à faire comme chez eux, et a un moment le bébé tombe par terre et les gens mangent le bébé - Stop. Y’a des trucs qu’on fait pas. On met pas en scène un bébé qui se fait dévorer par une foule de sauvages. Et pourtant, si j’en crois le film, je fais donc partie de ces gens qui piétinent sa création. Mais il y a une difference entre faire comprendre qu’on saccage sa création et montrer un nourrisson se faire déchiqueter par une foule sous les yeux de sa mère impuissante et de son père qui refuse d’agir Et à l’époque quand j’ai vu ça, ça m’a carrément énervé. Comment ça y’a un studio qui met en scène un truc comme ça et ça sort en salles et c’est acclamé par le public? On touche pas les bébés. Y’a des limites. Pour moi c’est de la branlette intellectuelle d’auteur. Si tu veux faire du sensationnel, fais confiance à ton public au lieu d’aller chercher dans un registre aussi malsain.

Aronofsky’s signature blend of terrifying, pretentious, and heavy symbolism gets me every time but this.... To give credit where it’s due, the allegories are sooo interesting, whether you view it as a critique of an artist's ego or a detailed allegory of the Bible (with the Husband as God, the guests as Adam and Eve making the crystal the forbidden fruit, the brothers' fight a Cain and Abel situation with the mark on the floor as Cain's mark). The frantic descent into chaos leading to the finale throws a harsh spotlight on societal collapse, throwing at thr audience brutal, inexplicable human crimes in rapid flashes without giving you a second to breathe. When it works, it’s dynamic and overwhelming. But all that madness in the final act couldn't rescue the fuuucking slow burn of the first half. The early narrative drags so much that it completely lost my interest. A brilliant concept wrapped in a disappointing viewing experience which is a shame cause I really had my hopes up..

Je trouve ça dommage de faire un huis clos pour y mettre tous les éléments de l'extérieur tels qu'ils sont. Par exemple une manif, la guerre, la police ? Dans une maison ? J'ai adoré la première partie, la tension est extrêmement forte, la mise en scène est vraiment plaisante, il y a un vrai jeu entre des plans très serrés et des plans en pdv subjectif plus larges. Ça donne une impression de voyeurisme, comme si la femme et la maison était la même personne (ce qui est le but). Ensuite il y a les premiers invités (la famille nucléaire), cette tension continue et en même temps des mystères se développent : qui sont ils ? Que se passe-t-il au sous sol ? Que signifie cette pierre ? Qu'écrit le mari ? C'est oppressant, on ne sait rien et tous les éléments sont stressants. À partir de ce moment là c'est très bien, les symboliques sont délicates, complètes et ça garde une forte puissance de propos. Personnellement j'y ai d'abord vu une idée féministe, la femme fait un travail monstrueux de rénovation pour que l'homme ait tout le buzz en écrivant (alors même qu'il écrit pas). Ensuite arrivent tout le reste de la famille, ça continue d'être stressant mais ça en devient ironique. C'est à dire qu'avant on savait que ça pouvait déraper puisqu'il y a avait un petit groupe d'intrus, mais là avec un groupe de 20 personnes, toutes différentes, la seule peur qui reste c'est la gêne qu'on ressent face à leurs comportements. Après que tout cela se calme, on revient sur du bon contenu : la relation dans le couple. Puis suite à la révélation de la grossesse et la fin de l'écriture, tout repars en couilles. Mais cette fois si c'est pire puisque plus rien n'a de symbolique. L'intérêt du début c'est surtout qu'il y a une symbolique cachée qui est la genèse de la bible. Mais passé cette étape là, on se lance dans une critique du christianisme d'une manière grossière. Pourquoi ne pas continuer le jeu de la symbolique ? Pourquoi faire des évènements aussi burlesques ? C'est vraiment de plus en plus grossier, tout ça pour avoir une critique très mid style "ah ouais la bible dit de tout partager, d'être gentil avec son prochain mais les gens ils sont pas gentils boubouuh 😣"  ou sinon une critique un peu incompréhensible qui est que Dieu ce flocko il veut trop la fame. Mouais à revoir. En plus le propos féministe que j'ai expliqué avant est bien estompé puisque ce n'est pas vraiment la femme qui charbonne (dans les 2 sens du terme) mais c'est Dieu qui crée Marie (la maison) comme hôte afin d'accueillir Jésus pendant qu'il écrit. C'est à dire qu'elle ne travaille pas vrm, c'est elle la maison et elle se prépare juste à son rôle premier : accoucher de l'autre pelo à l'auréole. Au global, le film avait un potentiel de fou, mais on ne sait pourquoi c'est passé du thriller horrifique à du comique.

Фильмы Даррена Аронофски надо чувствовать, а не смотреть. Они как голые провода заряженные чистыми эмоциями. В «мама!» они ещё и религиозно подкованные. Намёки на суть происходящего зрителю даются сразу же, в первые минуты. Здесь каждый элемент дома, не говоря о самом доме — метафора. Раковина — это ни что не иное, как закреплённый божий закон, а ебанутые гости – люди, и грехопадение Евы. I'm a big history buff, and this movie was painful both in historical context, and as a movie. I heard from some people that it was bad, and yeah, it is. I watched the directors cut, it was 3 1/2 hours of wasted time. The story is very inaccurate and focused too much on the least interesting things about Nepoleon's life, like parts of his relationship with his first wife Josephine, even when the battles happened and are shown, there's a time skip and don't get enough screen time. This movie completely omitted many battles, many events, and even many of the politics that Nepoleon took part in, like they omitted The Battle of the Nations, The Pininsular War, the fall of the Holy Roman Empire, which was a big deal at the time because the Holy Roman Empire had existed for a thousand years at that point. Both The Battle of the Nations and The Pininsular War also played a big role in Nepoleon's downfall, and both were some of the bloodiest events in the Nepoleonic Wars. If I go further with the historical inaccuracies, we'd be here all day, but it got so much wrong and even completely made things up. Despite the directors cut being 3 1/2 hours, it isn't enough to cover Nepoleon's life because of how much he did throughout his career as a soldier, general, consult, and emperor. On top of all that, this movie is boring,  like so boring, it made Nepoleon Bonaparte, one of the most interesting military generals in history, boring, that is an accomplishment. The effects were very good, the CGI, practical effects, the costumes were accurate to the time, the sets, the cinematography, and overall production quality was good. This movie cost about $200 million, and the production clearly shows. However the editing can at times be jarring, even the directors cut. The score was good, I really liked some of the tracks. Oh god, the acting was bad. Joaquin Phoenix was a horrible choice for Nepoleon, his acting didn't have the chops and he had some weird line deliveries. Everyone else was boring and dull, the only exception was Vanessa Kirby as Josephine, she looked and acted like she was trying, it wasn't much but she had the best proformance in the movie. In conclusion, Ridley Scott's Nepoleon is a god awful biopic, it doesn't cover everything about the titular historical figure, and what it does show is overshadowed by the inaccuracies and the fact that it's boring. The cherry on top was Ridley Scott's response to the criticisms from historians, he literally said and I quote "Were you there? No. So, shut the fuck up!" He wasn't there either, so what's he talking about? When French critics called the movie anti-french propaganda, which it kinda is, Scott said that the French hate themselves. What an asshole! If you are a history buff, don't watch this movie. 2/10

‘ France… Army… Joséphine .’ These are widely cited as the final words of Napoleon Bonaparte, encapsulating the three most important things that drove his 51 years of life. Ridley Scott’s 2023 Epic Historical Drama Napoleon feels like the culmination of two centuries of British propaganda; which reduces one of history’s most complex figures into a bumbling, pathetic character who’s only drive is his love for his wife to the point it comes off as a total mischaracterisation of the man. Despite my criticism of Napoleon’s characterisation Joaquin Phoenix’s performance is excellent and perfectly captures the character Scott intended to create. The portrayal of Napoleon as an insecure and emotionally immature man who lashes out at those around him and is only driven by having an heir to secure his imperial dynasty left me actively rooting against him at all times and sympathising with Joséphine. Vanessa Kirby’s performance of Joséphine rivals, if not overshadows that of her co-star. She brought a sense of warmth, struggle, and humanity to the screen. This makes Joséphine feel much more compelling than Napoleon and I found myself vividly enjoying her scenes; while having to suppress the fact the on-screen relationship’s historical accuracy is to be debated. Kirby’s performances was one of the only parts of the film I enjoyed as I felt it had decent emotional weight and focus compared to the other parts of the film. Scott’s attempt to encompass 22 years of the film’s namesakes’ life leads to many major moments in his military and political career are rushed through with little to no historical context or reduced to defining moments in the film created to impress and not inform. Moments such as the French Invasion of Egypt serve only to include notable monuments such as the Sphinx and the Giza Pyramids. Additionally, Napoleon’s eventual desertion of the campaign in order to attempt to seize the opportunity to gain power in the shadow of the French Revolution is instead used to further bolster the romance plot that plagues the film. Conflicts such as The Siege of Toulon , The Battle of the Three Emperors , and The Battle of Waterloo excel in being large eye-catching set-pieces with even those who are not interested in military history will find captivating. However, those who are fascinated in military history; myself included will find ourselves yelling at Scott to include what made those battles so important to the magnitude they are still studied today. I applaud Scott for attempting to create a film on one of history’s most fascinating and decisive figures; however the film fails to fulfil what an audience wishes to see in a two hour feature on Napoleon. Viewers wish to see the story of how an outsider from the Corsican gentry who was dismissed due to prejudice, uses the chaos France was in to become an Emperor. The Napoleonic Wars should have been the focal point of this film, however Scott creates an historical epic that is more focused on being a romance with hints of grandiose set-pieces with the intent to appeal to a large audience. Ultimately this leads to a film that appeals to no-one and is instead carried by the historical name associated to it and the performances of Phoenix and Kirby . As many grievances as I have with this film I would still recommend it if you are able to ignore the mischaracterisations and historical gaps. I understand that general audience may be able to ignore these due to not having enough knowledge on the time period or simply not caring, however as someone who’s always been captivated by the time period I simply could not.

critique, Napoléon – Director’s Cut (2023, Ridley Scott) J’avais découvert Napoléon au cinéma en 2023, et honnêtement, je n’avais pas tellement apprécié le moment. J’étais ressorti assez déçu, avec le sentiment que Ridley Scott passait complètement à côté de son sujet. Je viens enfin de voir la Director’s Cut, et je dois reconnaître une chose : je la trouve meilleure que la version sortie en salles. Les scènes supplémentaires apportent enfin un peu plus de respiration au récit, mais surtout elles développent davantage la relation entre Napoléon et Joséphine. C’est probablement ce qui manquait le plus dans la version cinéma. On comprend mieux leur dépendance affective, leurs tensions et la manière dont leur histoire influence le reste du film. Malgré tout, je reste persuadé que ces ajouts ne suffisent pas à transformer le film en grande fresque historique. Mon principal problème reste le même : je n’ai jamais réussi à m’attacher à ce Napoléon. Joaquin Phoenix est un immense acteur, mais ici je trouve que son interprétation ne fonctionne pas totalement sur moi. Le personnage paraît souvent distant, presque passif, et j’ai parfois eu du mal à retrouver le stratège, le chef militaire ou l’homme politique qui a profondément marqué l’histoire de la France et de l’Europe. Politiquement, c’est aussi ce qui me laisse sur ma faim. Napoléon est une figure complexe, à la fois héritier de la Révolution française et fondateur d’un Empire autoritaire. Le film effleure ces contradictions sans vraiment les explorer. J’aurais aimé qu’il s’intéresse davantage à son héritage politique, à ses réformes, à son rapport au pouvoir ou encore à l’impact immense de ses guerres sur l’Europe. Au final, beaucoup de ces enjeux restent en arrière-plan. Je trouve aussi que le récit manque parfois d’équilibre. Certaines batailles sont expédiées alors qu’elles auraient mérité davantage de temps, tandis que d’autres passages s’étirent sans toujours apporter quelque chose au personnage. En revanche, il y a des choses que je ne peux pas lui enlever. Les costumes sont magnifiques. Et surtout, j’ai beaucoup aimé la photographie. C’est assez paradoxal parce que je n’aime pas particulièrement le film, mais certaines images sont vraiment superbes. Ridley Scott conserve ce talent pour composer des cadres élégants et donner une véritable ampleur à certaines séquences. Visuellement, il y a plusieurs plans qui resteront gravés dans ma mémoire. Les batailles possèdent également une vraie puissance de mise en scène. Même si elles ne sont pas toutes développées comme je l’aurais souhaité, Scott reste un immense réalisateur lorsqu’il s’agit de filmer le chaos, les mouvements de troupes et la violence de la guerre. Au final, cette Director’s Cut améliore clairement le film. Mais pour moi, elle ne règle pas ses principaux problèmes. Je continue de penser que Napoléon est l’un des films les plus faibles de la filmographie de Ridley Scott. Quand on connaît ce qu’il est capable de faire avec Alien, Blade Runner, Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Kingdom of Heaven ou The Last Duel, j’attendais beaucoup plus d’un personnage aussi fascinant que Napoléon Bonaparte. Je suis heureux d’avoir revu cette nouvelle version. Mais je ne pense pas que j’y reviendrai une troisième fois.

I had sensed that I likely wouldn't be watching Napoleon twice, so I decided to watch the Director's Cut straightaway. What can I say, three stars just would have felt too generous for how completely uninvested I was after the first two hours and before Waterloo came. There is certainly merit in seeing this production staged at such an epic scale, and quite a bit of Napoleon is striking to look at in terms of what's on screen, but not in terms of how it looks. Overall, everything here just looks too clean, too digital and intangible for the battle images to move me in any meaningful way, even though they deserve to be praised from the position of technical accomplishment. By the dialogue and Joaquín Phoenix's performance you can certainly tell that Scott's film is openly mocking Napoleon the man, and making you question how a whole country could have been so enamored with him, but looking at today's tyrants and others in history they somehow always manage to sway considerable masses for their greedy and cruel purposes. Begrudgingly, the film also shows Napoleon's military successes, but still finds ways to show him either weak in them or cruel like in the battle of Austerlitz, and certainly singling out the losses his side sustained as ever increasing and ever more disastrous. A really exhausting watch and a far cry from Scott's own similar output.

Abba sung about Waterloo in under 3 minutes whereas, for Ridley Scott, his tale of that particular battle, and the life of Napoleon, is closer to 3 hours with an even longer, supposedly 4-hour version coming to AppleTV+. Enough with the facetiousness, Scott’s film of this titanic (but, ironically, pint-sized) figure unfortunately isn’t quite the definite article. Cramming the life of the Emperor, his myriad battles and the ongoing political circumstances, both in France and Europe at the time, into one film was always going to incur a long and unwieldy runtime. Scott does pretty well to keep proceedings clear and moving forward briskly but, because of this approach, a few spots of the history get muddled and you’re left with an interesting and broad overview, albeit one lacking true depth. Scott’s focus is more on the man himself and it works as a character study. On equal footing with the fighting is Napoleon’s relationship with his wife Josephine and it is in these scenes that we get our true glimpse into the man and the true brilliance of Joaquin Phoenix’s portrayal (excellent, as always, and bound to be awards-nominated.) Phoenix tows the line perfectly between showing the stern stoicism of the commander and the vulnerable insecurities of the man. It’s an unbiased and honest portrayal and it’s interesting to speculate and delve beyond just a timeline of events. However, despite attempts to lighten the mood at points with a spot of humour or an original take on the period drama concept, it suffers a little from fustiness and those bright spots only serve to show what this film potentially could have been under different circumstances. It feels like it can’t quite decide what to be and this scattershot nature lets it down. Those more speculative, intimate scenes of Napoleon and Josephine therefore stand as the film’s heart, beyond the wider historical context and scenes of war. It’s also, sadly, very difficult to follow what’s going on in those battle sequences. Great credit must go to all involved for staging such grand scenes but, unfortunately, all bar one suffer from some sort of debilitating factor: too dark, too fast in the edit, too confusing. The Battle of Austerlitz is the one true triumph here and is a sequence to place up there with cinematic large-scale battle scenes. It’s another example where the film shows what it could have been, only fuelling the frustration further. Sadly, Napoleon is just a teensy bit stale and a teensy bit boring. Too unforgivable adjectives in a film of this scale and with a figure of this much interest and importance at its centre (and also from the director of Gladiator.) Hopefully, the longer cut will prove to be the one but a little Swedish-pop, Midas-touch originality is needed here. ⭐️⭐️⭐️

I'm truly torn and fustrated with this. It's somewhere 3-3.5 for me and very hard to decide. It's fitting Ridley Scott did this, like so many of his films in between his masterpieces it leaves audiences divided. There are parts I think that are great. The production design is great, the winter ice lake battle scene was really good and the best part of the film, Phoenix & Kirby aren't bad together and have their moments, and it never is incoherent. It makes perfect sense and is easy enough to follow along with a deep dive into his relationship with his wife which is arguably the biggest aspect the film focuses on even more so than his battle victories, governing, childhood, relationship with his kids, friends, allies, or return from exile.  He's a fasinating figure and the film does keep an interest for me up until the final 40 minutes or so. The problem here is this probably needs anoth hour or hour thirty minutes to truly encompass everything needed for one of histories most fasinating figures. But also I feel it needs to scale back the focus on his wife. It's literally half the damn film. There needs to be more about his governance, his allies, going into the inner workings of his battle style, his friends and allies and making them as interesting as him. Acting isn't bad thanks to Kirby & Phoenix having their moments. But everyone else just blends in and is forgettable and at times it's too emotioness and wooden. The direction isn't bad either but i reminds me of Spielberg's post A.I. style which I'm not the biggest fan of. Editing and pacing is alright and everything else is half decent. The middle of the movie is the best part. But where this drops the ball for me is how they handled his invasion of Russia and his return to Waterloo. It just felt like it didn't even really dive into the inner working or politics of what happened to lead up to it. If you don't know anything about Napoleon or the Wars of this time I truly can't see how someone would understand what was happening or why. But they choose to continue to focus on his wife and the new wife which really made me baffled. It just doesn't provide enough background or clear motivation on the why's and also showing how he made France into the the envy of the world. And it just made me lose interest and it felt repetitive in a sense too because I knew what was coming. More battles and more drama with the wife which is exactly what I got for the fourth or fifth time. Again nothing is broken here and it does a serviceable enough job I guess. But it leaves a lot to be deisred I think summaries my thoughts here. I think unless your a die ahrd fan of Kirby/Phoenix there really isn't much here. Most could skip this sadly and not miss much. Waterloo (1970) is way better for learning about a specfic event and irnocially showing Bonaparte. And the definititve gold standard remains the 1927 Silent Era Masterpeice.

The year is 2023, and two new biopics have been released about some of the most destructive men known to our world. One of those films is named Oppenheimer, and it clocks in at roughly three hours and one minute. The other film is named Napoleon, and it clocks in at roughly two hours and thirty-eight minutes. Now ask yourself: Which film is longer? If you answered Oppenheimer, then you haven’t watched both films. After a rewatch the film decidedly conveys its points a lot better, and it’s a decent biopic that separates the man from the myth. That being said, decent is the word for it, because half of the time either Joaquin’s acting is meandering and aimless or Napoleon’s mood is being written to abruptly shift contradictory to how he should be acting. The one highlight of Napoleon’s writing is it at least shows the slow degradation of the main character’s mannerisms as they get overtaken by ambition. For anyone wondering, yes I have watched Oppenheimer before and yes at some point I will rewatch it and rate it accordingly. Anyways that’s it; no need to drag this review out in the way Napoleon drags out its runtime.

"Escribes con más cariño a tu perro que a mí. ¿Tengo yo que ladrar para ganarme tu afecto?" — Napoleón a Josefina. Desde hace tiempo siento una profunda admiración por Napoleón Bonaparte . No tanto por el conquistador, sino por el hombre. Siempre he sentido una extraña conexión con esa faceta suya que buscaba desesperadamente ser amado. Podrá sonar absurdo, pero mientras más leo sobre él, más entiendo que detrás del uniforme había alguien tan brillante como vulnerable. La película, con todos sus defectos —que son demasiados—, logra mostrar precisamente eso. No al estratega que puso de rodillas a media Europa, sino al hombre que parecía invencible en el campo de batalla y completamente indefenso frente al amor. Esa contradicción fue, para mí, lo más interesante del filme. Le sumo media estrella únicamente por esa representación. Porque, aunque la ejecución sea irregular, consiguió recordarme que Napoleón conquistó reinos enteros, pero jamás logró conquistar aquello que más deseaba. Hay algo profundamente trágico en morir siendo una leyenda y seguir sintiendo que el amor siempre te quedó demasiado lejos. Ahora bien, como película histórica deja mucho que desear. Hay errores difíciles de ignorar: el supuesto bombardeo a las pirámides de Guiza, la forma en que muestran a Napoleón liderando cargas de caballería o el encuentro cara a cara con Wellington, algo que nunca ocurrió. Aun así, me quedo con esa imagen del emperador derrotado no por un ejército, sino por sus propias carencias emocionales. Paradójicamente, esa fue la batalla que nunca pudo ganar. P.D Algo curioso. Si la numerología popular está en lo cierto, Napoleón tenía un Camino de Vida 1 y un número 6 . Yo , exactamente al revés: Camino de Vida 6 y número 1 . Como si fuéramos un espejo. Él parecía destinado a conquistar el mundo mientras anhelaba ser amado; yo sueño primero con amar y, luego con dejar también una huella en el mundo. No sé si la numerología significa algo. Pero admito que la coincidencia es brutal.

Seppur la director's cut non scomodi mai realmente la parola noia, ci troviamo di fronte ad una visione deliberatamente impegnativa, anche grazie ad una struttura narrativa ambiziosa che nel dilungarsi in alcune (spettacolari) sequenze sembra arrivare ai titoli di coda visibilmente stanca. -La mancanza di una soddisfacente lettura militare del protagonista. Un'assenza arginata molto bene dalla bravura del suo interprete (che di transalpino, nonostante la premessa fatta, ha veramente poco) ma che cede inevitabilmente di fronte ad una chiave di lettura maggiormente analitica: se sul fronte psicologico la figura di Napoleone Bonaparte, immersa nell'insicurezza e arroganza, è ben leggibile, dispiace non poter dire lo stesso del personaggio quando vediamo quest'ultimo muovere i propri passi nel contesto bellico. Puoi farmelo britannico, egiziano, senegalese, quello che vuoi, ma in un biopic di tale portata sarebbe necessario assaporare l'idea del genio militare e politico che la storia nel tempo ha più volte descritto. Sennò si rischia di restituire quasi più un'immagine di casualità piuttosto che di conquista dovuta al merito nel scalare le posizioni di potere dell'impero francese. Un peccato, visto il comparto scenico e tecnico che abbraccia l'intera pellicola e che rende a dir poco memorabili le battaglie combattute da Napoleone. Ed è per questo che mi sembrerebbe un torto dare meno di tre stelle e mezzo. Alors j’ai revu Napoléon de Ridley Scott, et je dois avouer que, malgré ce que j’avais dit dans ma précédente review, le film n’est pas catastrophique, loin de là. En fait, il est assez incompris, et au final pas si mal. En fait, l’erreur que j’avais commise à été de voir le film en salle, et non de voir la director’s cut, qui rajoute une cinquantaine de minutes au film. Si bien que ces problèmes de montage, de transitions, de lien entre les scènes, sont réglés en voyant la version finale. Ici, malgré quelques défauts qui persistent, tout est assez bien rythmé, bien filmé, si on évite les scènes de batailles qui sont le vrai point noir du film. Mais la ou mon point de vue a changé d’un vissionnage à un autre, c’est quand j’ai compris ce que Ridley Scott voulait faire avec ce film, et donc ce qu’il raconte réellement. En fait, Napoléon n’est pas un film sur la vision des français ou des anglais sur l’empereur, ni sur la vision réelle, historique, de ce personnages si ambigu et particulier, ni même de la vision de Scott sur Napoléon. En fait, ce film parle de la vision de Napoléon sur lui-meme, et ça, c’est très fort. Napoléon, dans le film, se raconte tout le temps, invente des histoire et s’invente des vies pour se prouver à lui même qu’il appartient à l’histoire, alors qu’il n’est au final qu’un grain de poussière dans l’existence. J’ai compris ça quand je me suis intéressé aux tableaux propagandistes de Jaques Louis David, qui sont repris dans le film. Mais, et c’est ce qui est intéressant, c’est que Scott montre l’avant et l’après du tableau, pour deconstruire le mythe et prouver à tout le monde la fraude qu’est Napoléon, qui a essayer de s’imiscer dans une histoire dont il n’aurait jamais du faire partie. Bref, une proposition très intéressante et très bien mise en scène, qui m’à fait évoluer et modifier mon appréciation de ce film. On est loin du niveau de Gance, mais ça reste un bon film, malgré quelques défauts.

Obsession | A Wildly Inventive Horror Spin on Love, Possession, and Personal Space Curry Barker’s Obsession takes a familiar romcom fantasy an awkward guy wishing his crush would love him back, and twists it into something deeply unsettling, darkly funny, and surprisingly sharp. Built on clever writing rather than scale, the film reimagines obsessive affection through grounded horror, where every scene, detail, and escalation serves a purpose. The storytelling constantly flips ordinary gestures of love into disturbing scenarios, creating tension without relying on conventional horror tricks. Michael Johnston convincingly captures the insecurity and panic of the protagonist, while Inde Navarrette is phenomenal in a role that shifts from warmth to terrifying emotional volatility. With inventive visual storytelling, precise atmosphere-building, and a script that finds horror in the collapse of emotional boundaries, Obsession feels refreshingly original. Bottom Line: A creative and confident approach that has been successfully delivered as a smart, unsettling and darkly hilarious horror flick.

Some people love Rollercoasters, or jumping out of planes for a rush or adrenaline; I watch horror films because I hate heights. The last three horror films I watched were Caveat, Oddity and Together; all three made me feel uncomfortable and creeped out. Together more than anything, I started watching it cuddling with my boyfriend, but by the end of the film, I didn't want him anywhere near me for at least 48 hours. But horror films lately have been missing something, something that I longed for. None of them scared me; all of them had a predictable plot, predictable characters, and predictable scares. Until my friend and I saw Obsession at the cinema on Wednesday. I could tell no one in the viewing was going to take it seriously, but we had hope from it being the first 18+ rated horror in a while. It was terrifying. The plot was amazing, and the acting was award-worthy, especially Inde Navarrette; she was absolutely brilliant, and I hope this projects her into more roles. I would love to see her in more horror films for sure. The scares and psychological turmoil were insaneee (in a good way), and you could never predict what was coming next. Even if you've seen clips or audio online and assume you know what it's about, you really don't. They all take you by surprise. I do believe it is more psychological for women to watch, so I suggest if you're a woman, go with your bestie/girlfriend, but if you have a good man, go with him, and he should understand why it's so insane. Nolan set out to make a film about the atomic bomb, working inside a framework that all but guarantees certain choices: the female characters stay thin, and the American establishment — despite building and deploying the most destructive weapon ever used — ends up framed as the aggrieved party. Three hours built around one event, and we never see that event’s human cost. No Hiroshima, no Nagasaki. What we get is Trinity shot with dread, and a hallucination of burned bodies mid-celebration — real craft, but it’s guilt filtered through Oppenheimer’s psychology, not the people who actually died. “We only see what we’re shown” isn’t a defence, it’s the problem — every war film would look blameless in its own cinema by that logic. This isn’t unique to Nolan either; American war films (Iraq, Korea, Vietnam) keep casting the US as victim in wars it started, the same way some WWII films let American soldiers alone liberate the camps and quietly cut the Soviets out. To be fair, the film’s real subject is different: Oppenheimer devoured by the establishment that used him. That’s honest, documented history. But it’s a different casualty from the nation, and the two blur together too easily. Even on its own terms, the pacing fails its nerve. The security hearing eats up the runtime; the actual moral reckoning gets compressed into mood and sound design instead of a position the film is willing to hold. A question this big — was this justified? — can’t be answered by half. Beautiful score, exceptional editing, a flawless cast. None of it amounts to an argument.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Oppenheimer is a technically extraordinary film that ultimately keeps its most serious question at arm's length. It flirts with self-criticism through the psychology of one man while leaving the nation's — and the weapon's — actual victims outside the frame entirely. Craft of this level deserves an equally serious answer to the question it raises, not an atmosphere of unease standing in for one.
