Another one for psych class. This is one of the worst films I've ever seen. The performances are mediocre, with DiCaprio's likely being the worst. The writing is incredibly juvenile, even with the plausible theory that the majority of the dialogue is filtered through the guy's warped mind. The film doesn't even look good or have an interesting aesthetic. The twist falls apart because it requires you to empathize with DiCaprio's character in the beginning, which I did not. Now, to the big problems. This film's portrayal of the mentally ill is disgusting. I understand that the facility is specifically meant to house people who've committed a violent crime, but the film was arguably still irresponsible in its perpetuation of the stereotype that all people with mental illness are scary, violent, completely irrational, and are deserving of no empathy whatsoever. There is no mention of the specific diagnosis that any patient, let alone the main character, has, which makes it impossible to understand the accuracy of the portrayals. This film was made too recently to still exhibit such an under-researched and outdated parody of what a real group of underprivileged people is like. Let's move on to another problem, the film's portrayal of both the Holocaust and the implications of Project MKUltra during the Cold War. These were both serious tragedies that I feel were not handled with appropriate sensitivity and were rather just half-baked elements seemingly thrown in for added novelty. With this film exhibiting these two themes in addition to its portrayal of extreme psychosis, there are too many things being explored and none of them are done properly. The main conspiracy is clearly supposed to be MKUltra, something that really did victimize psychiatric patients during the Cold War, and yet in the movie's cannon, it's confirmed to not be happening. I don't think this film is intentionally trying to say that MKUltra didn't happen, but it's a very strange and poorly thought-out choice that is completely at odds with the setting. This movie clearly did not have anything to say about any of the incredibly serious topics it includes, and thus has no comprehensive or unique thesis. It's an offensive, confused mess that frankly has no merit as a piece of art.

By the time poor Teddy (Leo DiCaprio) is told what we’re suppose to think, most wise guys have already solved the Big Mystery, thereafter becoming a Pile of Wet Clothes. Some of the acting is top-notch mad dog, principally Ted Levine ( Silence of the Lambs ), Patricia Clarkson ( The Green Mile ) and Jackie Earle Haley ( Breaking Away ) but Ben Kingsley and Max Von Sidow are committing petty larceny here. Marty, you’re a friend of ours and this hurts me but, hey . . . it’s business, not personal.

Le film se laisse agréablement suivre mais une fois la promenade terminée le point de vue où on arrive est décevant. Parce que c'est le même paysage qu'on voit depuis le début. Les ficelles qui sous-tendent l'ensemble sont trop visibles. En plus d'être visibles, elles sont trop serrées, elles contraignent la lecture d'un film qui a pourtant conscience de la force de l'ambiguïté émotionnelle qu'il pourrait produire chez le spectateur. La première mixture de réel et d'hallucination après un moment d'homogénéité apparente et intrigante finit par se soumettre aux lois physiques et se décante jusqu'à exposer clairement chacun de ses composants. La seconde mixture de monstruosité et d'humanité est juste insipide. Le crime qui est présenté n'est pas le crime d'un fou par perversion mais celui d'un fou de douleur. Le film justifie sa violence après avoir fait défendre la thèse d'une violence intraseque à l'humanité a l'un de ses personnages. Sauf qu'on ne le voit pas et l'ensemble échou à jeter le trouble dans lequel le regard de la femme qui pose son doigt sur sa bouche promettait de nous plonger.

"You have to let her go" "I can't!" "Then you'll never get off this island..." Enjoyed this more on rewatch, I was better able to appreciate how the mood of the island is developed, with the soundscape being particularly impressive, with original score, licensed music, and classical music all coming together really well. Weather is also used particularly effectively to make the island feel isolating and uncomfortable; there's something about heavy rain at night that makes me really uncomfortable and I love the way that is used in this film. The star segment here is Ward C, feeling like walking into a nightmare within an already dreadful environment - it feels like those segments in Silent Hill when you go from normal world to Otherworld, everything just gets so suddenly worse and terrifying with no end in sight. Despite this being a psychological thriller with heavy emphasis on its ending, it still does very little for me compared to the build up on the island (which I really enjoyed) and other films in the ending-heavy "genre" (Memento, Prestige, Fight Club, Total Recall, etc.). It just never feels like the reveals that happen meaningfully impact or re-contextualize the earlier scenes of the film. Of course the context does literally change but it doesn't really change the emotional impacts, at least for me

I personally think it is a psychedelic paranoid masterpiece that is a wonderful examination of the brain, trauma, and crisis of identity. All themes which Scorsese has used before for his movies. The film is creepy, beautifully shot, extremely well acted, and leaves you in suspense until the end. While it may not break new ground the way Taxi Driver, Mean Streets, and Goodfellas do, it is one of the most beautifully shot films I’ve ever seen, and I find it quite emotionally impactful. So why do you think Shutter Island hasn’t aged as well as his other works? Even Scorsese himself said he regrets being attached to it, and I think that’s wrong because it shows just how versatile the guy is. He can direct any genre to perfection.

Shutter Island is a psychological thriller film directed by Martin Scorsese and released in 2010. The movie stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Teddy Daniels, a U.S. Marshal who travels to a mysterious island with his partner, Chuck Aule, to investigate the disappearance of a patient from a psychiatric hospital. As Teddy investigates, strange events begin to happen, and he starts to question the hospital, the doctors, and even his own memories. The story becomes more mysterious and confusing as Teddy discovers that the island is hiding a dark secret. One of the best things about Shutter Island is its atmosphere. The dark setting, suspenseful music, and confusing events create a feeling of fear and mystery. Leonardo DiCaprio also gives a very strong performance as Teddy. The ending is one of the most surprising parts of the movie because it changes the way we understand the whole story. Overall, Shutter Island is an interesting and suspenseful movie that makes the audience think about reality, memory, and guilt. I would recommend it to people who enjoy psychological mystery films.

Let me begin this review by stating that "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" is an incredibly anticipated film, building upon the immense success of its predecessor, "Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse." However, I find myself deeply perturbed by one particular aspect of the film, an aspect that I simply cannot ignore—the shirt worn by the main character, Miles Morales. In the teaser for "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" introduced in "Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse," we were introduced to a visually stunning and utterly captivating Miles Morales, sporting a sleek black shirt, impeccably matching his stylish outfit. That image became etched into the minds of fans, sparking excitement for the sequel. Imagine my horror when I sat down in the theater, eagerly awaiting the film, only to discover that the shirt on Miles Morales did not match the outfit he wore in the teaser! It's as if a cosmic catastrophe had occurred, resulting in an outrageous wardrobe malfunction. The inconsistency is jarring and undermines the entire film-watching experience. How am I supposed to focus on the plot, the animation, or any other redeeming qualities of the movie when such a blatant contradiction stares me in the face? It's almost as if the filmmakers deliberately wanted to sabotage the enthusiasm of the audience. Now, some might argue that the color of a shirt is a minor detail that shouldn't detract from the overall enjoyment of the film. But let me remind you that it's these seemingly insignificant details that can make or break a cinematic experience. It's these nuances that contribute to the cohesiveness and believability of a fictional world. Furthermore, as a dedicated fan, I invest time and emotional energy into these characters. I expect consistency and continuity in their portrayal. Is it too much to ask for the same shirt Miles Morales wore in the teaser to be faithfully reproduced in the actual film? Apparently, it is. This grievous oversight makes me question the commitment of the filmmakers to their own creation. Did they forget what Miles Morales looked like in their own teaser? Did they think we wouldn't notice? Or, even worse, did they intentionally toy with our expectations, mocking our investment in the franchise? "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" may have its merits, but this shirt debacle overshadows any potential greatness it might possess. I implore the filmmakers to rectify this egregious error in future releases, providing fans with the consistency they deserve. Until then, I cannot in good conscience recommend this film to anyone who values attention to detail and artistic integrity.

Au moins aussi acclamé à sa sortie, ce second opus a le mérite d'être divertissant, mais à l'inverse du premier qui était une montée en puissance sur tous les plans, plus les enjeux multiversels prennent du poids, et moins il convainc. Spider-Man : Across the Spider-Verse est bien meilleur lorsqu'il se concentre sur l'intime, même s'il demeure à ce sujet très classique. D'ailleurs, j'ai bien cru que je le préférerais à en juger par son introduction, plus aboutie que celle du précédent, mais la suite m'a déçu. Il est très frustrant de regarder une œuvre qui s'étend sur autant de temps pour ne pas avoir le droit à une vraie fin, fut-elle ouverte. Sur le plan visuel, on est dans la continuité, avec un peu plus de variété issue de l'exploration du multivers. Toutefois, je regrette l'inclusion de live action qui me sort totalement du film. Ponctuellement, certains plans continuent de me gêner par leur façon de trancher avec d'autres mais je dois dire que cela a moins été le cas qu'auparavant. C'est peut-être une question d'habitude, mais je pense surtout que celui-ci est techniquement plus abouti. Quoi que je sois critique, cela reste à des années lumières des bouses super-heroïques que nous sert Marvel à son habitude. Le moment est plaisant mais hormis toute la séquence où Gwen et Miles se retrouvent puis papotent en se collant sur les bâtiments — qui est superbe — je ne sais pas si j'en retiendrais grand chose sur le long terme. En fait, je me rends bien compte que toutes mes scènes préférées sont dans le premier acte. Après, comme c'est une expérience formelle, je suppose qu'il a l'avantage de bien se revoir. La sortie de la suite sera l'occassion de le réévaluer.

50 Across the Spider-Verse is a film that promises everything and delivers... some of it. The multiverse concept, inherently thrilling on paper, remains the franchise's greatest asset. The sheer variety of Spider-People is a joy to behold. The film does not disappoint in its ambition. Yet for all its formal brilliance, Across the Spider-Verse stumbles badly in its handling of tone, and nowhere is this more evident than in its villain. His early appearances are played purely for laughs, and while the film eventually attempts to pivot toward genuine menace, the damage is already done. He becomes a symbol of the film's broader comedic excess: the relentless quipping and meta-references that undercut every moment of tension. By the time The Spot transforms into a world-ending threat, we cannot take him seriously because the film never taught us how. The film's incessant needle drops compound the problem, each licensed track feeling less like organic storytelling and more like a calculated monetization strategy. The soundtrack is curated not to serve the narrative but to populate Spotify playlists, a transparent effort to generate revenue streams beyond the box office. This commercial calculation extends beyond the music. The cliffhanger ending? It is difficult not to view it as a deliberate fragmentation, a way to stretch a single story across multiple releases and maximize returns. I do not envy anyone given the task of following Into the Spider-Verse. That film singularly injected so much new life and artistic innovation into an IP that was beginning to get stagnant. It took the time and consideration to acknowledge the foundation and rich history baked into the character of Spider-Man and gave it a loving sendoff before turning to a brand new chapter. Regrettably, Across the Spider-Verse feels like one step forward, two steps back. If there’s one thing my journey through the MCU has taught me, it’s that the multiverse fucking sucks. And I understand that’s a contentious position to hold against a series called “the Spider-Verse,” but hear me out. Into the Spider-Verse used the concept in the most effective way: minimalistic. The multiverse purely acted as the inciting incident for Miles’ story, much like time travel in the first Terminator movie. Yes, you had cheeky references to established Spider-Man iterations, their tropes and standing in pop culture, but ultimately it was a measuring stick to hold up to Miles’ own hero’s journey. A narrative device showing how the character inspired this new hero, much like he has countless others in our own world. Comparatively, Across the Spider-Verse becomes overindulgent, languishing in its multiverse setting and using it as an excuse to showcase the less popular Spider-Man content, or ride the coattails of the more popular content. Remember Andrew Garfield Spider-Man? Look, there he is! And Toby McGuire! Look, this multiversal Spider-Man agency knows about what Dr. Strange was doing! And the dimension-hopping films? He talks to Mrs. Chen, from our hit Venom film series! The SPUM-C is alive and well. And look, there’s Donald Glover as Prowler! Like he was gonna be in the MCU! There’s also an attempt to make each dimension extremely unique, which unfortunately comes across like a more obnoxious attempt to copy the uniqueness of Into the Spider-Verse’s art style, and the clashing artstyles tend to make it look like a big, muddled mess. Really, with a concept like the multiverse, the last thing you want to do is get technical. Where Deadpool & Wolverine had the braindead concept of an anchor being, Across the Spider-Verse presents the “canon events.” (Which felt like such a dumb attempt at meta, I threw up in my mouth a little bit.) Rather than the shared trauma being a bonding point between the different iterations of Spider-Man, it’s now an absolute event necessary for their journey, whose disruption could lead to the disintegration of their reality. Delving more into the multiverse also takes the wind out of the sails for Miles’ own character arc. Spoilers: we find out that he wasn’t meant to become Spider-Man, as the spider that bit him came from another dimension. So he is an anomaly, and his arc is that, even though it wasn’t his destiny…he is still Spider-Man. Because he chooses to be. Which isn’t nothing , but feels like a much more hollow echo of his arc in the first film. My own cynicism and hangups notwithstanding, Across the Spider-Verse is a fine film. A far fall from its predecessor, but if you’ve been missing the characters and world, it does feel like a welcome return. It’s overbloated, and its standing as a definitive “part one” further lessens its value on its own, but it’s ultimately competent enough.

Oh, what a tangled web [they] weave…with this cacophony of story threads. The highly anticipated sequel to the Best Animated Feature Oscar-winning Into the Spider-verse opens this week, but unfortunately, it suffers from a bad case of sequelitis brought on by a gluttonous consumption of excess. Spider-man: Across the Spider-verse works in title only–and all too well, as it were. The title says it all, and that is precisely what audiences get in this comic philhar-tragic symphony in the key of overindulgence. Across the Spider-verse is what happens when a story idea doesn’t pass the elevator pitch litmus test (wherein an idea can be explained sufficiently enough in three-minutes or less). Quite simply, there is such a proliferation of story webs that there is virtually no plot–there is certainly no resolution before the (and this isn’t a spoiler) cliffhanger ending. Story webs lead into story webs that leads into even more story webs. Suffice it to say, it’s as if writers and producers took every incarnation of Spider-man comic series, threw them into a blender, and served the concoction o audiences. Unless you are read up on decades of Spider-man comics, you will be hard-pressed to follow any storyline. Perhaps the better expression of a collision of Spider-verses would have been in a television series that could have explores a different thread of comics each season. Clearly, Sony took the extremely positive reception of the first one, focussed on recurring praises, and amplified those to the nth degree. Never mind that more than the visual expression of the story, plotting is crucial to structure, pacing, and coherency. The animators and artists are showcasing brilliance in animated filmmaking, but the clear evidence of screenwriting is nowhere to be found. Without a well-defined central character, a well-defined external goal, and a well-defined character of opposition between the central character and the goal, there is no plot–merely a sequence of loosely connected scenes or fragments of ideas. A fever dream, if you will. While Across the Spider-verse suffers narratively, it certainly excels in the art of animation. The stylistic animation and editing is outstanding! Much like with the first movie, this one takes the emotive detail found in a single frame of a comic book (or graphic novel) and combines that approach with hand-drawn inspired motion picture animation. There are certainly problems with the story (or stories, as it were), but Sony Pictures Animation has demonstrably shown commitment to the boundless imagination of and capabilities of animation. Across the Spider-verse, in how it is expressed in this movie, can only happen within the world of animation. In no way could this movie be expressed in a live-action way. Perhaps the writers were asleep at the wheel, but the animators gave each universe of Spider-man characters its own color palate and animation style. Make sure to watch Across the Spider-verse in a premium format at your cinema, because the strength in this animated movie has little to do with the story as much as it does the stylistic animation. When a film, animated or live action, strikes a balance between style and substance, it can be enjoyed on the big or small screen without detracting from the storytelling; but when the movie struggles narratively but excels in form, then experiencing it on the big screen is the best approach.

Man, I really wanted to like this movie more, I loved the first movie. And make no mistake, the first two thirds of this sequel were everything I'd hoped for, gorgeous animation and art style as expected, an interesting plot with a hilarious villain who unexpectedly goes through development into a more dangerous, malevolent foe. And the sheer amount of non-intrusive cameos when they arrive at Spider City, and Oscar Isaac's performance! But with the third act everything just... falls apart. All sense of momentum stops dead in its tracks. The bad guy fails to fulfill the menace and character growth he'd promised, because the movie never actually gets that far. What should be an exciting climax instead wastes time with useless drama and a misdirection that doesn't actually add anything to plot or character, but rather just bloats out the runtime to a level Eternals would have been proud of. And then.... "To Be Continued...... in Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse!" Uh.... okay. Sure. Cut out the third act of a film, the most important part of any movie where all the tension and drama pays off, and then relegate to a sequel which will likely not arrive for years to come. And instead of an alternate climax, just fill out the last 40 minutes with mind-numbingly boring and unsatisfactory screentime. Man, what a disappointment.

I wasn’t impressed when I saw this in theaters 3 years ago. I decided to give these movies a rewatch, to see if my opinion has changed. And I did like the first one more than I thought I did. As for this one? Unfortunately, still not very impressed. The weakest part of the first movie was the entire multiverse plot line. That idea has been taken and beaten to death over the years. In 2018, it was still relatively new. 2023 and now? I’ve lost all interest at this point. And this film took the multiverse concept and pushed it to the max. It did all the things that I’m already tired of. Relentless cameos and jumping across different universes at will. It’s a shame that such an original looking movie falls short in the original plot or concept department. And I’m a little iffy on the villain situation for this one. With the first, Kingpin was great because he wasn’t one note. He actually had a solid motivation for what he was trying to do. In this, it seems like Spot is the main villain, but really it’s Miguel. It’s mind boggling to me how any of the Spidermen could follow Miguel when he’s so clearly wrong. And even if he’s doing these things for the right reason, he’s a total dick about it. That’s another thing, if all these Spidermen are gathered in the same place trying to stop anomalies, who the hell is saving people in their own universes? It doesn’t make a whole lot of sense and just makes it all seem too gimmicky. This movie also lacks some of the charm that the first one had. It’s very dark and depressing, in comparison to the first which was fun and exciting. And the animation doesn’t seem as refined. I know that some of the different universes have different designs, but it’s an overall drop off from the first in quality. Now, it’s not all bad. I still enjoy the creativity and visuals overall. It’s not as good as the previous, but still better than most animated films visually. The story is also better than the first. It’s more complex and ambitious, despite being entwined in multiverse slop. And the voice acting is still top notch. But this film is also quite long. Especially when considering that it’s only half of a story. I feel like anything over 2 hours is just a little too long for any animated film. Even the higher quality ones like this series. Well, at least now I know. I do actually like the first Spiderverse movie, and this one isn’t bad, it’s just not as good as the first. It relies a little too much on the multiverse tropes while also losing some of the first’s luster. Final Verdict: 6.5/10

Я, лично, ничего тут не нашёл из «лучшей истории о Человеке-пауке», но она очень хорошая. Конечно, как гику такой фильм прикольно посмотреть, но явно не по мне. Да, тут много отсылок на пауков, много гик-намёков. По визуалу скажу: ЭТО САМЫЙ разнообразный СДВГ-контент вообще за всю Марвел. Первые 30 минут смотреть просто невозможно. ЭТОТ ФИЛЬМ ПРОСТО ОСТАНОВИТЬСЯ НЕ МОЖЕТ В ПОСТОЯННОЙ СМЕНЕ КАДРОВ И РИСОВКИ. Вырвиглазно порой было смотреть начало, но потом втягиваешься и фильм становится действительно хорошей личной историей Майлза Моралеса. Неплохо получается совмещать фильм-аттракцион, цветастое месиво для подростков, СДВГ-контент и неплохой сюжет о спасении и сохранении человечности. По сюжету в целом неплохо. Драматургия отличная и зашкаливает. Интересно, что всё таки фильм намного лучше развивает историю Мультивселенной, чем сами Marvel Studios. У Майлза, которому вообще 15 лет, начинаются самые тяжёлые годы в его жизни. Типичный подростковый период: с родителями плохо, друзей нет, в школе проблемы. После «Через Вселенных» у него ни осталось ни любимой девушки, ни друзей-пауков. Только обычная жизнь: родители, школа, несколько друзей и жизнь Человека-паука. Тем временем, у Гвен-паука тоже очень хорошая, даже местами чуть лучше, чем у Майлза, драматургическая сюжетная арка. Отлично раскрываются отношения Гвен Стейси и её отца, который искренне уверен, что Женщина-паук, которой является Гвен, убила местную версию Питера Паркера. В итоге, оказывается, что существует огромная мультвселенная, в которой вселенные пауков связаны Паутиной Вселенных. Мигель и его общество пауков очень хотят «защищать канон». И в момент жесточайшей битвы, она ссориться с отцом, который узнал её личность, и убегает вместе с другими версиями Человека-паука, в частности с Мигелем (чуть другой версией Человека-паука 2099). Интересно, кстати, сложилась химия отношений Майлза и Гвен. Им действительно веришь. Они выглядят, как хорошая пара-подростков. А ведь им действительно по 15 и 16-17 лет обоим. И когда наступает момент, очень больно они расстаются. Позже оказывается, что Мигель, пытаясь сохранять общие черты сюжета Пауков, хочет допустить смерть отца Майлза, который вот-вот стал капитаном. Типо якобы у Паука должны умирать всегда: Гвен Стейси, друг-капитан полиции и дядя Бэн. Ну, какой-то бред. В целом фильм хороший. Хоть и масштабно противоречит всем версиям Мультивселенной КВМ или «Человека-паука» 1994 года. Конечно, возможно, в этом и прикол, что Мигель врёт, удерживая собственное сообщество, как самопровозглашенную территорию, чтобы не пересекаться с Мадам-Паутиной из «Человека-паука» (1994) или УВИ из сериала «Локи» и типо это раскроется в третьей и финальной части. Например, чета никто не приходил в Киновселенную Марвел исправлять канон, лишь потому-что там не умирал дядя Бэн или не появлялась Гвен Стейси. Или никто не приходил во вселенную Тоби Магуайра, лишь потому-что его Гвен Стейси не умерла и её отец, капитан полиции, тоже не умер. Вот сюжетные противоречия, надеюсь в третьей части на этом они вывезут и всё свяжут отлично.

If Into the Spider-Verse felt like a comic book flipped at 24 frames per second, significant stretches of this one felt like it was flipped at 48. The animation is absolutely breathtaking, and the juggling act of all these characters, dimensions, and styles is remarkable, but the film’s constant need to stimulate becomes overstimulating: there’s always music, movement, and something happening in the background, rarely giving you room to breathe. The "Achilles' heel" of the multiverse concept is partly that there’s simply too much going on, and this movie occasionally falls into its own trap. The best parts are when it slows down. The Spot is introduced in an interesting way, but never really gets the one-on-one dynamic with Spider-Man you want from a central villain, partly because the emotional anchor is spread across so many characters that there’s nowhere obvious to attach yourself. It’s a double-edged sword: the concept is strong and the execution is often remarkable, but the emotional center is spread too thin. Still, the set pieces and animation are incredible, and the new dimensions it opens up are exciting. The ending leaves plenty on the table for the next chapter, and I’m excited to see where it goes. It’s still a very good animated film, but I prefer the first one, which somehow managed to balance all of this perfectly.

Across the Spider-verse es una colosal pieza de animación digital que no sólo es capaz de entender la idiosincrasia de todos sus personajes, si no que logra plasmarla en cada uno de sus increíbles universos e imágenes. Al mismo tiempo, teje de nuevo las reglas de un espacio-tiempo cambiante (siendo plenamente consciente del potencial del mismo) para poder brindar infinidad de nuevas e imaginativas set-pieces. Su ambición desmedida tiene doble filo: la mayor escala se traduce en una cantidad ingente de situaciones vibrantes, ideas asombrosas o cameos sorprendentes, pero también termina provocando una sobresaturación epiléptica que puede abrumar al espectador demasiado pronto. A pesar de ello, sus viñetas en movimiento parece que cobran vida frente a nuestros ojos, atrapandonos en sus redes. Un titánico trabajo visual, el diseño sonoro (acompañado de la pegajosa banda sonora firmada por Metro Boomin) y un tratamiento argumental fragmentado que reposa sobre el ABC del imaginario del hombre (no tan hombre) araña, hacen de ella un viaje imprescindible para todos los amantes del cómic.

Como su predecesora, obra maestra de la animación automática. No impacta igual que la primera, pero ya sabemos con las cartas que jugamos y aún así sorprende muchísimo. Una trama mucho más adulta, unos personajes mucho más ricos.

Cinq ans déjà qu'est sorti Spider-Man : New Generation (paye ton titre français concocté par des vieux) et qu'il a révolutionné le médium outre-Atlantique. Non content d'avoir extirpé l'animation US du film destiné aux plus jeunes et influencé plusieurs productions de studios différents par son style si particulier (Les Mitchell contre les machines, Le Chat Potté 2, Ninja Turtles : Teenage Years), le film a également ouvert la manne du multivers, subséquemment récupéré par Marvel (Spider-Man : No Way Home, Doctor Strange & the Multiverse of Madness) et transcendé par d'autres (Everything Everwhere All At Once). Maintenant que la nouveauté n'est plus de mise, comment l'inévitable suite allait-elle pouvoir continuer à innover? Dès les premières secondes, alors que la musique enfle sur une succession de logos qui glitchent, la sauce monte, comme un condensé de la hype à ne pas décevoir, et la séquence d'ouverture, magistrale, vient non pas simplement rassurer mais carrément subjuguer par sa réponse. Dès son introduction donc, Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse (paye ton titre original destiné à provoquer la confusion avec le premier film) ose tout. Il ose changer de protagoniste, il ose ressasser certaines choses mais en les détaillant, mais surtout, il ose pousser les potards du pop-art à fond. La première fois, des personnages issus d'univers différents intervenaient dans celui du héros et pouvaient arborer un dessin de manga ou bien de cartoon. Cette fois-ci, c'est nous qui basculons dans différents univers et ce sont par conséquent les décors qui se colorent de façons diverses, qui adoptent des styles variés, - et l’œuvre tout entière qui se fait plus expressionniste que jamais. Ainsi Gwen Stacy évolue-t-elle dans un monde d'aquarelle où les couleurs changent selon ses émotions, et où l'on croirait se balader dans une case de Bill Sienkewicz, avant d'affronter un Vautour tout droit échappé d'un croquis de Leonard de Vinci. Ces premières minutes ont provoqué un véritable coup de foudre. Je me suis dit "je suis en train de tomber amoureux de ce film". Spider-Man : Into the Spider-verse a marché pour que Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse puisse courir. Et putain, comment il court. Il court comme un enculé. Chaque univers a été conçu pour donner l'impression d'avoir été dessiné par un artiste différent. Rien d'étonnant vu qu'en BD, les dessinateurs se succèdent et réinterprètent les personnages à leur guise, qui plus est s'il s'agit de spin-offs ou d'univers alternatifs, mais au-delà des clins d'oeil qui reprennent délibérément à l'identique le dessin de tel comic book ou de telle série animée, l'équipe du film se permet d'aller encore plus loin. Le meilleur exemple n'est autre que le personnage de Spider-Punk, qui reprend l'esthétique du mouvement, du moins l'image que l'on s'en fait dans l'inconscient collectif, et qui incarne à merveille l'entreprise dans son ensemble : un patchwork rebelle, où le crayonné côtoie la texture 3D. Outre la valeur ajoutée cosmétique déjà enivrante de cette pluralité, réunie à l'écran dans une même œuvre, ce parti-pris illustre à lui seul l'approche de Phil Lord et Chris Miller, de retour au scénario et à la production, sur le fond. L'ouvrage n'est pas uniquement d'une densité formelle écrasante, il s'avère tout aussi riche d'un point de vue narratif, exploitant encore davantage que son prédécesseur la métatextualité pour tisser son histoire. Si le premier film s'amusait de l'inéluctable origin story commune à tous ses personnages, ce deuxième volet surenchérit en explorant les dynamiques familiales des différents protagonistes, précisément dans ce qu'elles ont d'identiques, pour semblablement remettre en question le trope en soi et la nécessité de souffrance et du sacrifice inscrit dans le code génétique de ces archétypes. Par son récit, le film se soulève contre le "canon", terme littéralement utilisé dans le texte ("canevas" dans les sous-titres), pour évoquer la possibilité de réfuter la fatalité. Que ce soit visuellement ou narrativement, le film entend de briser tous les moules. La suite, intitulée Spider-Man : Beyond the Spider-verse (oui ils cherchent la merde) et prévue pour le 29 mars 2024, apportera sans doute la réponse et c'est d'ailleurs mon seul regret face à ce film qui prend peut-être un peu trop son temps pour poser ses enjeux (même si c'était sans doute indispensable pour ancrer émotionnellement ce terreau théorique) : il s'agit encore une fois d'un film incomplet sans sa deuxième partie. Il y a cliffhanger et cliffhanger quoi. Faites des trilogies mais bouclez vos histoires, que chaque film puisse tenir indépendamment. Néanmoins, ce petit bémol ne saurait entamer l'incroyable expérience qu'est Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse. Régulièrement inventif, impressionnant dans l'action, toujours touchant, et résolument punk.

De startede karrieren på YouTube, ergo må de være indbegrebet af ungdom og kreativitet. Jeg har ikke det fjerneste imod, at man har franchisen for øje fra idéstadiet, men når den franchise, der søsættes, er 100 % genkendelig og ikke byder på et eneste lille my af egen-tænkning, så keder jeg mig altså ihjel.

Achei um filme interessante, mas a princípio fiquei com a sensação de que ele era um pouco raso. Eu estava esperando que algumas coisas fossem mais aprofundadas e, quando terminou, ainda senti que faltava alguma coisa. Mas é um daqueles filmes que continuam na cabeça depois dos créditos. Quanto mais eu pensava, mais percebia as coisas que ele deixa nas entrelinhas. Me chamou atenção como a mão funciona quase como uma metáfora para o vicio. Depois que os personagens experimentam aquele contato, eles passam a querer repetir a experiência cada vez mais, ignorando as possíveis consequências. Não parece ser só um filme sobre espíritos, mas também sobre dependência, impulsividade e a dificuldade de parar quando algo já tomou conta de você. Mia acaba sendo a maior prova disso. Carregando o luto pela mãe, ela se agarra à ilusão de que ainda pode falar com ela, mesmo quando fica evidente que aquilo não é realmente sua mãe. Também achei interessante como o filme trabalha os personagens. Apesar de serem um grupo de amigos, cada um mantém sua individualidade. A Mia, por exemplo, demonstra um carinho pelo Riley durante parte da história, mas, quando surge a possibilidade de conseguir algo que ela queria, ela acaba deixando esse cuidado de lado. No geral, achei uma produção bem feita, com uma boa construção dos personagens e uma atmosfera que funciona muito bem. Não foi um filme que me conquistou de imediato, mas definitivamente me fez pensar depois que terminou.

Considerando sucessos recentes de terror e seus impactos verdadeiros no cinema, como Midsommar, Obsession e A Hora do Mal, três títulos que gosto e aprecio o trabalho de direção, Fale Comigo possuía um aspecto semelhante, talvez pela boa propaganda que sempre tive de alguns veículos da informação que sigo. Adolescentes burros se reúnem para brincar com o que não se deve, usando uma mão decepada como portal pro outro mundo. Aí acontece uma merda e a partir daí, o filme começa a andar em círculos e atirar para todos os lados, quase gritando "me escuta aqui! Eu tenho metáforas pra fazer!" Enquanto não aproveita pra desenvolver de verdade, nada. É uma visão criativa limitada, com uma direção que eu não achei nada demais, e que na minha opinião, precisava de outro segmento e uma interpretação mais simples (talvez até momentânea) para agradar. No entanto, é preciso salientar que esse filme seria sim muito funcional se seu texto fosse mais sincero consigo mesmo, e não uma máquina aleatória de escrever subtramas. O primeiro terço do filme é muito legal e promissor em apresentar uma história simples, no qual o terror adolescente iria valer o seu tempo, mas ao longo do meio e do final, após acontecer o acidente principal na trama, ele se perde em tantas mensagens e o desenvolvimento chato do passado da protagonista. Os personagens são rasos, alguns em atuações bem fraquinhas e em dilemas que você simplesmente não acredita que essa besteirada propõe a discutir. É muito chato acompanhar essa situação dos protagonistas onde nada acontece e eles são poucos punidos pelos problemas que causaram a partir de uma brincadeira errada. Os relacionamentos entre os personagens são somente tristes de acompanhar, e a "tensão romântica", numa tentativa de colocar mais um arco a se desenvolver, é falha e uma das piores coisas do filme A parte gráfica, do body horror, é bem executada, porém me parece jogada na trama apenas para causar impacto. No geral, eu simplesmente não gostei do filme e talvez eu só tenha achado bem bobo e desrespeitoso, pelo tamanho da discussão e mensagem que estavam ali retratando. Esquecível

Um terror da Oceania que foca no abuso da tecnologia ganha espaço no streaming e  no boca boca da Austrália, ganhando ainda mais visibilidade por ter sido distribuída pela A24. Danny e Michael Phillipou dirigem e escrevem a obra sendo a primeira da dupla de irmãos. È evidente que Talk to Me teve como principal influencia a onda da incerteza do que a Tecnologia poderia ocasionar no pós anos 2000, visto em Future Days, ExistenZ e em Pulse (KAIRO) de Kyioshi Kurosawa. A abordagem do  filme ornamenta o titulo da obra, O Fale Comigo, cria a critica ao digital, ao não sentir e o ao não conversar, uma destituição de uma característica humana, mas puxada para uma visão do horror. A obra, influenciada por uma critica a tecnologia, sustenta a ideia do que passou para uma batalha da personagem principal, onde com insônia, as telas do celular viram uma espécie de refugio. Os irmãos Philipou, tomam cuidado para não escancarar a significância do filme, seja na forma poética ou simbológica, aproveitando bem o espaço real, fora do digital. As câmeras dos celulares se  comportam como seres transportadores da alegria, ao mesmo tempo, que os que tem a ferramenta da alegria nas suas mãos, almas vazias e loucas por atenção se mostram, e ai, Talk to Me começa. A obra, se difere da abordagem mais direta do terror ocidental, dando espaço para uma visão mais destoante, essa mesma diferença se comporta de forma fenomenal, mas ai, entra a abordagem da historia, onde a formula da distoancia entre o real e o virtual perde cada vez mais espaço para uma visão mais pé no chão e convencional. Pouco se salva da abordagem de terror desse filme, onde parece mais um filme de terror convencional, tendo como ponto altos, os ótimos ângulos de câmera. A personagem que e o centro da historia, se mete em um buraco sem escapatória, não em forma de ser o que deve ser, mas cansativo. Talk to Me dos irmãos Philipou é  uma carta escrita em papel de ouro, mas extremamente mal escrita com letras iguais, onde a cada paragrafo, não alcança lugar nenhum para querer ser lida.

Talk to Me tem uma premissa muito boa. A ideia de uma mão misteriosa que permite conversar com espíritos é criativa e encaixa muito bem no contexto de um grupo de adolescentes que transforma aquilo em uma brincadeira de festa. O filme também tenta construir um lado mais emocional ao explorar o trauma da Mia após a morte da mãe por suicídio e como isso influencia suas escolhas. O problema é que, para mim, essa parte da história simplesmente não funciona como deveria. Todo o conflito envolvendo o Riley, as consequências de ele usar a mão e a forma como a família passa a culpar a protagonista nunca conseguiu me envolver, então o peso dramático que o roteiro tenta criar acaba se perdendo. As atuações também não ajudam muito. A Sophie Wilde entrega uma boa performance como Mia e consegue carregar boa parte do filme nas costas, mas o restante do elenco passa uma sensação de ser apenas competente, sem interpretações que realmente se destaquem. Mesmo com algumas cenas de horror bem feitas e uma atmosfera desconfortável em certos momentos, fiquei com a impressão de que a execução ficou bem abaixo do potencial da ideia. Em compensação, a maquiagem merece muito destaque. Os ferimentos, as possessões e todo o visual dos espíritos são muito bem feitos e ajudam bastante na imersão, sendo facilmente um dos pontos altos do filme. Apesar disso, o final é, sem dúvida, a melhor parte. A conclusão amarra muito bem a trajetória da Mia e as regras da própria maldição. Ver a protagonista assumindo o lugar de um dos espíritos e sendo invocada por outras pessoas fecha o ciclo de uma forma muito inteligente e dá um novo significado a tudo o que aconteceu antes. É um desfecho forte e memorável, que quase faz o filme terminar melhor do que foi durante boa parte da sua duração. Ainda assim, no geral, Talk to Me acabou sendo uma experiência apenas mediana para mim.

Talk to Me propose un concept de possession particulièrement original grâce à cette mystérieuse main embaumée. J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé l’idée de voir des adolescents transformer une expérience aussi dangereuse en simple jeu, allant même jusqu’à se filmer. Honnêtement, j’ai trouvé cette idée très crédible : si un tel objet existait, il y a de fortes chances que ce soit exactement ce qui arriverait. Le film mise davantage sur le malaise que sur une accumulation de jump scares. Les scènes d’horreur sont brutales, dérangeantes et ponctuées d’un peu de body horror particulièrement efficace, même si elles ne sont finalement pas si nombreuses. Derrière son apparence de film d’épouvante, Talk to Me est avant tout un drame sur le deuil, la solitude et la dépendance. J’ai toutefois trouvé que la première moitié tournait un peu en rond. Le scénario tarde à véritablement décoller et le rythme manque d’équilibre avant que les enjeux prennent enfin de l’ampleur. Les personnages secondaires sont également peu développés, ce qui fait qu’on s’attache rarement à eux. Malgré ces défauts, Talk to Me demeure un film d’horreur original, moderne et efficace qui renouvelle intelligemment le cinéma de possession.

Talk to Me é um daqueles raros filmes de terror que compreende que o género não precisa de escolher entre a substância e o entretenimento. Pode ser profundamente alegórico sem deixar de ser genuinamente assustador. Pode falar sobre luto, dependência e autodestruição sem sacrificar a tensão em nome da mensagem. E é precisamente esse equilíbrio que faz do filme uma das obras mais marcantes do terror contemporâneo. À primeira vista, a sua premissa não parece particularmente inovadora. A possessão enquanto metáfora para o vício, a procura desesperada por uma fuga ao sofrimento e a sedução exercida por forças que prometem alívio imediato são temas que o cinema de terror tem explorado há décadas. No entanto, Talk to Me nunca depende da originalidade da ideia, depende da excelência da sua execução. Os irmãos Philippou demonstram uma confiança invulgar na realização, construindo uma atmosfera opressiva onde cada movimento de câmara, cada corte e cada silêncio contribuem para uma crescente sensação de inevitabilidade. O terror não nasce apenas daquilo que vemos, mas sobretudo da certeza de que a tragédia já começou muito antes de as personagens se aperceberem disso. O maior triunfo do filme reside na forma como recusa transformar a alegoria no seu principal espetáculo. Nos últimos anos, o chamado "elevated horror" tornou-se tão obcecado pelas suas leituras simbólicas que, muitas vezes, se esqueceu de provocar medo. Filmes excessivamente preocupados em explicar o trauma acabam frequentemente por neutralizar aquilo que torna o terror tão poderoso, a irracionalidade, a ansiedade e o desconhecido. Talk to Me faz exatamente o contrário. Primeiro assusta. Só depois convida à interpretação. A metáfora nunca sufoca a experiência, emerge naturalmente dela. A mão funciona como um objeto profundamente simbólico. Não representa apenas o contacto com os mortos, mas também a sedução de qualquer mecanismo de evasão que ofereça prazer imediato à custa da própria destruição. É impossível não estabelecer um paralelo com a dependência, a primeira experiência surge como uma curiosidade, transforma-se rapidamente num ritual coletivo e termina por consumir completamente quem já não consegue distinguir o controlo da ilusão de controlo. O filme evita qualquer moralismo simplista, preferindo mostrar como o sofrimento emocional cria terreno fértil para esse tipo de dependência. Grande parte da força dramática deve-se à extraordinária interpretação de Sophie Wilde. A sua performance nunca procura o exagero característico do cinema de possessão, pelo contrário, assenta numa vulnerabilidade constante que torna a deterioração psicológica da personagem devastadoramente convincente. Wilde consegue transmitir medo, culpa, isolamento, desespero e alienação com uma subtileza impressionante. Mesmo nos momentos mais extremos, nunca sentimos que estamos perante uma personagem, mas perante alguém que perdeu progressivamente a capacidade de distinguir a realidade daquilo que deseja desesperadamente acreditar. Também merece destaque a maturidade visual do filme. A fotografia utiliza uma paleta aparentemente banal para criar um universo onde o sobrenatural invade lentamente a normalidade quotidiana. Os efeitos práticos são utilizados com enorme inteligência, nunca como mero espetáculo grotesco, mas como extensões físicas do sofrimento psicológico das personagens. O design sonoro, por sua vez, torna-se quase uma personagem invisível, amplificando a tensão através de silêncios desconfortáveis e de uma presença constante que parece contaminar todos os espaços. Talvez o aspeto mais admirável seja a forma como os Philippou compreendem a essência do terror. O medo nunca é tratado como uma recompensa momentânea entre cenas de exposição, é uma atmosfera permanente. O filme recusa a estrutura previsível do susto fácil e opta por uma ansiedade lenta, quase insuportável, onde o espectador sente que cada decisão aproxima inevitavelmente as personagens da sua destruição. Infelizmente, existe hoje uma tendência para reduzir qualquer filme de terror que aborde o luto ou o trauma a uma simples tentativa de imitar Hereditary. Essa leitura ignora décadas de história do género. Muito antes disso, obras como Don't Look Now, The Changeling, Pet Sematary, The Orphanage ou The Descent já utilizavam o sobrenatural para explorar o peso da perda. O terror sempre foi uma linguagem privilegiada para falar do sofrimento humano. A diferença está na forma como cada filme escolhe fazê-lo. E Talk to Me escolhe fazê-lo através do medo. Medo genuíno. Daquele que não desaparece quando as luzes da sala se acendem. Daquele que permanece porque compreendemos que os verdadeiros demónios do filme nunca foram apenas os espíritos invocados, mas a facilidade com que o vazio emocional nos leva a abrir a porta a qualquer coisa que prometa preenchê-lo. Poucos filmes recentes conseguiram equilibrar de forma tão elegante o horror visceral, a tragédia íntima e a sofisticação formal. Sem reinventar completamente o género, Talk to Me demonstra que o terror continua a ser um dos meios mais poderosos para explorar aquilo que existe de mais frágil na condição humana. É um filme que assusta primeiro, pensa depois e permanece muito tempo connosco depois dos créditos terminarem.

El Padrino no es una película: es un tratado audiovisual sobre la inevitabilidad del poder, la herencia y la corrupción moral disfrazado de cine de gánsteres. Coppola toma el sueño americano, lo estrangula con una corbata italiana y lo convierte en una tragedia shakespeariana donde la familia funciona simultáneamente como refugio y condena. Lo verdaderamente fascinante no es la violencia, sino la burocracia con la que se ejerce. Michael Corleone no desciende al crimen por ambición, sino por la lógica casi determinista de un sistema donde la ética termina subordinada a la sangre. Cada decisión parece una tesis sobre cómo el poder deja de ser una herramienta para convertirse en una identidad. La fotografía de Gordon Willis, conocida con toda justicia como "el Príncipe de las Tinieblas", no ilumina a los personajes: los juzga. Las sombras no son una elección estética, sino una declaración filosófica de que toda autoridad nace parcialmente oculta. Y Nino Rota compone una partitura que suena menos a música y más a un lamento histórico por una familia condenada desde el primer brindis. Decir que El Padrino es "una película de mafiosos" es como decir que La Odisea trata sobre un hombre que vuelve a casa. Es una reducción casi ofensiva. Lo que Coppola construye es un mito moderno donde el capitalismo, el honor y la violencia dialogan hasta volverse indistinguibles. Obra maestra. No porque sea perfecta, sino porque redefine el lenguaje con el que el cine habla sobre el poder.

Man sollte keine Angst davor haben, Klassiker der Filmgeschichte zu kritisieren, bloß, weil dieser von der Masse gefeiert wird. The Godfather ist so ein Beispiel. Man kann nachvollziehen, wieso er ein großes Publikum erreicht: Der Plot ist gefällig erzählt , die Figuren sind schlicht und die Bildsprache eingängig. Wir verstehen sofort, was Sache ist. Copolla lässt kaum Raum für Ambivalentes, auch Politisches hält er hier vollkommen raus. Dabei kann gerade das Mafia-Genre rasant über die Entstehung von Kapital erzählen, doch das geschieht hier nur randständig. Stattdessen verschafft man dem Publikum Zugang zum Film durch die nervende Betonung von Familienwerten – ja, The Godfather ist ein durch und durch konservativer Film. Die Schwermütigkeit und die Länge des Films ist dabei nicht mit einer anspruchsvollen Kost zu verwechseln. Im Gegenteil kann man es sich immer ganz warm und gemütlich machen, wenn Don Vito Corleone vor dem Bildschirm läuft: Hier wird zwar geschossen und gemordet, aber immerhin ist hier das patriarchale Familienmodell noch intakt. An einem Scoresese-Gangster-Film, geschweige denn an einem Coppola, kommt dieser nicht ran.

He was definitely decent in this tho, and was far better than in the other films I have watched him star in. His ending was really cool as-well, and makes me a bit more excited for part2, where he is the ‘Godfather’ or whatever. I can see why people rate this five stars, but I just don’t think that three long dragged hours of pure talk can cut it for me. I did really like some of the performances, which made some memorable characters, yet I wouldn’t say I felt deeply connected with any, but maybe I wasn’t supposed to based on the genre of film. I don’t know it just felt like the middle 10 minutes of a sopranos episode, which is compared to three straight hours in this. In the sopranos there’s only really 5-10 minutes of pure dialogue, which is also compensated by Tony, however this pretty much starred an actor I am not very fond of, who speaks like you can’t hear him, and genuinely feels like ur sat down for 5 hours listening to a mumbling bafoon. I can call this movie decent, but I wouldn’t say it goes further than 3 stars. A product of its time. So many of the characters were so surface level for a fucking 3 hour long movie! I've unironically seen better character building over the course of 40 minute CW serials. I didn't find even Al Pacino that interesting/endearing, let alone any of the female characters. Don Corleone was the most interesting and complex to me, and I liked him - but unlike Tony Soprano, they didn't care to explore the moral implications and repercussions of his lifestyle. The people we see them kill are Bad and Evil and one-not and he Loves His Children and is Tough But Fair. The pacing was weird - I couldn't tell what the final act was leading up to, and then apparently it was the assassination of some randoms we've had 2 minutes of prior screentime of and who I couldn't feel the symbolic weight of anyways, by anonymous shooters we've never seen before. (That's not to say I didn't greatly enjoy mass-murder-baptism scene - in fact it was probably my favourite, in isolation - and I do appreciate that it represented a greater symbolic act of revenge for his brother's death, but it still didn't work for me.) And then we end with a brooding Al Pacino lying to his girlfriend who has no personality besides Pretty and I did not care about, and therefore fully adopting the new "don" role, becoming the new Godfather. And then a door slams. I guess. As the credits were rolling I was just left thinking... that's it? Where was the fallout, the consequences, for all that death and drama? Please, just one meaningful consequence? This pacing can only be justified if they were always intending on making a "Part II" to continue the story, because on its own it just feels incomplete to me. It was undeniably cinematically well-made and I recognise probably, to me, a victim of the "classic movie which was ground breaking and iconic for the time and was the first to do all these cool things that have now been done better a million times over and I take for granted" problem. Same as "Taxi Driver". But I'm not a film critic, I'm only going to review a movie taken on its own merit, and to me... I don't know. The themes were interesting...? I guess? The idea of Business getting conflated with the Personal was a throughline. Again, I've seen the revenge plot done better since. I recall enjoying the first part - the plot was well set up and the villains mysterious and threatening. But then they all just... die. With the fall-out captured in a five minute long montage of newspaper headlines. New villains appear, and then they die too. And this valiant "that's my familys work not mine" war hero just... flips, and becomes a mafioso the second he gets back from like a month max of exile in Italy where the most significant thing he did was watch his Italian wife get blown up in a car for no reason after having genuinely more dialogue with her father than her and then immediately forgetting about her. There's no consequences, no explicit moral reckoning, for what was supposed to be that climatic act of killing the men who shot his father earlier in the film. He doesn't even have one panic attack! The battered sister is used as a plot point and a pawn to advance the more important sophisticated business of mafia men. Even at the end when she's hysterically yelling at Pacino "you never even considered me [when you killed my abusive husband]" it's like... yeah, he didn't, in multiple ways. If he wasn't aware of his violence, he didn't care how she'd be affected by losing her loving husband, and if he was aware of his violence, that wasn't even the reason he killed him! He didn't care that she was being abused, he cared that he was part of some complex behind-the-scenes murder plot of him. That never went anywhere because everyone gets killed! Like, I get it. It was the 50s, who cares about women, but why include DV as a plot point - going so far as to have a too-long scene of a man chasing his pregnant wife around their house with a belt while she screams, and then beating her - and then just stomp on it? Maybe that was the point, that by the end of the film Pacino is just so far gone into the moral grey of the mob that he doesn't care and that's a bad thing. That would make it more interesting, but not necessarily better. He is explicitly positioned as the protagonist and yet shows so few positive qualities throughout the whole film. I just don't buy his character degradation, if that was the intention. These flat, tired depictions of women just cheapen any movie they're in. If you zoom out, you realise all you're watching is the product of a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking about a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking. Just jerk eachother off already. We want to believe the Author is this unbiased surveyor and imitator of the human condition, and that reckoning - it brings them down to earth for me. How brilliant can a man or his story be if they don't trascend or even attempt to transcend the cruelty and primitivism of their era? Oh well. It's fun to get all the Sopranos references now. Maybe watching that first was setting this film up for failure because there's so much more room over 6 seasons and 50+ hours for real, conscientious character development and moral complexity and getting attached to not just the people but the world being built, than a movie, even one as long as this. I should watch this again.

Well, “Leave the gun, take the cannolis ” is now officially my favorite line ever from a film. I love being part Italian so I can “claim” just a sliver of the vibes of this movie. I know these are quintessential movies, so I am so excited to finally watch the first part, but having just read the original book by Mario Puzo, I am left with three main takeaways: 1. This is a Peter Jackson, LOTR book adaptation level. Some scenes are truly ripped out the pages and shot exactly as they are written. Coppola consulted closely with Puzo and that shows. 2. Like most book to movie adaptations, I really do prefer the book to the movie. There is so much to love about the film. The acting is superb and so many scenes are beautifully shot, but so much of the context that I loved from reading the book is lost in translation. 3. For the second time this past month, I have watched a film based on a book that I really loved and appreciated. The first is the Odyssey and now the Godfather. Both movies I really loved, but my love for the ethos and deeper story in the written world makes me still feel like something is missing in the film. Both are still almost 3 hour movies, yet they felt so fast and are almost rushed in a way. I want to stay with Michael’s slow build into becoming a part of the family business. I want to see the full return of Odysseus to Ithaca and for it to feel the full completion and vindication. I know the mediums are different but I think these are connected in my mind and are resulting in me not feeling like they are “perfect” films. Still, this was an excellent watch, but my biggest recommendation is to read a copy of the book.

We know from Gay Talese’s book Honor Thy Father that being a professional mobster isn’t all sunshine and roses. More often, it’s the boredom of stuffy rooms and a bad diet of carry-out food, punctuated by brief, terrible bursts of violence. This is exactly the feel of “The Godfather,” which brushes aside the flashy glamour of the traditional gangster picture and gives us what’s left: fierce tribal loyalties, deadly little neighborhood quarrels in Brooklyn, and a form of vengeance to match every affront. The remarkable thing about Mario Puzo’s novel was the way it seemed to be told from the inside out; he didn’t give us a world of international intrigue, but a private club as constricted as the seventh grade. Everybody knew everybody else and had a pretty shrewd hunch what they were up to. The movie (based on a script labored over for some time by Puzo and then finally given form, I suspect, by director Francis Ford Coppola) gets the same feel. We tend to identify with Don Corleone’s family not because we dig gang wars, but because we have been with them from the beginning, watching them wait for battle while sitting at the kitchen table and eating chow mein out of paper cartons. “The Godfather” himself is not even the central character in the drama. That position goes to the youngest, brightest son, Michael, who understands the nature of his father’s position while revising his old-fashioned ways. The Godfather’s role in the family enterprise is described by his name; he stands outside the next generation which will carry on and, hopefully, angle the family into legitimate enterprises. Those who have read the novel may be surprised to find Michael at the center of the movie, instead of Don Corleone. In fact, this is simply an economical way for Coppola to get at the heart of the Puzo story, which dealt with the transfer of power within the family. Marlon Brando, who plays the Godfather as a shrewd, unbreakable old man, actually has the character lead in the movie; Al Pacino, with a brilliantly developed performance as Michael, is the lead. But Brando’s performance is a skillful throwaway, even though it earned him an Academy Award for best actor. His voice is wheezy and whispery, and his physical movements deliberately lack precision; the effect is of a man so accustomed to power that he no longer needs to remind others. Brando does look the part of old Don Corleone, mostly because of acting and partly because of the makeup, although he seems to have stuffed a little too much cotton into his jowls, making his lower face immobile. The rest of the actors supply one example after another of inspired casting. Although “The Godfather” is a long, minutely detailed movie of some three hours, there naturally isn’t time to go into the backgrounds and identities of such characters as Clemenza, the family lieutenant; Jack Woltz, the movie czar; Luca Brasi, the loyal professional killer; McCluskey, the crooked cop; and the rest. Coppola and producer Al Ruddy skirt this problem with understated typecasting. As the Irish cop, for example, they simply slide in Sterling Hayden and let the character go about his business. Richard Castellano is an unshakable Clemenza. John Marley makes a perfectly hateful Hollywood mogul (and, yes, he still wakes up to find he’ll have to cancel his day at the races). The success of “The Godfather” as a novel was largely due to a series of unforgettable scenes. Puzo is a good storyteller, but no great shakes as a writer. The movie gives almost everything in the novel except the gynecological repair job. It doesn’t miss a single killing; it opens with the wedding of Don Corleone’s daughter (and attendant upstairs activity); and there are the right number of auto bombs, double crosses, and garrotings. Coppola has found a style and a visual look for all this material so “The Godfather” becomes something of a rarity: a really good movie squeezed from a bestseller. The decision to shoot everything in period decor (the middle and late 1940s) was crucial; if they’d tried to save money as they originally planned, by bringing everything up-to-date, the movie simply wouldn’t have worked. But it’s uncannily successful as a period piece, filled with sleek, bulging limousines and postwar fedoras. Coppola and his cinematographer, Gordon Willis, also do some interesting things with the color photography. The earlier scenes have a reddish-brown tint, slightly overexposed and feeling like nothing so much as a 1946 newspaper rotogravure supplement. Although the movie is three hours long, it absorbs us so effectively it never has to hurry. There is something in the measured passage of time as Don Corleone hands over his reins of power that would have made a shorter, faster moving film unseemly. Even at this length, there are characters in relationships you can’t quite understand unless you’ve read the novel. Or perhaps you can, just by the way the characters look at each other.

Portuguese & English review Portuguese- Tarantino nunca conseguiu chegar a fazer um bom western nas suas tentativas, acaba por não haver uma compreensão de que o seu género de filmar quer realmente chegar ao com Django Unchained e The Hateful Eight, não há realmente uma correlação ou sensatez na utilização do Spaghetti Western. ​O grande problema destas tentativas de Tarantino, tanto em Django Unchained (2012) de forma mais gritante, como em The Hateful Eight, é que o realizador parece acreditar que fazer um Spaghetti Western se resume a decalcar a banda sonora de Ennio Morricone, usar lentes anamórficas de 70mm, filmar planos de pormenor de armas a saírem do coldre e carregar na violência hiperbolizada. Há uma total ausência de correlação e sensatez na utilização do género. O Spaghetti Western original aquele de Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci ou Giulio Questi nunca foi apenas sobre o estilo ou sobre "gajos fixes a disparar" era um cinema de urgência, seco, operático, que nascia de uma profunda desilusão do pós-guerra europeu, onde a violência era o reflexo de um mundo desprovido de Deus, de leis e de pátria, onde o silêncio e o deserto falavam mais do que os diálogos. ​Tarantino faz exatamente o oposto: ele sufoca o Western com o seu próprio estilo de filmar, transformando o que deveria ser um género visceral num exercício de autocomplacência verbal. The Hateful Eight falha na raiz porque renega o espaço do Western para se fechar numa peça de teatro filmada, claustrofóbica e tagarela, onde a dinâmica de "quem é quem" dentro duma cabana de neve se assemelha mais a um mistério de Agatha Christie reescrito com palavrões do que à crueza mítica de um clássico da fronteira. As personagens não são anti-heróis ambíguos e fascinantes na linha dos clássicos são apenas bonecos de cartão-canelado, odiosos e cínicos por decreto, criados para debitar monólogos intermináveis que tentam soar profundos mas que apenas revelam um realizador refém do seu próprio maneirismo. ​Não há sensatez moral na violência de Tarantino aqui. Enquanto no Spaghetti Western a brutalidade era trágica, suja e pesada, em The Hateful Eight ela torna-se meramente recreativa, um espetáculo gore gratuito e niilista que perde toda a força catártica. Ao tentar fundir a herança política da Guerra Civil Americana com o cinismo do Western europeu, Tarantino acaba por não chegar a lado nenhum. O filme arrasta-se num ritmo indulgente de três horas, onde a tensão nunca se traduz em peso dramático real, apenas numa contagem de corpos previsível. É o cinema transformado num parque de diversões temático para o próprio realizador, provando que, para se fazer um bom Western, não basta ter em arquivo uma gigantesca coleção de referências; é preciso compreender a mecânica do silêncio, a solidão do horizonte e a gravidade de um corpo que tomba no chão. Ainda um pouco melhor que Django Unchained. English- Tarantino never managed to make a good Western in his attempts, ultimately failing to understand what his genre of filmmaking really wants to achieve with Django Unchained and The Hateful Eight; there's really no correlation or common sense in the use of the Spaghetti Western. The big problem with Tarantino's attempts, both in Django Unchained (2012), most glaringly, and in The Hateful Eight, is that the director seems to believe that making a Spaghetti Western boils down to using Ennio Morricone's soundtrack, employing 70mm anamorphic lenses, filming close-ups of guns being drawn from holsters, and relying heavily on hyperbolized violence. There is a total lack of correlation and wisdom in the use of the genre. The original Spaghetti Western, the one by Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci, or Giulio Questi, was never just about style or "nice guys shooting." It was a cinema of urgency, dry, operatic, born from a profound disillusionment with postwar Europe, where violence reflected a world devoid of God, laws, and homeland, where silence and the desert spoke louder than dialogue. Tarantino does the exact opposite: he suffocates the Western with his own filming style, transforming what should be a visceral genre into an exercise in verbal self-indulgence. The Hateful Eight fails at its core because it rejects the space of the Western to enclose itself in a filmed, claustrophobic, and chatty play, where the "who's who" dynamic inside a snow cabin resembles more an Agatha Christie mystery rewritten with profanity than the mythical rawness of a frontier classic. The characters are not ambiguous and fascinating anti-heroes in the vein of the classics; they are merely corrugated cardboard puppets, hateful and cynical by decree, created to deliver endless monologues that attempt to sound profound but only reveal a director held hostage by his own mannerisms. There is no moral sense in Tarantino's violence here. While in the Spaghetti Western the brutality was tragic, dirty, and heavy, in The Hateful Eight it becomes merely recreational, a gratuitous and nihilistic gore spectacle that loses all cathartic force. In trying to merge the political legacy of the American Civil War with the cynicism of the European Western, Tarantino ends up getting nowhere. The film drags on at an indulgent three-hour pace, where the tension never translates into real dramatic weight, just a predictable body count. It is cinema transformed into a theme park for the director himself, proving that, to make a good Western, it is not enough to have a gigantic collection of references in the archives; It's necessary to understand the mechanics of silence, the solitude of the horizon, and the gravity of a body falling to the ground. Still a little better than Django Unchained.

Samuel L Jackson and Walton Goggins deliver great performances, the scope cinematography is excellent and Ennio Morricone’s music from The Thing and others is used to great effect. But I didn’t like this any more than the last time I saw it, which was in the cinema on release. It doesn’t hold together like other Tarantino movies for me, and the stylistic choices (particularly the director’s deliberately intrusive voiceover after the intermission) often come across as smug rather than clever. The worst thing is the way it wears its misogyny on its sleeve, not helped by the presence of the Weinstein name and logo all over the credits. It’s inspired by classic westerns of the 60s and 70s that have clearly racist and misogynistic moments… but those films were made over 50 years ago. This is from 2015 (although that’s a lifetime away in some respects). The use of slur words is extreme, even for Tarantino, and the final scene so grotesque that it overshadows anything good that came before. I don’t know anymore if it’s okay to admire the craft of a film if you find so much of the content repulsive.

Apparently unpopular opinion, but I really didn't like this movie. This movie truly felt like it was six hours long. It was a real chore to sit through. I don't mind dialogue driven films, but the dialogue has to actually be interesting and compelling. It should be additive and purposeful. But here it was mundane and repetitive. It felt like there were multiple conversations that just kept repeating themselves just with different people. Most of these conversations served no real purpose. I'd say a lot of scenes in general even beyond just the dialogue felt pointless. Every scene felt like it was lasting too long. I really did not need to see 10 different scenes of them nailing the door shut. I get it, the door is broken. Nor did I need to see the origin story for said broken door. I really didn't care how it broke. I get what the film was trying to do. It was trying to slowly build tension between everyone until it boils over and turns into a big brawl by the end. But the problem is I never felt this tension. First of all because I never cared about a single character in this movie. There was not a single person I was rooting for. But also because everything was so drawn out any tension that is built up runs out of steam and lost the tension for me because I just wanted them to get on with it. Characters choices just didn't often make sense either. But they had to do things to make it as drawn out as humanly possible. The film was well acted though, I would acknowledge that, at least from most people. Samuel L Jackson does a great job in particular. He probably has the best lines. The ones that actually feel like they mattered. So I don't think the film is without merit whatsoever. But there wasn't a moment in the film where I just was ready for the film to be over already.

QT’s There Will Be Blood, a violent, sadistic Western that amounts to something like an origin myth. It is easily his most alienating, least likable movie, and it competes with Django Unchained as his worst. It is baggy, self-indulgent, undisciplined filmmaking. You can sense the willful perversity behind it: It’s almost like a self-imposed challenge — how to make a 2-hour, 45-minute epic in the confines of a single location. (He fails his own challenge.) But despite my reservations, the go-for-broke, don’t-give-a-shit folly of it all earns respect, if not admiration. He knows exactly what he’s doing. I think he knows that there is not a single likable person here (see the title), that the violence is as over-the-top as it’s been in any of his movies, and that he’s pushing the limits of audience patience. He thinks his voice, his talent, his virtuosity, the power of his message, and his audience’s loyalty will carry him through. They don’t, not all the way at least.

Le risque de développer un style de mise en scène est à la longue de s'enfermer dedans et d'en être prisonnier. Peut être que certains esprits plus fermés et ayant une très grande confiance en eux sont moins propices à la remise en question et aux changements propres à la curiosité, ce qui en découle une certaine stagnation quel que soit ce que l'on fait. Ça fait 30 ans que Tarantino répète les mêmes schémas qu'ils narratifs ou dans sa mise en scène. Déjà très marqués dès Pulp fiction, j'ai l'impression que l'on atteint le plus haut dans Kill Bill. Depuis j'ai cette sensation de plus en plus présente dès Inglorious Bastard de revoir les mêmes mécaniques avec seul un décors en toile de fond qui changeait. Si dans ce dernier, cela passait encore, cette impression dérangeante s'est accentuée dans Jango. Ici avec Hateful Eight, cela en est presque une caricature de son propre style, tout devient trop un Déjà Vu et même les dialogues, souvent riches chez Tarantino sont un peu en deçà. Le film demeure agréable et sympathique mais je certaine lassitude l'emporte. Il a néanmoins rompu avec ce style avec Once upon a Time in Hollywood, ce que j'avais apprécié, même si il s'est rappelé à lui même dans les 15 dernieres minutes.

Wow, this movie is something else. I honestly didn't know what to expect going into The Hateful Eight, but I ended up really enjoying it. The movie is pretty slow at first, but I think that's what makes it work. Most of it takes place inside one cabin, with a bunch of strangers who don't trust each other. As the movie goes on, you start questioning everyone and wondering who's actually telling the truth. The line “I’m gonna get you” really fits the feeling of the movie because you constantly feel like someone is about to turn on someone else. The dialogue is probably my favorite part. There isn't always a lot happening, but the conversations are so interesting that I didn't really mind. Tarantino can make people sitting around a table talking feel more intense than an action scene. The characters are constantly trying to figure each other out, and that paranoia keeps building. I also really liked the setting. The snow and the huge amount of isolation make the whole movie feel trapped. They're stuck together with nowhere to go, which makes the tension even better. The cabin almost feels like its own character. The characters are also just crazy 😭. Pretty much everyone is a terrible person in some way, so you don't really know who to root for. Like the movie says, “No one’s gonna be leaving this place alive.” At that point, you already know things are about to go completely off the rails. Overall, The Hateful Eight is definitely a slow burn, but once it gets going, it's really entertaining. The dialogue, characters, setting, and mystery all work together really well. It's definitely worth watching if you're into Tarantino movies.

Bu adamın film tarzına bayılıyorum. Ne zaman elle tutulur bir hikaye yokmuş gibi gözükse bile inanılmaz keyif verici filmler ortaya koyuyor ve hikaye, diyologlarda araya sıkıştırdığı küçük sözlerle bile dallanıp budaklanabiliyor. Filmlerindeki o retro hava, nostaljik film vibeı, hikayeyi kitap okur gibi bölümlere ayrılması, hikaye akışında kronolojik sırayı bozup heyecan verici unsurları yayması ve özellikle filmin sonuna yerleştirmesi onu ayıran özellikleri bence. Ayrıca mizahı da çok iyi. Gerçekten bu adamın özellikle eski kovboy filmlerinin hastası olduğunu ve filmlerinde her alanda o eski, nostaljik havayı vermeye çalıştığına eminim. Öyle ki filmin opening ve ending kısmındaki akan yazıların kabartması ve puntosu bile eskiyi çağrıştırıyor. Ve film içerisindeki şakalar da o filmlerden çıkmış gibi, sadece eski film kasıntılığından uzak oluşu filmin mizah seviyesini yerinde, gülünebilir kılıyor. Bu filmin tek kötü yanı hikayenin kapsamlı olmayışı ve üç saat boyunca aynı mekanda olayları izlememiz. Ancak dediğim gibi söz konusu Tarantino filmi keyifli kılmayı biliyor. Adam hiç sanat sepet işlerine girmeden yalnızca keyif vermek üzerine mükemmel filmler ortaya koyuyor. Ancak bu filmde prensiplerinden birine rastlamamak üzmese de şaşırttı beni: filmde ayak yoktu. Bu alışıla gelmiş bir şey değil Tarantino için ama beni bağlayan bir sorun değil. Neyse son bir film daha kaldı Tarantinodan izleyeceğim sonra bu adamın külliyatı bitecek. Yazmayı unuttum film aynı RDR havası veriyor.

I do rather like The Hateful Eight, but it is my least favorite Tarantino film. While it is very violent, it almost feels goofy compared to some of his other movies (especially his earlier movies which often have real darkness and depth to them), and really leans into his more playful side, with comically over the top dialogue and blood, silly voiceovers and slow-motion effects, and a more laid-back vibe than his usual movies that feel like they have a lot more gravitas. This is my first time watching it, but I do feel like I will find this to be QT's least rewatchable film. I love how you can run his movies back and enjoy them just as much, if not more, the second time, but with this one I don't think I'll be compelled to return to it as much, largely because it's just a weaker, far more self-indulgent and dialogue-heavy movie than most of his other films, but all the characters are pretty much awful people (except Zoe Bell's minor character, love her), so there's not really anyone to root for in the movie. I don't know, I did really enjoy The Hateful 8 but it's definitely his least compelling film. I loved the wintry cinematography and remote cabin setting, and the variation of characters and performances, especially Walton Goggins and Jennifer Jason Leigh, but while it is quite enjoyable and a perfectly good western, it's Tarantino's least serious and worst movie.
