Et voilà enfin le dernier Tarentino, normalement, d'après ses dires, le dernier, dernier! On verra s'il respecte ce qu'il a dit par le passé. Bref, revenons à nos moutons. La bande-annonce laissait présager du meilleur puisque elle laisse entrevoir une situation de huis-clos, avec une tripotée de personnages haut en couleurs et armés jusqu'aux dents, ce qui, dans ses précédents films nous offre toujours des scènes d'anthologie. Premier constat, 2h45, c'est un peu long. On attend un peu trop de temps pour que le film démarre vraiment, puis le rythme s'accélère, s'emballe carrément, pour partir en vrille totale dans la dernière demi-heure. Finalement, le rythme assez lent du début se comprend car on est scotché par cette accélération progressive qui, si elle avait pu tenir en 30' maximum, Tarentino a la classe et la maîtrise de le faire sur presque 3h. Une très bonne production qui est un plaisir à regarder, mais peut-être pas à revoir, ne serait-ce que pour découvrir d'autres détails supplémentaires liés à la résolution finale.

One of Tarantino’s more underrated films, which is sad because this is him at his peak. A bunch of dudes sitting around talking to each other for two hours as tensions slowly build, capped off with a rather violent ending sequence. What more could you want? The build here is great, I’m glued to my screen waiting for the first pin to drop. But once it does, I found less of a reason to stay invested before having to sit through 20 minutes of building up the backstory. Realizing that no one was going to make it out of this alive, I found myself not as worried about the outcome. I think it’d be cooler if there were a few more twists and turns along the way, maybe having half the group have the same end goal wasn’t the best idea. But, still a very solid film nonetheless. The winter theme and cottage vibes make for a surprisingly cozy watch. I’d love to watch this around Christmas time, hot cocoa in hand (minus the poison). I’m glad that in the end, a union and confederate soldier were able to come together and unite over their hatred for women (satire… slightly).

This was such a well-rounded story to watch. I think what made this movie stand out to me, and therefore Tarantino’s style to me, is his chapter by chapter presentation of the film. Well, it is easy to label things up to an episodic format throughout the movie, but Tarantino’s dialogue and cinematography are straight out of a book. I could literally imagine a novel being written as I watched the movie with the grand details that Tarantino’s shots offer in addition to the character dynamics and the insane performances the cast displays throughout the movie. Getting to know the characters and the setting was entertaining, although some monologues and sequences may feel a bit of a drag, it didn’t hamper my attention enough and the movie always kept me at bay. This is the fourth movie I have watched from Tarantino, and this is probably the best one so far.

Aber Olivia Wilde setzt weniger auf Glaubwürdigkeit, sondern mehr auf Übertriebenheit und das von Beginn an: Kaum ein Dialog oder Gestik kommt in dem mit unzähligen Sticheleien versehenen Schlagabtausch ohne Hysterie und Theatralik aus. Subilität hat Sendepause und mit Authenzität hat das auch nicht mehr viel zu tun. Sinnbildlich der Score, der die Gefühlslagen stets (über-)präsent sowie penetrant mit schiefen oder sanften Klangteppichen ausrollt. Später, wenn Wilde den Fokus hinter der (bröckelnden) Fassade blicken möchte, bleibt dieser auch verschüchtert. Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen: Wilde bleibt bei A brav hängen. Allein nur explizit über sexuelle Vorlieben sprechen, ist halt lange nicht mutig genug, provokant erst recht nicht. Entsprechend gestaltet sich Eskalation ernüchternd inkonsequent, noch weniger entlarvend. Stattdessen werden dabei doch wieder die platten Gags rausgeholt. Das ist nicht pointiert, sondern peinlich. Die Komplexität der Konflikte um verschiedene Beziehungsformen und Liebe, aber auch Kommunikationsunfähigkeit, entfaltet sich dadurch selten schlagkräftig, auch da der Film lediglich auf konstruierte Zuspitzung aus ist. Am Ende stehen dann doch wieder Luxusprobleme im Vordergrund und die Tatsache, dass bei aller Offenheit andere Partnerschaftsmodelle außerhalb der traditionellen Ehe, doch nur pervertiert sind und Unruhe reinbringen. Ahja... Aber dann, die letzten 5 Minuten: Die sind plötzlich zutiefst menschlich. Olivia Wilde findet in der Ruhe nochmal leise Töne, die stark beeindrucken! Gerade hier ist zu spüren, was für ein reizvolles Potenzial 'The Invite' besitzt. Hätte sich der Film in den vorherigen 100 Minuten doch mal mehr aus der zahmen (Hollywood-)Komfortzone getraut.

It’s not the single most important takeaway but I’ve seen all three Olivia Wilde directed films and I’m now convinced she’s had exclusively terrible sex. That’s in spite of how sweaty and performatively preoccupied with the female orgasm her films claim to be–either within the text of the films or as part of the messy promotional tours surrounding them–yet they’re constantly engaging in mortifying coitus interruptus or something that’s adjacent to assault (wouldn’t even begin to know how to classify what’s happening in Don’t Worry Darling ). Something a bit doth protest too much, methinks. Wilde’s involvement notwithstanding (and isn’t it precious how the film quotes a different O. Wilde before the opening credits) the more identifiable authorial voice here belongs to Jones and McCormack in the sense that if I immediately recognized the sensibilities which led me to  shutting off Celeste And Jesse Forever after 40 minutes. A grab bag of emotionally stunted, shrill quirks and indignant bellowing with Rogen and Wilde coming across like a more broadly comedic George and Martha, largely defined by a single grating personality trait each (gruff obstinance and try-hard neediness, respectively). Goes through the sitcom-y motions of a straight-laced couple having their horizons expanded by a couple of swingers who saw them across their apartment building lobby and dug their vibe (Edward Norton and Penélope Cruz, also saddled with nonsensical characters but at least they’re allowed to have a little fun with all the pseudo-bohemian touchy-feeliness) only for the film to abruptly pull up short for a, I fucking kid you not, therapy session with a *literal* psychoanalyst who is able to accurately make a snap diagnosis of their long-simmering dysfunction. I don't know why I thought the film would actually follow through on its attention-grabbing premise but sure enough it beats a hasty retreat to squishy social conservatism and a plaintive, maybe-kinda-sorta reconciliation to send the audience out on a hopeful note. At an utter loss to see people praising Wilde’s direction as I found this to be mostly visually incoherent with no innate sense of how to block actors or convey evolving character dynamics via their placement within the frame. Instead it’s a blitzkrieg of alternating singles of varying focal lengths (I regularly found myself questioning whether all four actors were on set at the same time for more than a couple days of shooting) with the occasional racked focus between foreground and background and back to foreground for variety. Particularly frustrating to see this exalted in most corners–flashbacks of Booksmart 7 years ago–in that Splitsville tackled, more or less, this same premise last summer and was mostly met with polite indifference and nonexistent box office despite having the benefit of genuinely engaging with the emotional fallout and trade-offs of polyamory while being form-forward in its approach (also, was actually funny).

“I’m the only one who fucks me currently.” This is  atavistic chamber piece that recalls the cinematic pleasures of watching beautiful people crash out and argue. It flirts with incendiary melodrama before settling into a more tragic, hopeless register. Centering on two couples who gather for dinner, only to end up spilling secrets, desires, and resentment about each other over immaculately plated charcuterie, each conversation feels like watching technicians try to diffuse explosives. There’s an inherently performative aspect to any given social situation, and The Invite finds great humor and awkwardness in characters who explore the tension between what they say and what they think. Viewers who suffer from second-hand embarrassment might find their tolerance tested by characters’ tendency to walk right up to the line of what’s socially unacceptable. Hilariously acted by its four leads, thanks to Wilde’s effective direction and Adam Newport-Berra’s immersive cinematography, The Invite always feels like it’s more than the sum of its parts — although its thematic reach is often frustratingly in conflict with the realistic story it’s attempting to tell. As the same kind of enthusiasm-to-cynicism cycle that followed the Summer Of Love plays out in the internet age, some of the topical filmmaking from that earlier time is too. “Sex positivity” has replaced “free love,” but the emotions are very much the same. Curiosity, jealousy, embarrassment, doubt—the feelings that crawl under the skin of relationships emerge, sometimes ugly and raw, when people are frank about their romantic and sexual needs, especially when they extend beyond tradition. For anyone whose dating life has led them to run up against ethical non-monogamy, where asking about acronyms opens up a philosophical can of worms about the nature of personal relationships, The Invite provides plenty of embarrassing, familiar relationship comedy. But it’s director-star Olivia Wilde’s tight, warm control of her ensemble that keeps the awkwardly horny dinner party moving forward through its clunkier courses. Full review @ The A.V. Club

Sundance Film Festival Presents: The Invite Directed By: Olivia Wilde Based on the Spanish film from 2020 called The People’s Upstairs directed by Cesc Gray. Joe and Angela is having a very tough time maintaining their relationship and one night in San Francisco their neighbors decided to come over of what could be a night to remember. Olivia Wilde wowed us in the 2019 film Booksmart which became an instant coming to age classic with one of the best comedic films in recent memory. Unfortunately I couldn’t say the same with her 2022 film Don’t Worry Darling which is a trainwreck of a movie and its production history behind it is a stuff of legends. After being in director jail for nearly 4 years, her next project is a smaller indie film is Based on the Spanish film from 2020 called The People’s Upstairs directed by Cesc Gray and it stars Seth Rogen, Olivia Wilde, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton. So what do I think of the film, it’s a very provocative movie for adults that pays homage to the old school date movies. My only issue with the film is that the first 35-40 minutes didn’t find its footing yet and can feel a bit bloated at first but as soon as the comedy hits after those 35 minutes, the film eventually find its footing with some of the most silliest horniest scenes  during the film. Other than that issue, I do think this will be one of the most talked about films in the festival so far! Even though I like Seth Rogen and Olivia Wilde, it’s Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton’s show here that  I feel the film mostly worked because of their comedic timing and yet very horny character motives  that puts the film in insane situations. The film is also a one location film throughout the film and easily a very small cast but I feel the setting really create a far depressing tone that the film was going for and it worked for the most part. The Invite (2026) is easily one of this years Sundance’s better films so far! Even though it takes its time to get invested with the world and its characters, the film screenplay by Rashida Jones and Will McCormack gets better and gives uncomfortable horny jokes front and center and I feel Cruz and Norton understood the assignment the most. This is Wilde’s best film since Booksmart and easily the best directorial effort from Olivia Wilde that pays  homage to the old hangout films of the 1960s and 70s that managed to give the laughs and tears all throughout its official runtime.

THE INVITE is an uproariously funny yet profoundly sad dramedy about a deteriorating couple who invite their sexually confident, free-spirited neighbors over for what’s meant to be a pleasant evening, only for it to spiral into something painfully awkward, ugly, and brutally honest. Seth Rogen showcases remarkable range, blending his signature comedy with the finest dramatic work of his career. Olivia Wilde delivers a soul-crushing performance fueled by anxiety and secondhand embarrassment, while her precise, assured direction turns this intimate chamber piece into an astounding seamless balancing act between humor and heartbreak with something meaningful to say about marriage and relationships. Edward Norton and Penélope Cruz are the cherry on top of what is a delicious offering from Wilde and easily the best directorial work of her career so far.

The one-room film is certainly a rare breed, but certainly one of my favorites. With a stellar cast, raucously funny dialogue, and a fantastic script, it’s absolutely another win for Wilde. Plus, Seth Rogan twerks in this movie, so it gets some bonus points.

Contrary to some other film festivals out there, standing ovations don’t happen all of the time at Sundance. And, to be fair, getting one doesn’t mean the movie was necessarily great or will be a box office smash. But in the case of Olivia Wilde’s hilarious, rapid-fire marital comedy The Invite, I think both things are true. Wilde’s third time behind the camera, and a welcome return to comedy for the first time since Booksmart, the film is also a rebound from her polarizing suburban satire, Don’t Worry Darling. Underneath all of the witty one-liners, this is also a film that packs quite an emotional wallop, exploring love and sex between a longtime married couple that has lost that spark, and maybe needs a bit of neighborly advice to get it back. There are rare moments when a film comedy hits a gear where the big laughs are coming so fast, one on top of the other, that it becomes absolutely euphoric, no matter what other minor slips might occur along the way. You get one such occasion about mid-way through this farce about a married San Francisco couple, Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Olivia Wilde, who also directed), whose relationship difficulties come into focus when they host a dinner party for their upstairs neighbors, unconventional couple Hawk (Edward Norton) and Piña (Penélope Cruz). The script by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones adapts the 2020 Spanish feature Sentimental , and mixes farce with “comedy of remarriage” in a way that kind of rushes through the steps to figuring out whether Joe and Angela can work things out. But absolutely none of that matters at the peak of the gathering’s craziness, beginning with a wonderfully awkward search for a corkscrew and building to a conversation about Hawk and Piña’s sex life where the jokes come in a fusillade that barely lets you come up for air. All four of the performances are terrific while working in very different registers—Wilde’s reaction takes bouncing off Rogen’s ad-libs, with Cruz and Norton providing phenomenal straight-person counterpoint. The ending aims for a particular kind of sweetness, but really, nothing is sweeter than the sound of hundreds of people roaring in unison for several minutes straight.

The Invite is razor-sharp, as riotous as supremely tender. The sadness and anger that permeates it only makes it that much funnier. What a perfect quartet here, balanced and bouncing off each other flawlessly. Awkward, complex, hilarious. A beautiful tight-rope-walk of a film. Check out my full review over at Next Best Picture.

This was yet another insanely cool movie to see on my second day at Sundance! This was the world premiere of this movie which was wild and I got to see it with my dad which makes it an experience I’ll love and treasure forever. And then after the Q&A with Rogen and Norton and Wilde was so so cool. The energy in the room was unlike anything I’ve experienced before this festival. It’s one of the most electric theaters I’ve ever had the pleasure of being in. And as for the movie itself this is a genuine bonafide comedic masterpiece. You rarely see almost just pure throwback comedies like this now and this is pitched to perfection. Olivia Wilde makes a fantastic return to form with what is so far my favorite movie I’ve seen so far at this Sundance festival. Her direction is comedically razor sharp and brings so much delicious human comedy out of this premise. And the screenplay is the best script I’ve seen at this festival so far. It’s so sharp and insightful and it brings out so much of the comedy really organically which is just so satisfying to watch. And the score and production design and cinematography are all genius and bring brilliant shades of complexity to what is essentially Wildes Scenes from a marriage. And Rogen and Wilde and Norton and Cruz are all masterful in this and give some of the best performances I’ve seen this year. They are all so funny and it was so fun to see this with a world premiere crowd that got the joke. All in all this is the type of sharply assembled and cut to the bone dramedy that we simply don’t get anymore that’s extremely funny and also deeply poignant and insightful and just so so stirring. I love movies because of movies like this.

This movie has essentially the same premise as Gladiator, and it presents an interesting parallel. In Gladiator, the violence and evil has a purpose, and while it may not be fully historically accurate, the point is made and the emotions are evoked in the viewer. In the Northman, the violence and evil doesn't stop, and it seems to serve only to shock and disgust the viewer. It's dark and horrible just for the sake of being dark and horrible, and while that might work for somebody out there, I'm just not that person. I loved Gladiator because I could feel for Maximus and his struggle to avenge his family. Amleth is just angry and likes killing people. This movie probably isn't trying to be Gladiator or The Patriot, but for me those movies resonate in a way that this one misses the mark on.

I think the biggest consideration of period pieces is that their programming of speech and behaviour is of a time where different things were at stake, largely because ritual and power were at the forefront of the status quo, rather than, for an easy example, the possibility of the static lifestyle one can live now, of which human expedition then would ensure seriousness and expectation be within every walk of isolated thought and shared interaction. It’s against this backdrop that the opening stages’ questionable editing choices become most apparent: establishing that kind of world demands relaxation of a viewer’s experience through integration methods that are timeless in human history, and the film stumbles slightly out of the gate in giving us our footing. It is then the filmmaker’s job to ensure a universal entry point for even the most unintelligent of audience members to understand what is going on. Whilst it doesn’t contain the outstanding personality of The Lighthouse, instead here chasing spectacle in the traditional, predictable form (against its own intended “wow” factor) of “thing happens, get ready for next thing happening!! NEXT THING ARRIVES,” it does unquestionably provide the same fly-on-the-wall approach to that earlier work, giving us full spectator view of a meticulously designed production whose scale no one could argue with, and it’s here that the texture, where production design meets framing, makes a big bang. Where I’m less convinced is the camerawork itself. Eggers leans mechanical: constant pans, deliberate moves, in a way that keeps reminding you it’s camerawork rather than photography. These are undeniably seamless and the level of choreography required is evident in the final product, which is arguably perfect in achieving its intended circuitry (THE SEIGE!), yet there are moments that would’ve landed harder as a single, cleverly framed image of directed blocking, as a still image instead of motion for revelatory sake.

" Rewatch ( non in questo caso ) delle opere di Robert Eggers " Episodio 1 Robert, mi dispiace dirtelo, ma il tuo tentativo di fare qualcosa di diverso dal film dell'orrore non è andato a buon fine. Il film in sè, penso sia uno dei migliori film a livello tecnico che eggers abbia mai fatto. Con bellissimi paesaggi e una grande regia, che già dal primo minuto di visione si può già riconoscere chi lo ha diretto. Non parliamo poi della maniacale accuratezza storica che Eggers DEVE dare ai suoi film. I combattimenti che si vedono sono fantastici, e il come vengono mostrate certe scene: realistiche e crude, con il giusto quantitativo di violenza e una rappresentazione del periodo storico molto azzeccata. Il problema per me sta sopratutto nella storia che viene narrata, più che mai come viene narrata. La trama in sè, seppur non proprio all'apice dell'originalità, aveva una buona premessa. Essendo che c'era Eggers che lo scrive e dirige, mi faceva presagire già al mio nuovo film preferito. Invece no, dopo averlo finito mi sono sentito come ricevere un nuovo telefono solo per scoprire che all'interno c'è un mattone. Tutta la storia è strutturata con scene che portano avanti la trama, e sono divise da altre che servono a poco, con scene oniriche e piene di rituali ecc. Avendo visto anche the VVitch, era abbastanza prevedibile con Eggers, ma in questo caso non le ho viste come qualcosa che facesse parte della trama apparte qualche eccezione, come qualcosa che caratterizza il film e in molte occasioni non le ho trovate necessarie con il suo andazzo. Sopratutto nella seconda metà succede varie volte. Nonostante non sia un film horror, di soprannaturale ce ne è anche troppo. L'unico tocco di soprannaturale che ho gradito è il fatto che il Destino venga rappresentato come un'entità presente (come la morte in Final Destination ad esempio), se sia reale o solo un invenzione della capoccia del protagonista non lo sappiamo. Il Destino giuda Amleto per tutto il suo viaggio, anche quando cerca redenzione dalla sua vita piena di odio cercando di scappare da essa, il Destino torna e gli dice "Eh no, il tuo fato e già scritto, torna subito alla tua quest principale". Il finale, l'ho abbastanza gradito, anche se per il combattimento mi sarei aspettato tutt'altro epilogo, visto che per tutto il film il protagonista dice cosa farà una volta ottenuta vendetta. Per ora è il "peggior" film di Robert Eggers a mio parere.

It completely failed to make me care about any of the characters, especially Amleth, which is honestly the film’s biggest flaw. Not because of Alexander Skarsgård’s performance, he’s great and all, I’d definitely ride that even in the woods, but because the character writing never gives you enough to invest in. The film looks great, and there is something here which could be a decently powerful story about lost innocence, a certain conceptualisation of masculinity/manhood, patriarchal violence unto women, a more metaphorical violence unto one’s identity, etc. The problem is that there’s basically no character work here. There is barely any humanity or life in this story which, on paper, should be very close to that humanity and life. I simply didn’t care about what was happening, especially with regard to the character relationships. As another user has already said, there’s also not much forward momentum: things just happen one after the other. The characters I most sympathised with were Olga and Gudrún, but that’s less because of their characters and more just because of the horrors they’re forced to endure with, by virtue of their status as women in such a patriarchal society, very little opportunity to do much about that. It’s probably the understated victimhood of the other characters - the ones who aren’t royal men - that the film gets to its most interesting themes (most notably the radical self-involvement/selfishness of the core character motivations that move the plot forward), but this is (seemingly intentionally) left as an understated part of the film and, even if it wasn’t, it wouldn’t counterbalance the issues I’ve already spoken about. I did want to like this film because I love Eggers’ work but this just didn’t work for me.

Not once does this movie stop to ask if you are ok. It forces you to accept Norse theology (although gruesome) in order to understand the characters. Even until the final scene, the movie does not once question the beliefs of those it is betraying. This makes the film feel like it is being told to you from a storyteller in 900 AD. That being said, one of the greatest rules of storytelling is broken. Amleth has no character arc, nor does he learn any sort of lesson. He is told at the beginning of his life what his fait is, and that is exactly what ends up happening to him. This feels natural, in fact the story wouldn't make sense if it were any other way. Amleth wouldn't truly be who he is portrayed as if it weren't for his adherence to his Norse ideologies. This got me thinking on The Oddesy. This story was told very differently and Odyseus almost feels out of place in his world. These two films represent the two different ways to tell an old story. The Oddysey is a modernized version of a story that feels relatable, while The Northman is a no-apologies telling of a story that stays honest (although not fully based on a historical story). It seems unfair to compare this to a Nolan film but boy does it hold its ground well.

I don’t think any review puts together what exactly this film is like, but imagine you mix Requiem for a Dream with Dorian Gray, give it a Cronenberg twist and then write and direct it like Cat in the Hat or Catwoman and you’ve got this. Hollow from beginning to end, stupendously trite in all it wants to say and extremely dragged out. Everything is lacking, especially the weirdly bland production design for how cooky it’s trying to be. It’s putting weird on weird on weird and in the end, it doesn’t work. But mostly, my distaste for this came from the fact that this moves, looks and sounds like a YouTube video, or even a TikTok. Like one of those terrible short films you find in the recommended tab with really corny messaging, except here it never ends and you’re stuck with it for an excruciatingly long runtime. I appreciate how this could almost be seen as a silent film, but my god you could tell this story in 20 minutes. I give it some credit for the ending, which was pretty hilarious. Otherwise, this is quite bad.

it’s interesting and it has A Concept, i guess! i’m glad it was made and got a big theatrical release. but i’m not sure it quite nailed down what it wanted to be saying. it has the trappings of a movie about how beauty standards and ageism are bad for women, especially celebrities, but in light of that being (at least theoretically) its core, it came off to me weirdly critical of Demi Moore’s character for taking The Substance. like, the movie knows that beauty standards are bad for women, but for some reason all of the criticism and disdain it seems to have is for the women who are forced to abide by these beauty standards rather than the corporations that sell them or even the broader culture that enforces them. I think the whole “remember you are one” angle could have led to a movie that was more tied together, but i never actually got the sense that they were really one consciousness (beyond the times it was literally written out or said in as many words). basically from the point that The Substance is taken it seems that the Moore and Qualley characters are different people and entities and there’s never really anything done with the idea of one consciousness inhabiting two bodies. there is also more minor stuff that’s stupid - Dennis Quaid is playing a sleazy exec Harvey Weinstein reference but for some reason playing him as The Gayest Guy Of All Time so i could never believe the lechery; the talk show that is apparently the top of the mountain in the entertainment industry is called ‘The Show’. and it’s sooooooooo annoyingly heavy handed at some points, it comes off like it thinks the audience are truly deeply stupid people. think the worst example is the stuff with the doctor who administers The Substance who is himself on The Substance - they show his prominent birthmark, and for people who know how to watch movies (or, like, people who know how to think thoughts), when a much older man appears and the same prominent birthmark is shown, it’s like oh ok. so that doctor was also using The Substance. but then it tells you that hey this old guy is the doctor from before like five more times in increasingly obvious ways and it’s like…come on. that really rankled me honestly.

The problem is that the body horror is utilized in the most hollow attempt at satire, it fails to say anything of note  about youth, beauty and ageing. For all of its boundary pushing gore why is its commentary so one dimensional and bland. Its doesnt fully embrace the catharsis that is part of body horror. I absolutely adored her previous film Revenge in which that film successfully subverts the misogyny often a part of rape- revenge exploitation films and turns  her revenge against her abusers as a moment of catharsis and while  making it all feel incredibly visceral. I feel the Substance lacks that punch and brilliance that I was hoping for. I still had fun with it depsite my plethora of issues with its message. Demi moore is decent enough throughout, and its nice to see her in all of her bloody glory on the big screen.

Era pra ficar com nojo ou libido? CINEMATOGRAFIA Esse é, na minha concepção, o melhor parâmetro do filme. Temos aqui um aspecto bastante sólido em como tudo se constrói e se forma dentro das suas proposições. A estética é bastante sólida e a câmera é usada ativamente para passar as mensagens do filme. Existe sim um defeito em como o filme é extremamente expositivo, e isso é tosco, mas claramente esse é um defeito do roteiro, não de como a cinematografia opera as coisas. As atuações são sólidas. É interessante como o filme seria sim uma coisa completamente diferente sem a Demi Moore, apesar de eu sinceramente não achar que a Margaret Qualley seja a “perfeita” para o papel. Ela desempenha bem, mas eu consigo enxergar uma dúzia de atrizes que fariam um trabalho igual ou até melhor. No geral, o filme acerta bastante e entrega bem tudo aquilo que se propõe. Não há nada de outro mundo, mas sim algo muito consistente. NOTA: 4.7/5 TRILHA SONORA O filme utiliza muito sons graves e pesados, sempre num tom mais pop. É quase uma mistura grotesca do pop eletrônico clássico com tensão e atrito. O filme trabalha muito bem esse aspecto na sua própria proposta de estética e ambientação. Tudo é bastante coeso aqui. NOTA: 3.7/5 ROTEIRO A escrita tem sim seus méritos, mas não é algo perfeito na minha perspectiva. Os problemas se concentram principalmente em como o filme aborda suas mensagens. A escrita em si é fraca. O filme se sustenta 100% nas suas mensagens e tentativas de profundidade, e mesmo nisso ele não é tão efetivo. Começando com o maior problema de escrita, na minha visão: a escolha horrível de relembrar várias vezes tudo, seja com flashbacks ou coisas na tela mesmo — como as instruções de uso da substância, ou o momento em que ela encontra o outro usuário da substância e o filme não só coloca o flashback como faz questão de fazê-lo derrubar tudo e revelar o número dele. O filme meio que insulta a inteligência de quem assiste diversas vezes. Além disso, o filme tem um problema meio crônico nas críticas dele, que é justamente o melhor aspecto dele: como ele aborda a crítica à indústria. Se você reparar, o filme somente aborda que a indústria lucra com a beleza e que, a partir do ponto em que a personagem de Elisabeth não está mais nesse padrão, ela é demitida. E assim, desculpa acabar com o sonho de quem quer que seja, mas qualquer indústria funciona assim: você é contratado por um motivo; se esse motivo não existe mais, você tecnicamente não serve mais para a vaga. Obviamente tem toda a caricatura do chefe daquela indústria, sobre como ele enxerga as mulheres de uma forma objetificada, mas nitidamente é só um viés de como o filme decide retratá-lo. Se você realmente para para observar os “pecados” dele e da indústria, tudo o que há é o fato de ele demitir Elisabeth por ela não estar mais no padrão de beleza. Isso seria um absurdo se ela fosse engenheira, mas não: ela é uma espécie de idol pop sexualizada. Eu estou pegando tanto no pé desse aspecto específico porque ele era pra ser o mais fácil. A indústria se aproveita das mulheres há décadas, especialmente a indústria pornográfica, que lucra através do trauma das garotas que se submetem a estar naquela posição exposta e lucra também com o vício e a deturpação doentia da humanidade das pessoas que consomem isso. Mas não: o filme só aborda como a indústria é malvada por demitir Elisabeth e para aí. Pra fechar a sessão da negatividade, eu pontuo também como a parte da profundidade e crítica do filme não se encaixa com a realidade do roteiro quando você o enxerga de forma mais literal — como quando Elisabeth mantém Sue consigo sem qualquer razão válida —, mas obviamente faz sentido quando você considera a trama subjetiva e a crítica. Apesar dos pontos negativos, é muito interessante como o filme trabalha toda a questão interna de Elisabeth. Esse é totalmente o destaque do filme: a forma como ela luta com Sue, que se torna uma persona com vontade própria, através da distorção de imagem que ela sofre, é realmente muito bem demonstrada. Todo o gore e body-horror tem uma função bastante emblemática justamente por isso. No geral, é uma escrita bastante disfuncional, na minha visão, que mais erra do que de fato acerta. Eu acabei nem comentando tanto sobre como a história se escreve em si, ritmo, storytelling etc., mas saibam que também é ruim: não tem muito para se extrair daqui. NOTA: -2/5 CONSIDERAÇÕES FINAIS Gosto muito da proposta do filme e, sinceramente, apesar do final extremamente arrastado e repetitivo que irritou um pouco a minha experiência, eu gostei do filme. Todas essas questões precisam sim de luz, mas a forma como o filme trabalha esses tópicos é nada mais que decepcionante. NOTA FINAL: 6.4/10

Helping this film’s cause are a few things – firstly, it’s the second film from Coralie Fargeat, whose gory thriller Revenge marked her out as one to watch back in 2017 – but, secondly it marks a return-of-sorts for 1990s icon Demi Moore, who is fantastically cast as an ageing Hollywood star who takes a black market drug to create a younger version of herself. Writing this review at midnight so… I tried following along with Pump It Up as I watched it and dislocated my leg, this is ridiculous, I want a refund. 0/10. A grotesquely made satire, that can be best described as equal parts gross, depressing, funny, and raunchy. Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley brought a lot to this, playing Elisabeth/Sue playing the dual identities to feel like the same person (after all they are one) but different enough to feel distinct. Dennis Quaid is great at playing the most disgusting part of the movie, Harvey. The real star of the show here is Fargeat’s directing. A visual and audial treat of a movie. Not a treat like candy but the talent on display is stunning and I hope she continues making more movies (I also caught a bit of Revenge but not enough for a review). Stunning use of color and not to mention the creature and body horror effects. A lot of the creature stuff didn’t really freak me out but Elisabeth/Sue’s body mangling and decaying had mc flinching. There’s a bit to be said on the films similarities to the manga Helter Skelter and Oliver Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Grey. Which aren’t bad, nothing is original, and are distinct works but it’s interesting how they all handle the deterioration of self in search of beauty. How did Sue manage to build a small room in like, a few days. There’s a lot of heightened reality in this movie but that really took me out. I do think a few times the movie over explains its ideas, however that being said this is a thematically rich movie. The core is obvious, how women are treated within beauty standards, Elisabeth wants to maintain her youth and fame so she uses The Substance that’s the premise. The film shows that in a lot of ways how that’s enforced by men, Harvey’s introduction has him reference fertility ages, a note Elisabeth receives says “you WERE amazing, and when she interacts with the biker as Elisabeth and not as Sue, he yells at her. Harvey and the executives even say “pretty girls should always smile” before running off to chase dancers like dogs. Sue also enforces this. Giving Elisabeth an astronomically high standard, she cannot meet, although they are one. Both versions of Pump It Up are a good point here— Elisabeth’s show is mostly in a wideshot, instructions pretty clear. The leotard more of a cloth texture, though fitting, isn’t painted on. Then you have Sue’s… which is different. It’s a male gaze wet dream, a metallic bikini that’s practically spray painted on, is basically a thong on the bottom, and is cut to the point it can barely be considered athletic wear. It’s enforced on Elisabeth largely and more subtly on Sue. Funnily enough by the end, once everything goes wrong, that’s the only way the two could escape the cage of beauty standards. Two other threads I read in the film is within “respect the balance” is about self hatred and work life balance. Which going from male gaze to love yourself in theme is a leap but— Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother one considering her a “selfish bitch” the other an old woman who wastes her life. Yet they are the same person, they are one. Sue forces herself to work at Elisabteh’s expense, and Elisabeth does nothing in the meantime, just waiting for more Sue time. She buried herself in her career, and neglected any sort of relationships, that being familial, friendly, or otherwise. Her self-worth is her career, that’s all she has. And if she doesn’t have a career, she doesn’t have a self. Which she hates. While I just went on this whole thing about self hatred within the fact that though they are the same person Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother. I do think strangely enough, though it contradicts they have something that reads as a deeply messed up mother and daughter relationship. I think most of this comes from the interview scene. Elisabeth finds Sue spoiled, someone she gave life, someone who owes everything to her, and stealing away what she had. Sue thinks Elisabeth is jurassic, old, remarking she didn’t like the show but it was “inescapable”. Which does read a lot like a mother and daughters, not to so positive opinion of one another. It could be said that Elisabeth is exploiting the girl she created to extend her career, live through her, in this case literally. Though that does sort of ignore that Sue is defintley an extension of Elisabeth’s narcissism. Within that there’s two ways I see the Elisabeth/Sue fight. It’s either a manifestation of self hatred or a daughter trying to be her own person. Decide which one you like more, don’t debate in the comments. I do think the ending is far more campy than the first two hours but it’s not bad, a bloody wild climax. Anyways I’m glad to say The Substance has… The Substance in terms of theme and what it’s trying to say. Can’t wait to see whatever Fargeat does next, and though I’m not looking forward to it, I hope Demi Moore gets more work in the future, I’m sure Margaret Qualley will do great in the Posession remake.

I struggle to call this a mixed bag because the good is not nearly as present in quantity as the bad. The film is a bit too comfortable with it's source material I think. It most consistently preforms when it is working as closely to the stage show as possible, i.e. the famously good music is still good. However it does not manage to overcome any of the flaws of the original product, nor I think, particularly thrill in it's limited ability to translate stage to film. Choreography and set design are both at best, adequate which is a shame for a product which should shine in both areas. Costuming is a bit better, but is kept down by the Netflix gray smudge color grading. How can you produce a film in Oz and not have any color! A world of bright shades is reduced to smudgy pinks, dull greens, and little else that is not seemingly grey or earth tone. The film is far worse for not having put in the work to be as delightful to look at as the original Oz film. The story is not very good, there is basically no modification from the stage show to my understanding, and the show has always coasted by on the musical numbers over the story. The same structure remains here, made worse by the fact this is only part one and several more hours of story remain. Overall a pretty unremarkable thing, it managed to never make me consider stopping watching, but not much beyond that in terms of impact.

Pretty solid! This was certainly more up my alley than I expected it to be. Everything is very maximalist here, to the point of being visually overwhelming at times. There was clearly a great amount of care and detail put into the set design. The dialogue was fun and I was a big fan of all the words they came up with in here. It's a fun twist on The Wizard of Oz, which I'm ashamed to say I only generally know the story of. I also only just found out that Wicked is not, in fact, an original screenplay and was adapted from a play. Apparently I live under a rock. There are certainly some gripes I have here, with the biggest one being the music. Composition felt very flat and just unmoving to me despite all of its attempts at grandness. Mixing was horrible, you can't hear any of the instruments over the vocals half the time. Vocal performances are reminiscent of how I feel about TOOL and Angine de Poitrine; there's a high level of technicality and little to no feeling. Music can be a make or break thing in a MUSICAL, but this seems to be mostly genre-based personal taste whatever so I won't be too harsh. I also thought it looked very visually fake a lot of the time. My girlfriend pointed out that a lot of the sets were actually real, and a surprising amount of the movie was done practically, which I found difficult to believe cause, well... look!! It just looks CGI as all hell!! But apparently it's true, there was a lot of work on the set designs here, and maybe it's that they did TOO good of a job that my brain fills in that it must be fake. Even then, so many shots have this sort of saccharinity to them that feels very common in these high-budget blockbusters where everything is filmed in a green room. Speaking of green... I felt like they didn't know how to deal with the main character being green. I wanted them to either REALLY lean into her sticking out visually or actually coordinate the shots so that the colors all go together (bonus points for all the nature-y segments that are super green and she's sort of like camouflaged almost I thought that was kind of funny) but most of the movie seemed to be in this sort of awkward middle ground between the two. Maybe it's supposed to say something about her lived experience or whatever but I didn't get that from it either. It suffers from the same problem a lot of blockbusters with A-list actors do, which is that they spend all this money on the background and hardly have the characters interact with it! Maybe it's some shallow depth of field so we can't even see anything, or maybe there's a bunch of cuts so that they can split a complicated shot into more manageable chunks, or any number of other things, but it never feels like we're actually supposed to explore the frame!! Everything happens in the middle, everything is immediately apparent what it means and where you're supposed to look and the subtext always finds a way to rise to the level of text and yada yada yada yada boring pretentious stuff YES I KNOW ITS A CHILDRENS MOVIE YES I HAD THE SAME COMPLAINTS WITH STAR WARS YES THE PROBLEM IS PROBABLY ME but still!! Like I go on and on about, can we please just stop with the medium close up over the shoulder dialogue shots!? I guess through all the rambling what I'm really trying to say is that so much of the technical side of things is done right. It's got the budget, the sweeping sets, all the lighting equipment you could ever ask for, super high quality cameras, and yet... it feels like they just stopped there. You got the cameras, now USE them!! In all the grandiosity of the sets, it feels like there wasn't much thought put into visual language. I think this could have been a better movie if the budget was cut by 90%, because it would have forced people to think and get creative about how to film stuff! I think the whole writing a blank check is detrimental because creativity so often is fostered by limitation. But even after saying all that, it is undeniable that this movie is very fun to just sit back and watch. It's almost 3 hours but doesn't even feel like 2. Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande have wonderful chemistry, the writing here is very entertaining, and if I turn off the pretentious side of my brain, it's very easy to get swept away by all of the visual sugar here. I am even excited to see the second part!!

Okay, I am by no means a musical fan, I know blasphemy for a theater kid! Shoot me, but honestly I usually find them straight up just not interesting. So I'll start with the bad here and end with the good. The color grading is all over the place, some shots look phenomenal while others look incredibly bland or washed out. The pacing is also pretty rough, it's hard to care about the building of relationships when everything feels like it's happening within the same week, or even sometimes the same day. Like I don't give a fuck about the love triangle or Boq's lil romance suplot...most of the romance done in this is pretty wack. Finally the worst offender of it all...the fucking references towards the Wizard of Oz! Maybe it's not as egregious as I felt it was but like...it really feels like every little fucking thing needs to have a pointless explanation and cheeky little nod at the audience. The member berries are on crack and it made me roll my eyes every single time. Now the good, it's a fun watch, I was never bored. Maybe one scene had me slightly uninterested, but there's enough going on that it keeps your attention. The costumes and set design are really well done. Honestly, perfectly casted too, the characters are fun but the preformances are what stand out. For the most part the music is really good, Defying Gravity being the obvious stand out, I got straight chills in that scene. All in all, this is a fun but muddled concept, and obviously this isn't the films fault but the source material it is adapting. The conflicts are halfbaked and most of the time done in such a cartoonish manner you can't take anything seriously. While that is a huge blow to the entire plot...unfortunately the biggest blow is the relationship at the center of the film, the most important part, is just straight up not strong enough. I do not buy these two as friends. It feels like two people pretending to be friends or just keeping the peace because it's more work to be enemies. It's not tragic when the true goat of our story Elphaba loses her Glinda, cuz Glinda has always been a posh selfish person and one dance or the fact that she's not actively being an asshole is enough. There's no real growth or scenes of them being actual friends (besides a song of them at the Emerald City) to justify any of this crying. Maybe my mind will change when I get to the second part, but right now, it's a fine movie, an enjoyable time, but carries no real emotional weight for me.

Best moment: “Defying gravity”. That song and scene is the centerpiece of the musical and this (and the other) movie. It doesn’t disappoint. The song by itself already feels epic but the movie version puts a cherry on top. This small action interlude on the broom is a fun little break before it works toward that climax and note we have all been waiting for. Best quote: “I don’t cause commotions. I am one.” MVP: Cynthia Erivo. First, her voice is stunning. It is so crystal clear and she switches between emotional to powerful with the flip of vocal cord. Second, the acting matches the vocal performance. She gives Elphaba so much heart and a deep compassion but that fury beneath the surface is always brewing. It is an emotional performance in all areas. Best visual: The wizard’s room. The rest of the movie is so bright, colorful and joyful. That set, however, is darker and there isn’t any of the joy of the Emerald City. The design of the big head also looks really cool and ominous. Best showstopper: “Dancing through life” is just so much fun. The part in the library has so much cool choreography with the books and the spinning set. The ballroom looks stunning and also has some fun choreography. In all of this I ask myself one important question: How can someone be as charming as Jonathan Bailey? Rating: 9 out of 10 flying monkeys

Le film de Paul King sur le biopic de Wonka est une oeuvre orienté jeunesse. On sens une très grande inspiration cartoon de NOS jeunes années. Les chansons et danses omniprésentes parlent d'eux même mais ne sont pas les seuls points caractérisant ce coté cartoons. Les cadrages et décors colorés rappellent des prises de vue non habituelle du cinéma et une autre facon de retourner dans notre enfance. Le scénario va de paire avec cette idée, pas très elaboré ni très originale, cependant efficace. Le seul point noir de ce film est sa pâte graphique. Quelques manques de qualité de 3D se font ressentir. Surtout lors de deux scenes, les bonbons volants et la scène final de la fabrique. Malgré tout la girafe CGI fait très bien son effet. C'est avec plaisir que j'ai vu ce film de Paul King qui m'a encore renvoyé en enfance après ma découverte de ce réalisateur avec les deux films Paddington qui m'ont émerveillé.

❝ we are the music makers, and we are the dreamers of dreams. ❞ wonka felt like walking through a sweet shop at christmas — warm lights, colourful wrappers, and the smell of chocolate drifting through the air before you’ve even stepped inside. i went into it expecting something whimsical, and it certainly has that storybook charm. the film moves with a kind of cheerful optimism that feels very disney-coded, as though the world might become kinder if everyone sang at the right moment and shared a piece of chocolate. timothée chalamet brings a gentle sweetness to wonka that makes him easy to root for. this version of the character feels less eccentric genius and more hopeful dreamer, which gives the film a softer, more fairy-tale quality. what i enjoyed most was the atmosphere. there are moments that genuinely feel magical — little bursts of colour and wonder that reminded me of opening a childhood book and finding illustrations tucked between the pages. at the same time, i found myself wanting a little more of the strange edge that makes willy wonka such a fascinating character. the film is so determined to be charming that it occasionally feels a bit too safe, and some of the magic slips through my fingers before it can fully settle. still, there’s something comforting about it. it feels like a rainy-afternoon film: cosy, sugary, and easy to spend time with, even if it didn’t completely enchant me. a sweet, whimsical adventure that made me smile, even if it never quite became the golden-ticket experience i hoped for.

Wonka is exactly what I need a tale from the mind of the wonderful Roald Dahl to be, a delightfully fun and whimsical romp with a bit of fun and heart to it, I was obsessed with Roald Dahl books growing up, yet Wonka never took my fancy as a film, I’m not sure if it’s because I’m not a massive musicals guy, or just because I was more of a fan of works like The Twits growing up, but if this wasn’t put on in work it probably wouldn’t of been one I was watching any time soon, However within a minute of this being put on I was hooked, drawn to the screen by the energetic performance of Timothée Chalamet, he’s probably my favourite young actor today and he brings to life the energy and charisma of Willy Wonka just like those who have come before, it’s not just Chalamet who holds up his end of the bargain either, everyone holds there own in this film through there magical performances and looking a the cast list it’s not hard to see why, but as a Brit who loves Peep Show I’ve got to give a special mention to Paterson Joseph, his role as Johnson is my favourite in Peep Show, he’s electric in every role I’ve seen him in and often steals the show, he goes toe to toe with the eccentric Wonka as the evil businessman Slugworth and I’d be lying if there both not as good as each other here, But even if the performances and whimsical world of Roald Dahl isn’t enough to sell you this movie breezes by you with its fun nature, I said to the people in work it boils down really to a serious crime/thriller movie for families, Wonka trying to take and supply on the Businessmen Turf , the evil Businessmen trying to take down the honourable man, but it’s set in the world of Wonka , so it’s fun whimsical and a really enjoyable time for all ages, Wonka is a extremely fun time filled with great music and perfectly capturing the spirit and childhood imagination that all good Roald Dahl stories/worlds have, Chalamet oozes out the seems in the role of Wonka and it would be a crime if we never got to see him portray the role again, the rest of the cast hold there own and it wears its heart and emotions on it sleeves, colourful and dreamy yet serious when it needs to be, Wonka is a fun time that never feels like it outstays its welcome for to long and if your a fan of the Willy Wonka character or any other Dahl’s works, you won’t be left feeling disappointed

‘Tis the season for a sweet treat and, whilst not anything to do with Christmas, Wonka hits quite a lot of the festive buttons: fun, light-hearted, colourful and one for all the family. With much of the Paddington team behind this, it delivers that quintessentially English, quirky family film that its forebear (pun intended) achieved but sprinkled with a little bit of Cruella in its prequel backstory to a familiar character. It doesn’t present the titular chocolatier as a villain though, and rubs maybe just a little too much mystery off of the character, but does still feel very much a Roald Dahl tale. Wonka’s dream is to open a chocolate shop and he arrives in an alt-Paris (I think it’s meant to be Paris) to compete against the most famous chocolate makers of the time. From there, frolics, mishaps and big musical numbers ensue. Yes, this is a full musical like the OG Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory. Taking a couple of the songs but throwing in some excellent originals, this could well be destined for a stage run itself in the future. It’s cut through with a particularly English sense of humour and a brilliant ‘spot the famous person’ cast with a, hopefully intended, hat tip to Peep Show and yet another turn from Hugh Grant’s new comedy persona as an Oompa-Loompa. It’s just an utter delight, against all the odds, much like the aforementioned Cruella. A brisk and breezy one-for-all-the-family movie to smack a smile on your face. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️
